items.title: Indian Financial System Basics: NISM III-A Revision Notes
items.description: Revise markets, instruments, intermediaries and the flow of savings in India's financial system, with examples and the traps NISM III-A papers set.
items.intro: This opening chapter of NISM Series III-A sets the stage for every regulation that follows. It explains how savings travel from households to companies and government through markets, instruments and intermediaries. Questions are usually definitional: classify an instrument by market and maturity, identify whether money reaches the issuer, or pick which intermediary performs a given function. Expect three to five easy marks if the vocabulary is clear.

points.heading: Purpose of a financial system
points.text: A financial system links surplus units (mainly households) with deficit units (companies, government). It mobilises savings, allocates capital, provides payment services, spreads risk and produces prices. When a Pune salaried saver buys a corporate bond, her surplus funds a factory expansion she will never see; the system makes that transfer cheap and trusted.

points.heading: Direct versus intermediated finance
points.text: In direct finance the saver buys the security issued by the user of funds, such as shares in an IPO. In intermediated finance an institution stands in between: a bank takes deposits and makes loans, carrying the credit risk itself. Mutual funds are a middle path: they pool money but the investor bears the market risk.

points.heading: Primary and secondary markets
points.text: The primary market is where securities are created and sold for the first time; money flows to the issuer. The secondary market is where existing securities change hands between investors on exchanges; the issuer receives nothing. A healthy secondary market matters to issuers anyway, because investors pay more for securities they can easily sell.

points.heading: Money market versus capital market
points.text: Money market instruments have original maturity up to one year: call money, treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, repos. Capital market instruments fund long-term needs: equity shares, corporate bonds, government securities beyond one year. A 364-day T-bill is still money market; a 5-year NCD is capital market.

points.heading: Main participants
points.text: Issuers (companies, governments, banks), investors (retail, HNIs, institutions, FPIs), intermediaries (stock brokers, depository participants, merchant bankers, registrars, custodians, credit rating agencies, debenture trustees), market infrastructure institutions (stock exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories) and regulators (SEBI, RBI, IRDAI, PFRDA). The rest of III-A regulates exactly these intermediaries.

points.heading: Market infrastructure institutions
points.text: Stock exchanges provide the trading platform, clearing corporations guarantee settlement through novation and margins, and depositories hold securities in electronic form. Together they are called MIIs and are treated as systemically important, so SEBI holds them to higher net worth, governance and ownership standards than ordinary intermediaries.

points.heading: Functions the system performs
points.text: Remember the classic list: pooling of funds, transfer of resources across time and space, risk management (insurance, derivatives, diversification), price discovery, liquidity, reduction of information and transaction costs, and a payment and settlement mechanism. Exam stems often describe one function in plain words and ask you to name it.

points.heading: Financial instruments by claim
points.text: Equity is an ownership claim with residual, variable returns. Debt is a contractual claim with fixed or floating interest and priority over equity in liquidation. Hybrids such as convertible debentures and preference shares sit between. Derivatives derive value from an underlying asset and are used to hedge, speculate or arbitrage.

points.heading: Why intermediaries need regulation
points.text: Intermediaries hold client money and securities and know more than their clients. That information gap and custody of assets create room for misuse, which is why each one needs SEBI registration, a capital cushion, a code of conduct, segregation of client assets and grievance redressal. This logic explains the structure of the whole III-A syllabus.

traps: An IPO and an offer for sale both happen in the primary market, but in a pure OFS the money goes to selling shareholders, not the company.
Original maturity decides money versus capital market: a 10-year bond with six months left to redemption is still a capital market instrument.
Mutual funds are intermediaries, but unlike banks they do not guarantee principal; the investor carries the market risk.
Clearing corporations, not stock exchanges, guarantee settlement of trades through novation.
items.recap: Savings move from surplus to deficit units either directly through markets or through intermediaries. Primary market creates securities; secondary market trades them. Money market means up to one year original maturity; capital market is longer. Exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories are MIIs. Intermediaries are regulated because they hold client assets and information, which is the thread running through the rest of NISM III-A.

items.title: Securities Regulatory Framework in India: III-A Notes
items.description: Who regulates what in Indian finance: SEBI, RBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, MCA, the key Acts and the appeal route through SAT, revised for NISM Series III-A.
items.intro: This chapter maps the legal and regulatory architecture of Indian securities markets: which regulator controls which activity, which Act gives that power, and how disputes travel from an order to an appeal. Examiners like matching questions (law to regulator, activity to authority) and the appeal route from SEBI to the Securities Appellate Tribunal and then the Supreme Court.

points.heading: The main regulators
points.text: SEBI regulates securities markets and intermediaries; RBI regulates banks, NBFCs, money, forex and government securities markets; IRDAI regulates insurance; PFRDA regulates the National Pension System; the Ministry of Corporate Affairs administers the Companies Act; the Department of Economic Affairs in the Finance Ministry frames policy and administers SCRA rules.

points.heading: Core securities laws
points.text: SEBI Act, 1992 (creates SEBI and its powers); Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 (stock exchanges, contracts, listing); Depositories Act, 1996 (demat holding); Companies Act, 2013 (issue and transfer of securities, prospectus, disclosures for unlisted companies). FEMA, 1999 and PMLA, 2002 also bind market intermediaries.

points.heading: Shared jurisdiction
points.text: Some areas overlap. Issue and transfer of securities of listed companies or companies proposing to list is administered by SEBI, while unlisted companies stay with MCA. Government securities trading is regulated by RBI even when it happens on stock exchanges. Interest rate and currency derivatives on exchanges are jointly governed by RBI and SEBI.

points.heading: Delegated legislation
points.text: Acts give the framework; regulations, circulars and master circulars fill in the detail. SEBI frames regulations under Section 30 of the SEBI Act with Parliament's approval process, and issues circulars under Section 11. Exchanges and depositories add bye-laws and business rules that members must follow. All layers are binding on intermediaries.

points.heading: Self-regulatory role of MIIs
points.text: Stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories act as first-level regulators of their members: they inspect brokers and DPs, impose penalties, and suspend or expel members. SEBI oversees the MIIs themselves. This is why compliance officers report to both the exchange or depository and to SEBI.

points.heading: Appeals and the SAT
points.text: A person aggrieved by an order of SEBI, an adjudicating officer, or certain RBI, IRDAI and PFRDA orders can appeal to the Securities Appellate Tribunal within 45 days of receiving the order. A SAT decision can be challenged before the Supreme Court within 60 days on a question of law. Civil courts cannot entertain matters within SAT's jurisdiction.

points.heading: Financial Stability and Development Council
points.text: The FSDC, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, brings together the heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA and others to monitor systemic risk and coordinate inter-regulatory issues. It is not a super-regulator and does not replace any individual regulator's powers; exams test this distinction.

points.heading: Why a framework matters to an intermediary
points.text: A broker who is also a mutual fund distributor and an insurance agent answers to SEBI, the exchange, AMFI rules and IRDAI simultaneously. Knowing which rulebook applies to which product avoids mis-selling, wrong disclosures and duplicate violations. The compliance function exists to keep this map current.

traps: SAT hears appeals against SEBI; the Supreme Court hears appeals against SAT. An appeal does not go from SEBI directly to the High Court as a matter of routine.
Government securities are RBI territory even when traded on NSE or BSE platforms.
FSDC coordinates regulators; it does not issue registrations or penalise intermediaries.
Unlisted company securities are mostly MCA's domain, not SEBI's, unless the company proposes to list.
items.recap: SEBI for securities, RBI for banks, money and forex, IRDAI for insurance, PFRDA for pensions, MCA for company law. Four core laws: SEBI Act, SCRA, Depositories Act, Companies Act. Exchanges and depositories are frontline regulators of their members. Appeal against SEBI goes to SAT within 45 days and then to the Supreme Court within 60 days.

items.title: Compliance Function Basics: NISM III-A Revision Notes
items.description: Meaning of compliance, the compliance officer's role, compliance risk, policies, reporting and internal controls for SEBI intermediaries, in exam-ready form.
items.intro: Before the Act-by-Act chapters, NISM III-A explains what compliance means inside a securities intermediary: following laws, regulations, circulars and internal policies, and proving that you did. Questions test the compliance officer's role, independence, reporting lines, the difference between compliance and audit, and consequences of failure. Expect scenario stems where you choose the most appropriate compliance response.

points.heading: What compliance means
points.text: Compliance is the process of making sure an organisation and its people follow applicable laws, regulations, exchange and depository bye-laws, circulars and internal codes. It covers both the letter (filing a report on time) and the spirit (not designing products to sidestep a rule). It is ongoing, not a one-time certification.

points.heading: Compliance risk
points.text: Compliance risk is the risk of legal or regulatory sanctions, financial loss or loss of reputation from failing to comply. For a broker this could be a penalty for late margin reporting, suspension of trading terminals, or clients leaving after adverse media coverage. Reputation loss is often costlier than the fine.

points.heading: The compliance officer
points.text: SEBI regulations require most intermediaries to appoint a compliance officer who monitors compliance with the Act, rules, regulations and circulars and reports non-compliance to the board or senior management and, where required, to SEBI. The officer is also usually responsible for investor grievance redressal.

points.heading: Independence and authority
points.text: A compliance function works only if it is independent of business targets, has direct access to the board, adequate resources and the authority to see any record. A compliance head who reports to the sales head creates a conflict. Many regulators prefer a separate compliance reporting line to the board or its committee.

points.heading: Compliance policy and manual
points.text: Good practice is a board-approved compliance policy, a manual setting out procedures, a calendar of regulatory filings, and periodic testing. New circulars should be tracked, impact-assessed and communicated to the staff who must act on them, with records showing that this was done.

points.heading: Compliance versus internal audit
points.text: Compliance is the second line of defence: it advises, monitors and tests on a continuous basis. Internal audit is the third line: it independently reviews whether controls, including compliance, actually work. Business units are the first line and own their risks. Exams often swap these roles.

points.heading: Training and culture
points.text: Rules are followed when staff understand them. Regular training, certification requirements (for example NISM certificates for associated persons), whistle-blower channels and visible senior management support create a compliance culture. A tick-box approach without culture tends to fail during market stress.

points.heading: Consequences of non-compliance
points.text: SEBI and MIIs can issue warnings, levy monetary penalties, suspend or cancel registration, debar individuals and order disgorgement. Serious violations can also lead to prosecution. Repeated minor lapses can lead to a finding that the intermediary is no longer 'fit and proper'.

traps: The compliance officer advises and monitors; the board and senior management remain ultimately responsible for compliance.
Compliance is not the same as internal audit; audit independently checks the compliance function too.
Following only the letter of a circular while defeating its purpose can still be treated as a violation.
Fit and proper status is continuous; an intermediary can lose it after registration.
items.recap: Compliance means following law, regulation, bye-laws and internal codes, and being able to prove it. Compliance risk covers penalties, losses and reputation. Every SEBI intermediary needs an independent compliance officer with board access, usually also handling grievances. Business is the first line, compliance the second, internal audit the third. Ultimate responsibility stays with the board.

items.title: SEBI Act 1992 Revision Notes for NISM III-A
items.description: SEBI's constitution, functions under Section 11, registration under Section 12, penalties, settlement and SAT appeals, revised with exam traps for III-A.
items.intro: The SEBI Act, 1992 is the parent law for most of NISM III-A. It creates SEBI, lists its duties and powers, requires intermediaries to register, sets out penalties and provides for appeals. Questions commonly ask section-wise powers, the composition of the Board, who can be penalised for what, and appeal time limits. Section numbers are tested, so revise the main ones.

points.heading: Origin and objective
points.text: SEBI was set up in 1988 as a non-statutory body and became statutory in 1992 through the SEBI Act. Its preamble states three aims: protect the interests of investors in securities, promote the development of the securities market, and regulate it. Many exam options paraphrase these three objectives.

points.heading: Composition of the Board
points.text: The Board has a Chairman, two members from Central Government ministries dealing with finance and company law, one member from RBI, and five other members of whom at least three are whole-time members. All are appointed by the Central Government. Know this nine-member structure.

points.heading: Section 11: functions and powers
points.text: Section 11 gives SEBI its broad mandate: regulating stock exchanges and intermediaries, registering collective investment schemes and mutual funds, prohibiting fraudulent and unfair trade practices and insider trading, promoting investor education, and conducting inspections and inquiries. Section 11(4) allows interim measures such as impounding proceeds or restraining persons from the market.

points.heading: Section 11B directions
points.text: Under Section 11B SEBI can issue directions in the interest of investors or orderly market development, including directions to disgorge wrongful gains. A typical order: a promoter is barred from the securities market for two years and told to disgorge ₹3 crore with interest.

points.heading: Section 12: registration
points.text: No stock broker, sub-broker or other intermediary associated with the securities market may buy, sell or deal in securities except under a certificate of registration from SEBI. Depositories, DPs, custodians, credit rating agencies, venture capital funds and collective investment schemes are also covered. Operating without registration is a serious violation.

points.heading: Penalties under Chapter VIA
points.text: Sections 15A to 15HB prescribe adjudication penalties: failure to furnish information or returns (15A), failure by intermediaries to enter agreements with clients (15B), failure to redress investor grievances (15C), insider trading (15G), fraudulent and unfair trade practices (15HA), and a residual penalty for any other violation (15HB). Amounts are revised from time to time, so learn the heads rather than figures.

points.heading: Adjudication factors
points.text: When fixing a penalty the adjudicating officer considers the disproportionate gain or unfair advantage made, the loss caused to investors and whether the default is repetitive (Section 15J). This is why two similar violations can attract different penalties.

points.heading: Settlement and recovery
points.text: Section 15JB permits settlement of proceedings on payment of a settlement amount, without admission or denial of guilt, under the Settlement Proceedings Regulations. Section 28A lets the recovery officer attach bank accounts and property when penalties or disgorgement are not paid.

points.heading: Appeals
points.text: Appeals against SEBI or adjudicating officer orders lie to the Securities Appellate Tribunal within 45 days (Section 15T); SAT may condone delay for sufficient cause. Appeals from SAT go to the Supreme Court within 60 days (Section 15Z). Civil courts have no jurisdiction over matters SAT can decide (Section 15Y).

traps: Section 11 is about functions and powers; Section 12 is about registration. Options often swap these.
The SAT limit is 45 days; the Supreme Court limit after SAT is 60 days.
Settlement under 15JB does not require the noticee to admit guilt.
The RBI nominee is one member; two members come from the Central Government ministries.
items.recap: SEBI Act 1992: protect investors, develop and regulate the market. Board of nine: Chairman, two Central Government, one RBI, five others with at least three whole-time. Section 11 powers, 11B directions and disgorgement, 12 registration, 15A to 15HB penalties, 15J penalty factors, 15JB settlement, 28A recovery, 15T appeal to SAT in 45 days, 15Z appeal to Supreme Court in 60 days.

items.title: SCRA 1956 and SCRR 1957: NISM III-A Revision Notes
items.description: Definition of securities, recognised stock exchanges, contracts, listing, delisting and minimum public shareholding under SCRA and SCRR, made exam-ready.
items.intro: The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and the rules made under it in 1957 control stock exchanges, the contracts traded on them and the listing of securities. The Act is older than SEBI and is administered jointly with the Central Government. Expect questions on the definition of securities, recognition of exchanges, listing and delisting, and the minimum public shareholding rule in Rule 19A.

points.heading: Definition of securities
points.text: Section 2(h) defines securities widely: shares, scrips, stocks, bonds, debentures and other marketable securities of a company or body corporate; derivatives; units of collective investment schemes and mutual funds; government securities; security receipts; and rights or interests in securities. Because derivatives are included, exchange-traded F&O falls within SCRA.

points.heading: Recognised stock exchanges
points.text: An exchange must be recognised under Section 4 to operate. Recognition is granted by the Central Government (powers delegated to SEBI) after checking rules, bye-laws and investor protection. Contracts in securities outside a recognised exchange in a notified area are restricted, which channels trading into regulated platforms.

points.heading: Corporatisation and demutualisation
points.text: Exchanges were once broker-owned mutual bodies. Section 4B required corporatisation and demutualisation so that ownership, management and trading rights are separated. Brokers can no longer control the board of the exchange whose rules they must obey. SEBI's SECC Regulations now govern exchange and clearing corporation ownership.

points.heading: Clearing corporations
points.text: SCRA recognises clearing corporations, which clear and settle trades executed on exchanges. Separation of trading (exchange) and settlement (clearing corporation) strengthens risk management. Clearing corporations act as central counterparty to every trade.

points.heading: Listing under Section 21
points.text: Where securities are listed, the company must comply with the listing conditions of the exchange, now largely contained in the SEBI LODR Regulations. Rule 19 of SCRR sets the requirements to be met for listing, including the minimum offer to the public at the time of an IPO, which varies with post-issue market capitalisation.

points.heading: Delisting under Section 21A
points.text: A recognised exchange may delist securities on grounds specified in the rules, for example repeated non-compliance or failure to pay listing fees, after giving the company a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The company can appeal to SAT. Voluntary delisting by promoters follows the SEBI Delisting Regulations with a reverse book-building or other prescribed price discovery.

points.heading: Minimum public shareholding
points.text: Rule 19A requires every listed company, other than certain public sector and specified companies, to maintain public shareholding of at least 25%. A company that falls below must restore it within the period allowed, using methods such as offer for sale, QIP or rights issue. Example: if promoters hold 82%, at least 7% must be diluted.

points.heading: Penalties and powers
points.text: SCRA lets SEBI call for periodic returns, direct exchanges to amend rules, supersede an exchange's governing board in extreme cases, and impose penalties for failures like not furnishing information or violating listing conditions. Appeals lie to SAT, like SEBI Act matters.

traps: Rule 19A is minimum public shareholding (25%); Rule 19(2)(b) is about the minimum offer size at IPO. Do not mix them.
Derivatives are 'securities' under SCRA Section 2(h), so derivative contracts are regulated under it.
Demutualisation separates ownership and trading rights; it does not mean exchanges stop having broker members.
Compulsory delisting by an exchange is different from voluntary delisting by promoters; both are covered but under different procedures.
items.recap: SCRA 1956 governs securities contracts, exchanges, clearing corporations and listing; SCRR 1957 adds the detail. Section 2(h) defines securities including derivatives and MF units. Section 4 recognition, 4B demutualisation, 21 listing, 21A delisting with SAT appeal. Rule 19A: listed companies must keep at least 25% public shareholding and restore shortfalls within the permitted time.

items.title: SEBI Intermediaries Regulations 2008: III-A Revision
items.description: Common registration process, fit and proper criteria, general obligations, code of conduct and enforcement actions under SEBI Intermediaries Regulations 2008.
items.intro: The Intermediaries Regulations, 2008 give a common procedure for registering, supervising and acting against all SEBI intermediaries, so that individual regulations only add activity-specific rules. Examiners focus on the fit and proper person test, the validity of registration, general obligations and the range of actions SEBI can take after an enquiry.

points.heading: Why a common regulation
points.text: Before 2008, each intermediary regulation had its own registration and enforcement procedure. The 2008 regulations standardised these, covering application, grant of certificate, conditions, inspection and enforcement for brokers, DPs, merchant bankers, RTAs, investment advisers and others. Activity-specific regulations then add capital, qualification and conduct requirements.

points.heading: Application and grant
points.text: An applicant files the prescribed form with fees and documents through the route specified (for brokers and DPs, through the exchange or depository). SEBI checks eligibility and fit and proper status, may seek clarifications, and grants a certificate. Rejection must be communicated with reasons, giving the applicant a chance to be heard.

points.heading: Validity of registration
points.text: Registration granted under these regulations is generally permanent, subject to payment of fees and continued compliance, unless suspended, cancelled or surrendered. Earlier, many certificates had to be renewed every few years. Any material change in control requires SEBI's prior approval.

points.heading: Fit and proper person criteria
points.text: Schedule II assesses integrity, reputation, character, absence of convictions and restraint orders, and financial soundness of the applicant and its principal officers, directors, promoters and key managerial persons. A person against whom a criminal complaint involving economic offences has been filed by SEBI, or who is declared a wilful defaulter, is generally not fit and proper.

points.heading: Continuous obligations
points.text: Intermediaries must abide by the code of conduct, keep books and records, submit information SEBI asks for, inform SEBI of material changes, and redress investor grievances promptly through SCORES and other channels. Fit and proper status must continue throughout the life of the registration.

points.heading: Code of conduct essentials
points.text: Act with integrity, due skill, care and diligence; avoid conflicts of interest or disclose and manage them; do not make exaggerated statements about services; keep client information confidential; maintain adequate infrastructure and trained staff. These generic principles appear in Schedule III and in each specific regulation.

points.heading: Enquiry and actions
points.text: After an inspection or complaint, a designated authority may conduct an enquiry and recommend action. SEBI can then pass orders such as warning, suspension of registration for a period, cancellation of registration, prohibition from taking new clients, or debarment of principal officers. The intermediary must be given a show-cause notice and a hearing.

points.heading: Effect of suspension or cancellation
points.text: On suspension or cancellation the intermediary must stop the activity, allow clients to withdraw or transfer funds and securities, and hand over records as directed. Client protection continues even after the business stops. Cancellation does not wipe out liability for past violations.

traps: Registration is now largely permanent, but fit and proper status must be maintained continuously, not just at the time of application.
A warning is the mildest action; cancellation is the most severe. Options sometimes rank them in the wrong order.
A change in control needs SEBI's prior approval, not merely intimation afterwards.
Fit and proper criteria apply to promoters, directors and key managerial persons, not just the entity.
items.recap: Intermediaries Regulations 2008 give one procedure for registration, inspection and enforcement across SEBI intermediaries. Registration is generally permanent but fit and proper status (Schedule II) must continue. Duties include records, information to SEBI, grievance redressal and code of conduct. Enforcement range: warning, suspension, cancellation, prohibition, debarment, always after notice and hearing. Change in control needs prior approval.

items.title: SEBI Insider Trading Regulations: NISM III-A Notes
items.description: UPSI, insiders, connected persons, trading window, trading plans, contra trades and disclosure duties under SEBI PIT Regulations 2015, with exam traps.
items.intro: The SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 stop people from trading on unpublished price sensitive information. They apply to listed companies, intermediaries and fiduciaries, and to anyone holding UPSI. Expect questions on who is an insider, what counts as UPSI, the trading window, trading plans, contra trades, disclosure triggers and the informant reward mechanism.

points.heading: UPSI
points.text: Unpublished price sensitive information is information about a company or its securities, not generally available, which on becoming available is likely to materially affect the price. Typical examples: financial results, dividends, changes in capital structure, mergers and acquisitions, delistings, and changes in key managerial personnel. Information on the exchange website is 'generally available'.

points.heading: Who is an insider
points.text: An insider is a connected person or anyone in possession of or having access to UPSI. A connected person is someone associated with the company in the six months before the act, in a way that gives access to UPSI: directors, employees, auditors, bankers, consultants and their relatives. A stranger who overhears a director in a lift and trades can also be an insider.

points.heading: Communication and trading prohibited
points.text: Insiders must not communicate UPSI except for legitimate purposes, performance of duties or legal obligations, and no one may procure UPSI. Trading while in possession of UPSI is prohibited. Defences exist, such as off-market inter-se transfers between promoters who both had the same UPSI, block deals and trades under an approved trading plan.

points.heading: Trading window
points.text: Listed companies close a trading window for designated persons and their relatives during which they cannot trade. For financial results it usually runs from the end of each quarter until 48 hours after the results are made public. The compliance officer can also close it when other UPSI exists.

points.heading: Trading plans
points.text: An insider who perpetually holds UPSI may submit a trading plan to the compliance officer for approval, which is then disclosed to the exchanges. The plan must start only after a cool-off period, cannot cover the period around results, and once approved must be executed irrevocably. Cool-off and plan-length rules were revised in 2024; check the latest SEBI text.

points.heading: Pre-clearance and contra trade
points.text: Designated persons need pre-clearance from the compliance officer above thresholds set in the company's code, and must execute within seven trading days of approval. They must not enter an opposite (contra) trade within six months of the earlier trade; profits from a contra trade are disgorged to SEBI's Investor Protection and Education Fund.

points.heading: Disclosures
points.text: Promoters, KMP and directors disclose holdings on appointment within 7 days. Continual disclosure applies when the value traded in a calendar quarter exceeds ₹10 lakh (single or a series of transactions): the person informs the company within 2 trading days, and the company informs the exchanges within 2 trading days of receipt.

points.heading: Codes, database and informants
points.text: Every listed company and intermediary must have a code of conduct to regulate trading and a code of fair disclosure. A structured digital database records who shared UPSI with whom. Informants can report violations to SEBI's Office of Informant Protection and may receive a reward, subject to a cap set by SEBI.

traps: A connected person includes anyone connected in the six months before the act, not only current employees.
The ₹10 lakh continual disclosure threshold is per calendar quarter, not per financial year.
The trading window reopens 48 hours after results are made public, not on the day of the board meeting.
Contra trade profits go to the IPEF administered by SEBI, not to the company.
Once approved, a trading plan cannot be withdrawn or deviated from.
items.recap: UPSI is non-public, price-moving information. Insiders include connected persons (six-month look-back) and anyone holding UPSI. No trading or communication while in possession of UPSI. Trading window closes from quarter end till 48 hours after results. Trading plans are irrevocable after approval. Contra trade bar: six months. Continual disclosure above ₹10 lakh per quarter within 2 trading days.

items.title: SEBI PFUTP Regulations 2003: Fraud and Manipulation Notes
items.description: Fraud, manipulative and unfair trade practices under SEBI PFUTP Regulations 2003: circular trading, front running, false statements and mis-selling explained.
items.intro: The Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market Regulations, 2003 target manipulation, fraud and deception in the securities market. They are broad and principles-based, so questions describe a behaviour and ask whether it is a violation and of what kind. Learn the definition of fraud, the deemed manipulative practices listed in Regulation 4 and how intermediaries are covered.

points.heading: Definition of fraud
points.text: Fraud is defined very widely: any act, expression, omission or concealment, whether in a deceitful manner or not, by a person or by anyone else with his connivance, to induce another person to deal in securities. It need not involve proof that anyone actually lost money or that the person intended to deceive in the criminal sense.

points.heading: General prohibition
points.text: No person may buy, sell or deal in securities in a fraudulent manner, use any manipulative or deceptive device, employ any scheme to defraud, or engage in any act that operates as fraud or deceit on any person in connection with dealing in securities. The rule applies to everyone, not only registered intermediaries.

points.heading: Market manipulation examples
points.text: Regulation 4 deems certain acts manipulative: creating a false appearance of trading, dealing in a security without intention of change in ownership (wash trades), circular trading among a group, inflating or depressing prices through artificial volume, and advancing or delaying the settlement price. Example: three related accounts trading a thinly traded scrip back and forth to raise its price.

points.heading: Misleading information
points.text: Publishing or spreading false information that is likely to influence investors is prohibited, including through social media, tips groups and paid stock recommendations. Planting bullish news before selling (pump and dump) is a classic violation. Companies that publish misleading financial statements are also covered.

points.heading: Front running
points.text: An intermediary or its employee who trades ahead of a large client order, using knowledge of that order, commits a fraudulent practice. Example: a dealer at a broking firm buys shares minutes before executing a mutual fund's large buy order and sells after the price rises. Front running by any person with access to such information is covered.

points.heading: Mis-selling
points.text: Selling securities or services by making false or misleading statements, concealing material facts or risks, or ignoring suitability is mis-selling. Selling a complex structured product to a retiree who asked for safe income, without explaining risks, is an example. Mutual fund unit mis-selling is explicitly covered.

points.heading: Intermediary-specific practices
points.text: Intermediaries must not churn client accounts to earn brokerage, issue false contract notes, misuse client funds or securities, or deliberately misreport prices. Knowingly assisting a manipulation, for example lending accounts to an operator, can make the intermediary liable.

points.heading: Consequences
points.text: SEBI may suspend trading, restrain persons from the market, impound gains, order disgorgement with interest, impose penalties under Section 15HA of the SEBI Act and launch prosecution. Investigations commonly use trade logs, phone records and connections between accounts to establish the pattern.

traps: Fraud under PFUTP does not require proof of an actual loss to investors.
Wash trades are about no real change in ownership; circular trades are rotation within a group. Both are manipulative.
PFUTP applies to any person, not only SEBI-registered intermediaries.
Front running uses knowledge of a pending order; insider trading uses UPSI about the company. Do not confuse the two.
items.recap: PFUTP 2003 bans fraud, manipulation and unfair trade practices in securities by anyone. Fraud is defined broadly and needs no proof of loss. Deemed manipulative acts include wash and circular trades, false volume, price rigging and spreading false information. Front running, churning and mis-selling are unfair practices. Penalties include restraint, disgorgement and Section 15HA penalties.

items.title: PMLA 2002 for Securities Intermediaries: III-A Notes
items.description: Money laundering stages, reporting entity duties, CDD, beneficial ownership, CTR and STR timelines and record keeping under PMLA, revised for NISM III-A.
items.intro: Every SEBI intermediary is a reporting entity under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. This chapter covers what money laundering is, the obligations of brokers, DPs and others to verify clients and report suspicious activity to FIU-IND, and the record keeping rules. Questions often test reporting deadlines, the principal officer's role, beneficial ownership and red-flag scenarios.

points.heading: Stages of money laundering
points.text: Placement puts illegal cash into the financial system (for example, many small cash deposits). Layering hides the trail through a series of transactions, such as rapid buying and selling of illiquid shares across accounts. Integration brings the money back looking legitimate, for instance as sale proceeds of investments. Exam stems describe one stage and ask you to name it.

points.heading: Offence and punishment
points.text: Section 3 makes it an offence to be involved in any process or activity connected with proceeds of crime, including concealment, possession, use or projecting it as untainted. Punishment under Section 4 is rigorous imprisonment of three to seven years and fine, extendable to ten years where the predicate offence is under the NDPS Act.

points.heading: Reporting entities and FIU-IND
points.text: Banks, financial institutions and intermediaries such as stock brokers, DPs, mutual funds, portfolio managers and RTAs are reporting entities. They report to the Financial Intelligence Unit-India, the central agency that receives, analyses and disseminates information on suspicious financial transactions to enforcement agencies.

points.heading: Principal officer and designated director
points.text: Each reporting entity appoints a principal officer, a senior person responsible for monitoring and reporting transactions to FIU-IND, and a designated director responsible for overall compliance with PMLA obligations. Their names and changes must be communicated to FIU-IND.

points.heading: Client due diligence
points.text: Before opening an account, the intermediary identifies the client and verifies identity using officially valid documents, identifies the beneficial owner, understands the purpose of the relationship and does ongoing monitoring. Enhanced due diligence applies to high-risk clients such as politically exposed persons, non-face-to-face clients from high-risk jurisdictions and clients with unusual patterns.

points.heading: Beneficial ownership
points.text: For a company, the beneficial owner is the natural person who ultimately owns or controls a specified percentage of shares, capital or profits, or exercises control by other means. The thresholds were tightened in 2023 (to 10% for companies, as of 2026 — check the PML Rules). If no natural person qualifies, the senior managing official is treated as the beneficial owner.

points.heading: Reports and timelines
points.text: Cash Transaction Reports cover cash transactions above ₹10 lakh (or integrally connected series) and are filed monthly by the 15th of the following month. Suspicious Transaction Reports must be filed within 7 days of the principal officer concluding that a transaction is suspicious. Securities intermediaries rarely handle cash, so STRs are the main obligation.

points.heading: Record keeping and tipping off
points.text: Records of transactions and of identity must be kept for at least five years after the transaction or after the business relationship ends, whichever is later. Staff must not tell the client that an STR has been or will be filed; tipping off defeats the investigation. Filing an STR does not require stopping the account unless directed.

traps: STR is due within 7 days of the conclusion of suspicion, not 7 days from the transaction date.
CTR is monthly, by the 15th of the next month; STR is event-based.
Records must be kept five years from the end of the relationship, not just five years from account opening.
Informing the client about an STR (tipping off) is prohibited even if the client asks why there is a delay.
items.recap: Placement, layering, integration. PMLA Section 3 offence, Section 4 punishment of 3 to 7 years (10 for NDPS). Intermediaries are reporting entities reporting to FIU-IND through a principal officer, with a designated director accountable. Do CDD, identify the beneficial owner, apply EDD to high-risk clients. CTR monthly by the 15th; STR within 7 days of suspicion; keep records five years; never tip off.

items.title: KYC Registration Agency Regulations 2011: III-A Notes
items.description: How KRAs centralise investor KYC, duties of intermediaries and KRAs, record validation, confidentiality and KYC statuses under SEBI KRA Regulations 2011.
items.intro: The KRA Regulations, 2011 created a single-KYC system for the securities market. An investor completes KYC once with any SEBI intermediary, and the record is uploaded to a KYC Registration Agency so that other intermediaries can rely on it. Questions test the roles of intermediary and KRA, eligibility to become a KRA, confidentiality and the meaning of KYC statuses.

points.heading: Why KRAs exist
points.text: Before 2011 an investor had to repeat KYC with every broker, DP and mutual fund. KRAs centralise KYC records so that an investor who completed KYC with a broker in Chennai can open a mutual fund folio in Delhi without resubmitting documents. This reduces duplication and inconsistency across intermediaries.

points.heading: Who can be a KRA
points.text: A KRA must be registered with SEBI and must meet net worth and infrastructure requirements. Depositories and their subsidiaries and other entities meeting SEBI's criteria have operated KRAs; examples include CDSL Ventures (CVL) and NSDL's KRA. Registration follows the common process under the Intermediaries Regulations.

points.heading: Intermediary's duties
points.text: The intermediary performs initial KYC: collects documents, does in-person verification (or approved video/digital verification), and uploads the details and scanned documents to the KRA system within the time SEBI specifies. It remains responsible for the accuracy of what it uploads and must keep original records.

points.heading: KRA's duties
points.text: The KRA stores KYC records securely, allows intermediaries to access them, sends confirmation to the investor on upload and on modification, and validates key attributes such as PAN, name, address and mobile or email against official sources. It must maintain confidentiality and audit trails of every access.

points.heading: Reliance by other intermediaries
points.text: A second intermediary can download the record from the KRA and need not repeat full KYC, though it may perform additional due diligence and must still do its own risk categorisation and in-person verification where required. It cannot use the KRA data for any purpose other than KYC.

points.heading: KYC statuses
points.text: Records can show statuses such as registered, validated, on hold or rejected. A record goes on hold when, for example, PAN is not linked with Aadhaar or the email or mobile could not be verified, and the investor cannot transact in new accounts until it is fixed. Status names and conditions are updated by SEBI periodically.

points.heading: Modification of details
points.text: Changes in address, contact details or name are submitted to any intermediary, which updates the KRA. The KRA then notifies the other intermediaries holding that client, so records stay consistent. The client should not have to inform each intermediary separately.

points.heading: Confidentiality and data protection
points.text: KRAs and intermediaries must not share KYC data with anyone except as permitted by law. They must have systems to prevent unauthorised access, maintain logs and keep records for the period specified. Using KYC data for marketing is not permitted.

traps: The intermediary, not the KRA, performs the initial KYC and in-person verification.
Relying on a KRA record does not remove the second intermediary's own risk-based due diligence obligations.
A KYC record on hold blocks new transactions until deficiencies are cured; it is not the same as rejection.
KRAs must notify all linked intermediaries of changes; the investor need not update each one.
items.recap: KRAs, registered with SEBI, hold a central KYC record for securities market investors. The intermediary collects documents and verifies in person, then uploads to the KRA; the KRA validates, stores, confirms to the investor and shares with other intermediaries. Others can rely on it but still do their own risk checks. Data is confidential and changes flow to all linked intermediaries.

items.title: SEBI FPI Regulations 2019: NISM III-A Revision Notes
items.description: FPI categories, DDP registration, investment limits, ODIs and investor-group rules under SEBI FPI Regulations 2019, with common NISM III-A exam traps.
items.intro: The FPI Regulations, 2019 govern how foreign investors buy Indian securities through portfolio routes. They define who may register, how registration is granted through designated depository participants, what an FPI can invest in and the limits that separate portfolio investment from FDI. Questions test the two categories, the DDP's role, the below-10% limit and offshore derivative instruments.

points.heading: Meaning of FPI
points.text: A foreign portfolio investor is a person registered under these regulations to invest in Indian securities. Portfolio investment means holdings below the FDI threshold, intended for financial return rather than management control. Residents cannot be FPIs, but NRIs, OCIs and resident Indians may participate in an FPI within limits set by SEBI.

points.heading: Two categories
points.text: Category I includes government and government-related investors (central banks, sovereign wealth funds), pension funds, regulated entities like banks, insurers, asset managers and broker-dealers from FATF-member jurisdictions, and entities from India's IFSC. Category II includes everyone else eligible, such as appropriately regulated funds not in Category I, unregulated funds, corporates, family offices and individuals.

points.heading: Registration through DDP
points.text: SEBI has authorised designated depository participants, typically custodian banks, to grant FPI registration on its behalf after due diligence. The DDP checks eligibility, KYC and beneficial ownership. Registration is permanent unless suspended, cancelled or surrendered, subject to payment of fees for the applicable block period.

points.heading: Eligibility conditions
points.text: The applicant must not be resident in India, must be from a jurisdiction that is not identified by FATF as high risk, must be eligible to invest under its home laws, and must be fit and proper. Its beneficial owners must be identified under the PMLA framework.

points.heading: Investment limits
points.text: Purchase of equity shares of a company by a single FPI or an investor group must be below 10% of the total paid-up equity capital on a fully diluted basis. If it crosses 10%, the FPI must divest the excess within five trading days or the holding is reclassified as FDI. Aggregate FPI holding is subject to the sectoral cap.

points.heading: Investor group concept
points.text: FPIs with common ownership of more than 50% or common control are treated as one investor group for the 10% limit. This stops a single foreign investor from splitting money across several entities to cross the portfolio limit indirectly.

points.heading: Permitted instruments
points.text: FPIs may invest in listed or to-be-listed equity, units of mutual funds, AIFs and REITs/InvITs, government and corporate debt (subject to RBI limits), derivatives traded on recognised exchanges, and security receipts, among others. Debt investments follow RBI's FPI debt framework and route-specific limits.

points.heading: Offshore derivative instruments
points.text: ODIs such as participatory notes are issued abroad by Category I FPIs with Indian securities as underlying. They can be issued only to persons regulated in their home jurisdiction and fit and proper, not to unregulated entities, and must be reported to SEBI. ODI holdings are clubbed with the FPI holdings of the same investor group for limits.

traps: The DDP grants registration on behalf of SEBI; the applicant does not apply directly to SEBI.
The limit is 'below 10%'; crossing it requires divestment within five trading days or reclassification as FDI.
Only Category I FPIs can issue ODIs, and only to regulated subscribers.
Investor-group clubbing applies at more than 50% common ownership or common control.
items.recap: FPIs are non-resident portfolio investors registered through DDPs on SEBI's behalf. Category I: governments, pension funds and regulated entities from FATF jurisdictions; Category II: the rest. Single FPI or investor group must hold below 10% of a company; excess divested in five trading days or treated as FDI. ODIs issued only by Category I FPIs to regulated persons, with reporting to SEBI.

items.title: SEBI Stock Brokers Regulations: III-A Revision Notes
items.description: Broker registration, clearing member types, client funds segregation, margins, contract notes, settlement of accounts and authorised persons, in brief.
items.intro: The Stock Brokers Regulations and the many SEBI circulars built around them set out how brokers and clearing members are registered and how they must deal with clients. This chapter is heavy in operational rules: client onboarding, handling of client funds and securities, margins, contract notes and grievance redressal. SEBI revises broker regulations often, so focus on principles and check current limits.

points.heading: Registration and membership
points.text: A stock broker must be a member of a recognised stock exchange and registered with SEBI, applying through the exchange. Clearing members must also register. Net worth and deposit requirements vary by segment and are prescribed by SEBI and the exchanges. Brokers must have qualified, NISM-certified staff dealing with clients.

points.heading: Types of clearing members
points.text: A self-clearing member clears only its own and its clients' trades. A trading-cum-clearing member clears its own trades and also those of other trading members. A professional clearing member does not trade but clears for others, often a bank or large firm. Know which type clears for whom.

points.heading: Client onboarding
points.text: Brokers complete KYC (often through KRAs), collect the account opening form including rights and obligations, risk disclosure document and policies, and allot each client a Unique Client Code. Trades must be placed only under the correct UCC. Nomination or an explicit opt-out is required for new accounts.

points.heading: Segregation of client assets
points.text: Client money must be kept in a separate client bank account, and client securities in separate client accounts, never mixed with the broker's own. Using one client's funds for another client's obligations or for proprietary trading is prohibited. Clearing corporations now track client collateral at the individual client level.

points.heading: Margins
points.text: Brokers must collect upfront margins (initial margin plus exposure or extreme loss margin) from clients before trades in the derivatives and cash segments and report collections to the clearing corporation. Short collection attracts penalties. Example: if the SPAN plus exposure margin for a Nifty futures lot is ₹1.4 lakh, the client must have that available upfront.

points.heading: Contract notes and statements
points.text: A contract note, physical or electronic with a digital signature, must be issued within 24 hours of the trade, showing order and trade numbers, time, quantity, price, brokerage and taxes. Brokers also send periodic statements of funds and securities so that clients can reconcile.

points.heading: Running account settlement
points.text: Unless the client asks otherwise, funds and securities left with the broker must be settled by returning them on a periodic basis, monthly or quarterly as the client chooses, after retaining only the amount needed for obligations. This limits the broker's ability to hold idle client money.

points.heading: Authorised persons and grievances
points.text: Authorised persons are agents of the broker approved by the exchange; the broker remains responsible for their acts. Brokers must resolve complaints quickly, publish grievance details and participate in SCORES and the online dispute resolution mechanism for disputes not settled directly.

traps: A professional clearing member clears for others but does not trade itself.
Contract notes are due within 24 hours of the trade, not by T+1 evening.
The broker is liable for the acts of its authorised persons.
Running account settlement must happen monthly or quarterly as chosen by the client; it cannot be skipped indefinitely.
items.recap: Brokers register with SEBI through the exchange and must hold client money and securities separately. Three clearing member types: self, trading-cum-clearing and professional. Onboarding needs KYC, UCC, rights and obligations and risk disclosure. Collect upfront margins, issue contract notes within 24 hours, settle running accounts monthly or quarterly, and answer for authorised persons' acts.

items.title: Merchant Bankers, Underwriters and Bankers to an Issue
items.description: Merchant banker registration, issue management duties, due diligence, underwriting obligations and the role of bankers to an issue, for NISM Series III-A.
items.intro: This chapter groups the intermediaries who bring securities to market: merchant bankers who manage issues, underwriters who promise to buy unsubscribed portions, and bankers to an issue who collect application money. Questions test who can act as lead manager, merchant banker obligations under ICDR, the underwriter's commitment and restrictions on conflicts of interest.

points.heading: Who is a merchant banker
points.text: A merchant banker manages issues of securities, acting as manager, consultant or adviser, including preparing offer documents, arranging underwriters and coordinating with other intermediaries. Only a SEBI-registered merchant banker may act as lead manager for public issues, rights issues above the specified size, buybacks and open offers.

points.heading: Registration and capital
points.text: Merchant bankers must be body corporates (not NBFCs in the earlier sense), meet capital adequacy or net worth norms, employ experienced professionals and have necessary infrastructure. SEBI raised net worth requirements and introduced categories in 2024 amendments; check the current figures before quoting a number.

points.heading: Due diligence role
points.text: The lead manager must exercise due diligence and certify that the offer document is fair and adequate to enable investors to make an informed decision. If disclosures later turn out to be false, the merchant banker can be held responsible. Exams stress that the due diligence certificate is filed with SEBI.

points.heading: Restrictions and conflicts
points.text: A merchant banker cannot lead manage an issue of its associate, and must not deal in the securities of the issuer it is managing in a way that uses unpublished information. It cannot carry on business other than in the securities market, apart from permitted financial services. It must disclose any underwriting and stake details.

points.heading: Underwriters
points.text: An underwriter agrees to subscribe to securities not taken up by the public, up to the amount underwritten. Example: if ₹100 crore is underwritten and the public subscribes ₹85 crore, the underwriter must take up ₹15 crore of securities. Underwriting obligations must be met within the time set in the agreement. Registered merchant bankers can act as underwriters.

points.heading: Bankers to an issue
points.text: Bankers to an issue are scheduled banks registered with SEBI to accept application money, handle refunds and pay interest or dividends if engaged. Under ASBA, self-certified syndicate banks block funds in the applicant's account instead of collecting it. They must keep records and report collection details to the registrar and lead manager.

points.heading: Code of conduct
points.text: Merchant bankers must act with integrity and fairness, avoid misleading statements about issues, keep client information confidential, not create a false market and not divulge confidential information about the issuer. Breaches can lead to suspension or cancellation under the Intermediaries Regulations.

points.heading: Records and inspection
points.text: They must keep books of account, records and documents for the specified period, submit half-yearly results and reports on issues managed, and allow SEBI inspection. A compliance officer monitors adherence and reports to senior management and SEBI.

traps: A merchant banker cannot act as lead manager to an issue of its own associate.
Underwriters take up only the unsubscribed portion up to their commitment, not the whole issue.
Under ASBA the bank blocks money rather than debiting it, so investors earn interest until allotment.
Due diligence responsibility rests with the lead manager even when the issuer prepares the draft.
items.recap: Merchant bankers manage issues, prepare offer documents and certify due diligence; only registered ones may lead public issues, buybacks and open offers, and never for associates. Underwriters take up the shortfall up to their commitment. Bankers to an issue collect or block application money and handle refunds. All follow a code of conduct, keep records and face Intermediaries Regulations enforcement.

items.title: SEBI ICDR Regulations 2018: IPO Rules Revision Notes
items.description: IPO eligibility routes, allocation to QIBs, NIIs and retail, promoter contribution and lock-in, anchor investors, price band and listing timeline under ICDR.
items.intro: The Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2018 govern public issues, rights issues, preferential allotments, QIPs and bonus issues. For NISM III-A, IPO eligibility, investor allocation, promoter contribution, lock-in and anchor investor rules are the most tested. Numbers appear frequently in questions; learn the standard ones and remember that SEBI amends timelines often.

points.heading: Eligibility under Regulation 6(1)
points.text: An issuer may do an IPO through the profitability route if it has net tangible assets of at least ₹3 crore in each of the preceding three years, average operating profit of at least ₹15 crore in the preceding three years with operating profit in each year, and net worth of at least ₹1 crore in each of the preceding three years, among other conditions.

points.heading: Regulation 6(2) route
points.text: An issuer that does not meet the profitability tests can still go public if at least 75% of the net offer is allotted to qualified institutional buyers. Retail allocation is then capped at 10% and non-institutional at 15%. This route suits loss-making technology companies; if the QIB portion is not met, money must be refunded.

points.heading: Allocation under 6(1)
points.text: For issues under 6(1), not more than 50% of the net offer goes to QIBs, not less than 15% to non-institutional investors and not less than 35% to retail individual investors (applications up to ₹2 lakh). Up to 5% of the QIB portion is reserved for mutual funds.

points.heading: Anchor investors
points.text: Up to 60% of the QIB portion can be allotted to anchor investors one working day before the issue opens, with a minimum application of ₹10 crore. A share of the anchor portion is reserved for domestic mutual funds (and, after 2025 changes, for insurers and pension funds; check current SEBI text). Half of anchor shares are locked in for 30 days and the rest for 90 days after allotment.

points.heading: Promoter contribution and lock-in
points.text: Promoters must contribute at least 20% of post-issue capital, locked in for 18 months from allotment (three years where the issue objects include capital expenditure for a project). Promoter holding in excess of the minimum contribution is locked in for six months. Pre-IPO non-promoter shares are generally locked in for six months.

points.heading: Pricing and price band
points.text: Issues can be fixed price or book built. In book building, the cap of the price band must not exceed 120% of the floor, and the cap must be at least 105% of the floor. The price band is announced at least two working days before opening. Retail investors may bid at the cut-off price.

points.heading: Minimum subscription and timelines
points.text: If minimum subscription of 90% of the fresh issue is not received, the entire amount is refunded. Issues stay open at least three working days. Listing must happen within three working days of issue closure (T+3), as of 2026 — check SEBI's latest circular for any changes.

points.heading: Offer documents
points.text: The draft red herring prospectus is filed with SEBI for observations and made public for comments. The red herring prospectus omits final price and size; the prospectus filed after pricing contains them. SEBI observations are valid for a limited period (12 months) within which the issue must open.

formulas: Promoter minimum contribution = 20% x post-issue paid-up capital (e.g. post-issue capital ₹500 crore means at least ₹100 crore held by promoters and locked in).
traps: Under 6(2), QIBs get at least 75% and retail at most 10%; under 6(1) QIBs get at most 50% and retail at least 35%.
Anchor lock-in is 50% for 30 days and 50% for 90 days, not the whole for 30 days.
The 120% rule is the maximum cap over the floor; at least 105% is the minimum gap.
Minimum subscription is 90% of the fresh issue, not 90% of the total including OFS.
items.recap: ICDR 2018: Reg 6(1) profitability route (NTA ₹3 crore, average operating profit ₹15 crore, net worth ₹1 crore); 6(2) route needs 75% QIB. Allocation under 6(1): QIB up to 50%, NII at least 15%, retail at least 35%. Anchors up to 60% of QIB, locked 30/90 days. Promoters 20% locked 18 months. Cap up to 120% of floor. Minimum subscription 90%. Listing T+3.

items.title: Depositories Act 1996: Demat Holding Revision Notes
items.description: Registered vs beneficial owner, fungibility, option to hold in demat, pledge and hypothecation and depository liability under the Depositories Act 1996.
items.intro: The Depositories Act, 1996 made it possible to hold and transfer securities in electronic form. It defines the relationship between the investor, the depository participant, the depository and the issuer, and changes how ownership is recorded. Exams test the registered-versus-beneficial-owner concept, fungibility, pledge procedures and the immunity from stamp duty and Companies Act transfer rules for demat transfers.

points.heading: Need for the Act
points.text: Paper certificates caused bad deliveries, forgery, loss in transit and long transfer delays. The Act allowed securities to be dematerialised and transferred by book entry. NSDL began operations in 1996 and CDSL in 1999. Since April 2019, transfer of listed securities is permitted only in demat form, except for transmission and transposition.

points.heading: Key parties
points.text: The depository holds securities electronically and maintains records; the depository participant is the agent through which investors open accounts and give instructions; the beneficial owner is the investor; the issuer is the company whose securities are held. Each depository must be registered with SEBI and be a company formed and registered under company law.

points.heading: Registered owner versus beneficial owner
points.text: Section 10 deems the depository to be the registered owner of securities held in demat form for the purpose of effecting transfers, but it has no voting rights or economic interest. The beneficial owner enjoys all rights and liabilities, including dividends, bonuses and voting. The issuer's register of members shows the depository; the depository's records show the beneficial owner.

points.heading: Fungibility
points.text: Section 9 makes demat securities fungible: they have no distinctive numbers, so any 100 shares of a company in demat form are identical to any other 100 shares. This is why demat holdings show quantity, not certificate numbers.

points.heading: Option to hold in demat
points.text: Section 8 gives the investor the option to hold securities in physical or demat form, though SEBI rules now require demat for transfer of listed securities and for public issues. An investor who wishes to dematerialise surrenders certificates through the DP; the issuer cancels them and credits the depository.

points.heading: Pledge and hypothecation
points.text: Section 12 lets a beneficial owner pledge or hypothecate demat securities with the depository's approval. The pledgor initiates through its DP, the pledgee accepts, and the depository records the pledge. On default the pledgee can invoke the pledge and get the securities transferred. Margin pledges for brokers follow this mechanism.

points.heading: Transfer simplified
points.text: Transfers between beneficial owners happen by book entry on instruction to the DP. No transfer deed or stamp duty under the old physical procedure is needed for transfers within the depository, though stamp duty applies on market transactions under the Indian Stamp Act as amended.

points.heading: Liability and penalties
points.text: The depository indemnifies beneficial owners for loss caused by negligence of the depository or its participant, and may recover it from the DP. Penalties apply for failure to furnish information, failure to reconcile records and other violations. Appeals lie to SAT.

traps: The depository is the registered owner only for effecting transfer; voting rights stay with the beneficial owner.
Fungibility is Section 9; registered and beneficial ownership is Section 10. Don't swap them.
The option to hold physical shares still exists in the Act, but transfers of listed securities now must be in demat.
The depository compensates the investor first and then recovers from the negligent DP.
items.recap: Depositories Act 1996 enables book-entry holding and transfer. Depository is registered owner (Section 10) but beneficial owner holds all rights. Demat securities are fungible (Section 9). Investors may choose demat (Section 8). Pledge and hypothecation via Section 12. Depository indemnifies investors for losses from its or its DP's negligence. NSDL 1996, CDSL 1999.

items.title: Depositories and Participants Regulations 2018 Notes
items.description: Depository and DP eligibility, account opening, BSDA, DIS controls, nomination, transmission, reconciliation and grievance duties under SEBI D&P Regulations.
items.intro: While the Depositories Act creates the legal framework, the SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 2018 contain the working rules: who can become a depository or DP, governance of depositories, and how DPs must open accounts, handle instructions and protect investors. Exams favour operational scenarios such as DIS misuse, transmission, nomination and reconciliation.

points.heading: Depository eligibility
points.text: A depository must be a company with a minimum net worth of ₹100 crore, sponsored by eligible institutions, and must meet ownership limits applicable to market infrastructure institutions. It is a first-line regulator of DPs and must have governing board independence and a separate regulatory department.

points.heading: Who can be a DP
points.text: Banks, financial institutions, custodians, clearing corporations, registered stock brokers, NBFCs and RTAs meeting net worth criteria can be DPs. Each DP must be registered with SEBI through the depository and comply with depository bye-laws and operating instructions.

points.heading: Account opening
points.text: The DP does KYC (through a KRA where possible), executes the account opening form, gives the rights and obligations and tariff sheet, and collects nomination or an explicit opt-out declaration. A Basic Services Demat Account is a low-cost account for individuals holding small values of securities, with reduced or nil maintenance charges below SEBI's thresholds.

points.heading: Delivery instruction slips
points.text: DIS booklets are issued only on request and serially numbered. Pre-signed blank DIS, loose slips and slips with alterations not countersigned should not be accepted. Many transfers now happen through electronic instructions with OTP or through the DDPI given to a broker. Misuse of DIS is a classic DP compliance failure.

points.heading: Nomination and transmission
points.text: Individual account holders can nominate up to the number of nominees SEBI permits with percentage shares. On death of a sole holder, securities are transmitted to the nominee after documents such as death certificate and KYC. In joint accounts, the surviving holders get the securities first; nominees come in only if all holders die.

points.heading: Freezing and closure
points.text: An investor can freeze the account against debits, credits or both, useful when travelling abroad. Accounts with no securities and no transactions can be closed on request; balances must first be transferred. Regulator or court orders can also freeze accounts.

points.heading: Reconciliation and audit
points.text: DPs reconcile records with the depository daily, and depositories reconcile with issuers and RTAs. Internal audit and concurrent audit of DP operations are required at intervals specified by SEBI and depositories. Mismatches must be resolved promptly to prevent unauthorised transfers.

points.heading: Investor protection
points.text: Depositories maintain an investor protection fund, monitor grievances against DPs and conduct inspections. DPs send transaction statements periodically and holding statements at least annually, and alert investors by SMS or email on debits. Complaints can be escalated to the depository and then SCORES.

traps: In a joint account the surviving joint holders inherit first; the nominee receives securities only when no joint holder survives.
BSDA is a reduced-cost demat account for small holdings, not a separate category of depository.
Blank pre-signed DIS must not be accepted from clients or retained by the DP.
Depositories, not SEBI directly, are the first-level regulators that inspect DPs.
items.recap: D&P Regulations 2018: depositories need ₹100 crore net worth and act as frontline regulators of DPs. Eligible DPs include banks, brokers, custodians and NBFCs. DPs open accounts with KYC, nomination, BSDA option; control DIS strictly; transmit to nominee or surviving joint holders; reconcile daily; send statements and debit alerts; handle grievances with escalation to depository and SCORES.

items.title: Registrars and Share Transfer Agents: III-A Revision
items.description: Category I and II RTAs, their role in issues and investor servicing, record keeping, grievance handling and code of conduct under SEBI RTA Regulations 1993.
items.intro: Registrars to an issue and share transfer agents keep the records that connect investors with the companies they own. This chapter covers who they are, how they are registered, what they do during an issue and afterwards, and the conduct and record-keeping obligations SEBI imposes. Questions often test the categories, the activities that belong to each, and grievance timelines.

points.heading: Two activities, one regulation
points.text: A registrar to an issue collects applications, keeps records of applicants and money received, finalises the basis of allotment with the exchange, and arranges credit of securities or refunds. A share transfer agent maintains the register of members after listing and handles transfers, transmission, dividend payments and corporate actions on behalf of the company.

points.heading: Categories
points.text: Category I RTAs can act as both registrar to an issue and share transfer agent. Category II can act as only one of them. Capital requirements differ between the two categories, with Category I needing more. Companies may also handle transfers in-house, but then cannot act as STA for others without registration.

points.heading: Role during an IPO
points.text: The registrar receives bid data from exchanges and SCSBs, rejects technically invalid applications, works out the basis of allotment in consultation with the designated stock exchange, issues allotment advice, and instructs depositories to credit shares and SCSBs to unblock funds for unsuccessful bids. Speed and accuracy matter under T+3 listing.

points.heading: Investor servicing
points.text: After listing, the STA processes transmission on death, change of address and bank details, issue of duplicate certificates for remaining physical holders, dematerialisation and rematerialisation requests and dividend or interest payments. Requests need the documents prescribed by SEBI, such as standard forms for KYC updates of physical holders.

points.heading: Records and inspection
points.text: RTAs keep records of applications, allotments, transfers, refunds and complaints for the period SEBI specifies, and permit inspection by SEBI. They must have adequate systems, a disaster recovery site and periodic audit, since they hold sensitive investor data for many issuers.

points.heading: Grievance redressal
points.text: RTAs must resolve investor complaints quickly, maintain a register of complaints and report status to the issuer and SEBI. Unresolved complaints can be escalated through SCORES and the online dispute resolution mechanism. Investors can also approach the company, which remains responsible to its shareholders.

points.heading: Code of conduct
points.text: An RTA must act fairly, not favour any issuer or investor, maintain confidentiality, not misuse information about allotments, and avoid conflicts such as acting for an associate's issue without disclosure. It must not delay transfers or refunds without valid reasons.

points.heading: Relationship with the issuer
points.text: The RTA acts under an agreement with the company, which defines duties, fees and data handling. The company cannot escape its own obligations under LODR by outsourcing them; both can be held responsible for delays in investor servicing.

traps: Category I can do both activities; Category II only one. Options sometimes reverse this.
The basis of allotment is finalised by the registrar with the designated stock exchange, not by the merchant banker alone.
Outsourcing to an RTA does not remove the listed company's own responsibility to shareholders.
Transmission (on death) is not a transfer and remains possible for physical shares.
items.recap: RTAs handle two jobs: registrar to an issue (applications, allotment, refunds) and share transfer agent (register of members, transmission, corporate actions). Category I does both, Category II one. They keep records, permit SEBI inspection, resolve grievances with SCORES escalation and follow a code of fairness and confidentiality. The issuer remains responsible alongside the RTA.

items.title: SEBI Research Analysts Regulations 2014: Exam Notes
items.description: Who needs RA registration, qualifications, conflicts, trading restrictions, report disclosures and fee rules under SEBI Research Analysts Regulations.
items.intro: The Research Analysts Regulations, 2014 govern anyone who prepares research reports or makes buy, sell or hold recommendations on securities for consideration. They aim to reduce conflicts of interest and improve disclosure. Questions test who must register, qualifications, trading restrictions around reports, mandatory disclosures and the separation of research from other businesses.

points.heading: Who is a research analyst
points.text: A research analyst prepares or publishes research reports, makes buy, sell or hold recommendations, gives price targets or offers opinions on public offers. Example: a firm sending paid stock tips with targets through a messaging channel must register as an RA. Journalists writing general market news, or advisers giving advice only to their own clients, may fall outside.

points.heading: Registration
points.text: Individuals, partnership firms, LLPs and body corporates can register. An entity with RA activity must ensure employees involved in research hold required qualifications and certifications, primarily NISM Series XV. Individuals and entities must meet net worth or deposit conditions specified by SEBI.

points.heading: Qualifications
points.text: Research analysts need a qualifying educational background as specified by SEBI (graduate-level qualifications, with SEBI having eased the discipline requirements in recent amendments) and the NISM Series XV certification, with periodic renewal through continuing education or re-examination.

points.heading: Conflict management
points.text: An entity doing research alongside investment banking or broking must separate the research function by Chinese walls. Research analysts cannot report to the investment banking or sales team, and their pay cannot be tied to specific investment banking deals. Research must be independent of the business that benefits from it.

points.heading: Trading restrictions
points.text: Research analysts and their associates must not trade in a security from 30 days before to 5 days after publishing a report on it, and must not trade contrary to their recommendation. Exceptions exist with compliance approval for genuine personal hardship. This prevents front running of their own reports.

points.heading: Disclosures in reports
points.text: Reports must disclose the RA's financial interest or that of associates in the subject company, holdings of 1% or more, compensation received from the company in the past twelve months, whether the analyst has served as an officer, and any other material conflict. Recommendations must have a reasonable basis and be fair.

points.heading: Fees and client dealings
