points.text: RAs dealing with individual and HUF clients must follow SEBI's fee limits, client agreement and advance-fee rules introduced in 2024 amendments (as of 2026 — check the latest SEBI circular). They must not promise returns or assure profits, and must maintain records of research, recommendations and the rationale.

points.heading: Proxy advisors and records
points.text: The regulations also contain a chapter for proxy advisers, which advise institutions on voting. All RAs must keep records for five years, have a compliance officer where applicable, and undergo annual compliance audits.

traps: The trading restriction is 30 days before and 5 days after the report, not the other way round.
Holding of 1% or more in the subject company must be disclosed in the report.
An RA cannot report to investment banking or sales staff, even if research is in the same group.
Assuring returns or profit in recommendations is prohibited for registered RAs as well.
items.recap: Anyone publishing research or buy/sell/hold calls for payment needs RA registration with NISM XV certification. Research must be separated from investment banking and sales. No trading in the covered stock 30 days before to 5 days after a report or against the call. Disclose financial interests, 1% holdings and compensation from the company. Follow fee rules, keep records five years.

items.title: SEBI Investment Advisers Regulations 2013: Revision
items.description: Investment adviser registration, qualifications, segregation from distribution, risk profiling, suitability, fee modes and records under SEBI IA rules.
items.intro: The Investment Advisers Regulations, 2013 bring fee-based investment advice under SEBI registration and separate it from commission-based distribution. Questions test who needs registration, exemptions, qualification and certification rules, segregation of advisory and distribution, risk profiling and suitability, and fee limits. Several provisions were amended in 2024 and 2025, so treat limits as 'as of 2026 — check SEBI'.

points.heading: Who must register
points.text: Anyone giving investment advice for consideration, directly or indirectly, and holding out as an adviser must register. Exemptions include advice given incidentally by professionals like chartered accountants and lawyers, insurance agents advising only on insurance, and distributors giving incidental advice on products they distribute without charging an advisory fee.

points.heading: Qualifications and certification
points.text: Individual advisers and principal officers need prescribed education and experience and must pass NISM Series X-A and X-B certifications, renewing them periodically. Persons associated with advice in a non-individual IA need the same certifications. SEBI relaxed some educational criteria in recent amendments.

points.heading: Segregation from distribution
points.text: An IA cannot provide distribution services to its advisory clients, and the separation applies at the client's family level. A body corporate must keep advisory and distribution in separate subsidiaries or divisions with an arm's-length relationship. An individual IA cannot offer distribution services at all.

points.heading: Risk profiling
points.text: Before advising, the IA must collect information on the client's age, income, liabilities, investment objective, horizon, risk appetite and capacity to absorb loss, and assign a risk profile. The profile must be communicated to the client and updated periodically. Advice must follow the profile.

points.heading: Suitability
points.text: Recommendations must be suitable to the client's risk profile and needs. Example: suggesting small-cap equity funds and options strategies to a 68-year-old with a conservative profile and short horizon would breach suitability even if the client agreed. The IA should document the reason for each recommendation.

points.heading: Fees
points.text: Fees are charged under one of two modes per family: as a percentage of assets under advice or as a fixed fee, within limits SEBI specifies (for example, the AUA mode cap of 2.5% a year; as of 2026 — check the latest SEBI circular). Limits apply to individual and HUF clients. Fees should be paid through banking channels, not cash.

points.heading: Agreement and disclosures
points.text: An IA must sign a client agreement containing mandatory terms, disclose conflicts of interest, its registration details, and any consideration received from product manufacturers. Disclaimers cannot hide material risks. Advertisements must follow SEBI's advertisement code and avoid promising returns.

points.heading: Records and audit
points.text: IAs keep records of risk profiles, suitability, advice given with rationale, client agreements, fees and complaints for five years, and undergo annual compliance audits. Grievances must be addressed promptly and can be escalated through SCORES and ODR.

traps: An individual IA cannot act as a distributor for anyone, not just for advisory clients.
Segregation applies at family level: advising a husband and distributing to his wife counts as the same client family.
A client's signed agreement to unsuitable advice does not cure a suitability failure.
Mutual fund distributors giving incidental advice without a fee are exempt; charging an advisory fee needs registration.
items.recap: Fee-based investment advice needs SEBI IA registration with NISM X-A and X-B. Advisory and distribution must be separated, at family level; individuals cannot distribute at all. Do risk profiling, give only suitable advice, document rationale, sign a client agreement with disclosures. Fees by AUA or fixed mode within SEBI limits. Keep records five years and do annual compliance audit.

items.title: SEBI Debenture Trustees Regulations 1993: Notes
items.description: Who can be a debenture trustee, eligibility, duties to debenture holders, security creation, covenant monitoring and enforcement under SEBI DT Regulations.
items.intro: Debenture trustees protect the interests of debenture holders, who are often numerous and unable to monitor the issuer themselves. The Debenture Trustees Regulations, 1993 set eligibility, conflict rules and a detailed list of duties from before issue to redemption. Exam questions test who may be a DT, the restrictions on associates and what the trustee must do when the issuer defaults.

points.heading: Need for a trustee
points.text: When a company raises ₹500 crore through listed NCDs held by thousands of investors, no individual holder can verify that assets were charged or covenants followed. A debenture trustee acts as the single representative of all holders, monitors the issuer and enforces security on their behalf. Companies Act and SEBI rules require a DT for listed and public debt issues.

points.heading: Who can be a DT
points.text: Scheduled banks carrying on commercial activity, public financial institutions, insurance companies and body corporates can register as debenture trustees. A body corporate needs minimum net worth as specified by SEBI (raised to ₹10 crore through amendments) and adequate infrastructure and professionals.

points.heading: Conflict restrictions
points.text: A DT cannot act for an issue if it is an associate of the issuer, has lent money to the issuer in a way that creates conflict (unless permitted), or is a beneficial holder of the issuer's shares. Independence from the issuer is central to the role.

points.heading: Due diligence before issue
points.text: Before the issue, the DT verifies that assets offered as security are free from encumbrances or that existing charge holders have consented, checks valuation and insurance, and confirms adequacy of security cover. It gives a due diligence certificate to be filed with the exchange and disclosed in the offer document.

points.heading: Monitoring during the life
points.text: The DT calls for periodic reports on utilisation of funds, security cover and covenant compliance, ensures that the issuer creates the charge and executes the trust deed within the specified time, and checks that interest and principal are paid on schedule. It monitors the recovery expense fund created by issuers.

points.heading: Action on default
points.text: On default, the DT informs debenture holders, convenes meetings, obtains their consent for enforcement, and may take steps such as enforcing security, filing under IBC or SARFAESI, or entering inter-creditor agreements. It must act with the required majority consent as specified by SEBI.

points.heading: Duties to holders
points.text: The DT must act in the interest of holders, keep them informed, ensure that the issuer redresses complaints, and disclose relevant information on its website. It must exercise due diligence and is liable for breach of trust if it fails to act.

points.heading: Records and compliance
points.text: DTs keep records of each issue, reports received, meetings held and actions taken, and submit periodic reports to SEBI and exchanges. A compliance officer is appointed to monitor adherence to regulations and circulars.

traps: An associate of the issuer cannot act as its debenture trustee.
The DT verifies and monitors security; it does not guarantee repayment to holders.
Enforcement on default generally needs approval of the required majority of holders.
Creation of charge and trust deed execution are monitored by the DT, but the obligation to create them is the issuer's.
items.recap: Debenture trustees represent all debenture holders. Eligible: scheduled banks, PFIs, insurers and body corporates meeting net worth. No associates of the issuer. Before issue: due diligence on assets and security cover. During: monitor charge creation, covenants, fund use and payments. On default: inform holders, convene meetings, enforce security with consent. DTs do not guarantee repayment.

items.title: SEBI Credit Rating Agency Regulations 1999: Notes
items.description: CRA promoter eligibility, rating process, committees, surveillance, conflict restrictions and disclosures under SEBI Credit Rating Agencies Regulations 1999.
items.intro: Credit rating agencies give opinions on the likelihood of timely repayment of debt. Since investors and regulators rely on these ratings, SEBI regulates who can set up a CRA, how ratings are assigned and reviewed, and how conflicts are handled. Exam questions focus on promoter eligibility, rating process steps, surveillance, restrictions on rating associates, and the nature of a rating.

points.heading: What a rating is
points.text: A credit rating is an opinion on the relative ability and willingness of an issuer to meet debt obligations on time. It is not a recommendation to buy, sell or hold, and does not comment on market price or suitability. AAA indicates the highest safety; ratings below BBB- are speculative grade.

points.heading: Eligible promoters
points.text: A CRA must be promoted by a public financial institution, a scheduled commercial bank, a foreign bank operating in India, a foreign credit rating agency with at least five years' experience, or a company or body corporate with continuous net worth of at least ₹100 crore for the previous five years. This keeps the business with established institutions.

points.heading: Net worth and registration
points.text: The CRA itself must be a company with minimum net worth of ₹25 crore and adequate professionals, and must be registered with SEBI. Its memorandum must include rating as a main object.

points.heading: Restrictions on rating
points.text: A CRA cannot rate securities issued by its promoter, by entities that are its associates, or by entities in which its promoter holds a significant stake beyond the specified limit. It cannot rate an issuer if it has a conflict that impairs independence, such as consulting assignments for the same entity.

points.heading: Rating process
points.text: The CRA signs a rating agreement, gathers information from the issuer and public sources, analysts meet management and prepare a rating note, and a rating committee assigns the rating. The issuer can appeal once with additional information. The rating, rationale and key drivers are published.

points.heading: Surveillance
points.text: Ratings must be reviewed at least annually for the life of the instrument, and continuously monitored. If the issuer stops cooperating, the CRA continues with available information and flags the rating as 'issuer not cooperating'. Defaults must be recognised promptly as per SEBI's timelines.

points.heading: Disclosures and rating shopping
points.text: CRAs disclose rating methodologies, default rates, transition matrices and rating history on their websites. Issuers must disclose all ratings obtained, including those not accepted, so they cannot hide unfavourable ratings by 'rating shopping'.

points.heading: Code of conduct
points.text: CRAs must act independently, avoid conflicts, keep information confidential, separate rating from other business, and have rating committee members free from conflicts. Analysts' compensation should not depend on the revenue from the rated entity.

traps: A rating is an opinion on credit risk, not a recommendation to invest or a guarantee of repayment.
The ₹100 crore five-year net worth test applies to a company promoter; the CRA's own minimum net worth is ₹25 crore.
Non-accepted ratings must still be disclosed to stop rating shopping.
Ratings are reviewed at least annually, not only when the issuer requests.
items.recap: CRAs give opinions on timely debt repayment, not buy or sell calls. Promoters: PFIs, scheduled banks, foreign banks, foreign CRAs with five years' experience, or companies with ₹100 crore net worth for five years. CRA net worth ₹25 crore. No rating of promoters or associates. Committee-based ratings, annual surveillance, disclosure of methodologies and non-accepted ratings.

items.title: SEBI Custodian Regulations 1996: III-A Revision Notes
items.description: Custodial services, net worth, segregation of client assets, internal controls, corporate actions and conflicts under SEBI Custodian Regulations 1996.
items.intro: Custodians safeguard securities and related assets for institutional clients such as mutual funds, FPIs, insurers and portfolio managers. The Custodian Regulations, 1996 define custodial services, set eligibility and capital norms and require strict segregation and controls. Exams test the scope of services, the net worth requirement, conflicts of interest and the custodian's duties on corporate actions.

points.heading: Custodial services
points.text: Custodial services mean safekeeping of securities, gold and other assets of a client, along with related services such as collecting dividends and interest, tracking and acting on corporate actions, maintaining accounts of holdings, and settling trades by receiving or delivering securities and funds. A mutual fund cannot operate without a custodian.

points.heading: Eligibility
points.text: Only an entity registered with SEBI may act as custodian. It must have a minimum net worth of ₹50 crore, adequate infrastructure, trained staff and systems for safekeeping and record keeping. Most custodians in India are banks or bank subsidiaries.

points.heading: Segregation of assets
points.text: Client assets must be held separately from the custodian's own assets and from those of other clients. Each client's holdings must be identifiable at all times. If the custodian fails, client assets are not available to its creditors.

points.heading: Internal controls
points.text: The custodian must have controls to prevent fraud, errors and unauthorised transfers, conduct regular reconciliation with depositories and clients, and undergo periodic audit. Instructions must come from authorised signatories under agreed procedures.

points.heading: Corporate actions
points.text: The custodian informs the client of rights issues, bonuses, buybacks, mergers and voting events, acts on instructions within deadlines, and collects entitlements. Missing a rights issue deadline for an FPI client due to delay in passing on information would be a service failure.

points.heading: Conflicts of interest
points.text: A custodian should not act for a mutual fund whose sponsor or AMC is its associate unless specified conditions on independence (such as minimum directors who are independent) are met. It must avoid conflicts between its own business and its role as custodian, and disclose any that arise.

points.heading: Agreement and reporting
points.text: Each client relationship is governed by a written agreement setting out duties, fees, liability and reporting. Custodians report holdings and transactions to clients and file periodic reports with SEBI. They also often act as DDPs for FPI registration.

points.heading: Records and inspection
points.text: Records of client holdings, instructions and correspondence must be maintained for the period specified and are open to SEBI inspection. A compliance officer oversees adherence.

traps: The custodian's minimum net worth is ₹50 crore, higher than many other intermediaries.
Custodians safekeep and service assets; they do not decide what to buy or sell for the client.
Client assets are not part of the custodian's estate on insolvency.
Associate relationships with an AMC need independence safeguards; they are not automatically allowed.
items.recap: Custodians safekeep securities and other assets for institutional clients and service them: settlements, dividends, corporate actions and records. SEBI registration and ₹50 crore net worth are required. Client assets are segregated and protected from the custodian's creditors. Strong internal controls, reconciliation and written agreements are mandatory. Conflicts with associated AMCs need independence safeguards.

items.title: Proxy Advisors in India: NISM III-A Revision Notes
items.description: Role of proxy advisers, SEBI registration under RA rules, conflicts, voting recommendation methodology, disclosures and company responses, with exam traps.
items.intro: Proxy advisers analyse shareholder resolutions and recommend how institutional investors should vote. Their influence on corporate governance outcomes led SEBI to regulate them through a dedicated chapter in the Research Analysts Regulations and later procedural guidelines. Questions test their role, registration route, conflict management, disclosure of methodology and the process for sharing reports with companies.

points.heading: Who is a proxy adviser
points.text: A proxy adviser provides advice to institutional investors or shareholders, through any means, on exercising their rights in a listed company, including recommendations on public offers or voting on agenda items. In India, firms such as IiAS, InGovern and SES are well-known proxy advisers.

points.heading: Why they matter
points.text: Mutual funds, insurers and FPIs vote on thousands of resolutions each year and often rely on proxy research. A negative recommendation on a related-party transaction or director appointment can sway enough votes to defeat a resolution, so accuracy and independence matter.

points.heading: Registration route
points.text: Proxy advisers must register with SEBI under the Research Analysts Regulations, 2014, which contain a separate chapter on proxy advisers. They must meet eligibility conditions, employ qualified staff and comply with the code of conduct applicable to research analysts and the specific proxy adviser provisions.

points.heading: Conflict of interest
points.text: Proxy advisers must disclose conflicts such as consulting relationships with the company being evaluated, or holdings of the firm or its clients in the company. Where a conflict exists, they must manage it through policies and disclosure, and may need to refrain from recommending.

points.heading: Voting recommendation methodology
points.text: They must publish their voting policies and methodologies, review them at least annually and disclose material changes. Recommendations should be based on these policies and publicly available information, with reasons stated so that investors can judge rather than follow blindly.

points.heading: Sharing reports with companies
points.text: Under SEBI's procedural guidelines, proxy advisers share their reports with clients and the company at the same time, and the company may send comments. If received, the comments are circulated to clients. Factual errors must be corrected promptly and the correction communicated.

points.heading: Not a decision-maker
points.text: Final voting decisions rest with the institutional investor, which must follow its own stewardship code and disclose votes and rationale. Proxy advice is an input; investors cannot transfer their fiduciary responsibility to the adviser.

points.heading: Records and grievance
points.text: Proxy advisers keep records of reports, recommendations, policies and communications, and must address complaints from clients and companies. Annual compliance audits are required as for other research analysts.

traps: Proxy advisers register under the Research Analysts Regulations, not under a separate standalone regulation.
The report goes to clients and the company at the same time; the company does not get a pre-approval right.
Institutional investors remain responsible for their votes even if they follow proxy advice.
Voting policies must be reviewed at least annually and published.
items.recap: Proxy advisers recommend how institutions should vote at shareholder meetings. They register with SEBI under the RA Regulations, disclose conflicts, publish and annually review voting methodologies, share reports with clients and companies simultaneously, circulate company comments and fix errors fast. Institutions still own their voting decisions under stewardship codes.

items.title: Basics of Derivatives: NISM XIII Revision Notes
items.description: Meaning of derivatives, forwards, futures, options and swaps, OTC vs exchange-traded, and the roles of hedgers, speculators and arbitrageurs in India.
items.intro: NISM Series XIII (Common Derivatives) covers equity, currency and interest rate derivatives together. This first chapter defines a derivative, compares the basic contract types and explains why markets need them. Questions are mostly conceptual: identify the instrument from a description, classify a participant by motive, or contrast exchange-traded and OTC contracts.

points.heading: Definition
points.text: A derivative is a contract whose value depends on an underlying asset, index or rate: shares, Nifty, USD/INR, government bond prices, interest rates or commodities. Under SCRA, derivatives are securities. The contract itself usually requires little or no upfront payment beyond margin or premium, which creates leverage.

points.heading: Forwards
points.text: A forward is a customised bilateral agreement to buy or sell an asset at a fixed price on a future date. An importer agreeing with a bank today to buy USD 50,000 in three months at ₹84.20 has a forward. Terms are flexible, but there is counterparty risk and no easy exit before maturity.

points.heading: Futures
points.text: Futures are standardised forwards traded on an exchange, with fixed lot size, expiry and settlement, and a clearing corporation guaranteeing performance. Daily mark-to-market settles gains and losses, so credit risk is limited. Positions can be closed any time before expiry by an opposite trade.

points.heading: Options
points.text: An option gives the buyer the right, not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying at a strike price on or before expiry, in exchange for a premium. The seller (writer) has the obligation if exercised. Buyers have limited loss; sellers have limited gain and potentially large losses.

points.heading: Swaps
points.text: A swap exchanges one set of cash flows for another, for example fixed interest for floating (interest rate swap) or principal and interest in one currency for another (currency swap). Swaps are mostly OTC between banks and corporates in India, though they are covered in the syllabus as a basic type.

points.heading: Exchange-traded versus OTC
points.text: Exchange-traded contracts are standardised, transparent, margined and centrally cleared. OTC contracts are customised and negotiated privately, with higher counterparty and liquidity risk, though many OTC derivatives are now reported to trade repositories and some are centrally cleared through CCIL.

points.heading: Market participants
points.text: Hedgers use derivatives to reduce existing risk, such as an exporter selling USD futures. Speculators take positions to profit from expected price moves, accepting risk. Arbitrageurs lock in riskless profit from price differences between markets, such as buying shares in cash and selling futures when futures are overpriced. Each role adds liquidity.

points.heading: Economic functions
points.text: Derivatives help price discovery, transfer risk to those willing to bear it, increase market liquidity and lower transaction costs. Misused, leverage can amplify losses, which is why margins, position limits and suitability checks exist. Index futures began in India in June 2000, followed by index options, stock options and stock futures.

traps: Forwards carry counterparty risk; exchange-traded futures replace it with the clearing corporation's guarantee.
The option buyer pays premium and has a right; the seller receives premium and has an obligation.
An arbitrageur seeks riskless profit; a speculator accepts risk for expected profit.
Swaps are derivatives too, even though most trade OTC.
items.recap: A derivative derives value from an underlying. Forwards are customised OTC contracts with counterparty risk; futures are standardised, exchange-traded and marked to market daily; options give buyers a right for a premium; swaps exchange cash flows. Hedgers reduce risk, speculators take it, arbitrageurs exploit mispricing. Benefits: price discovery, risk transfer, liquidity.

items.title: Equity, Currency and Bond Markets for NISM XIII
items.description: Index construction, free float, USD/INR quotes and cross rates, G-sec prices and yields, and benchmark rates that underlie Indian derivatives, revised.
items.intro: Before trading derivatives you must understand the underlying markets: equity indices and stocks, the foreign exchange market and the government bond market. This chapter is wide, covering index construction, exchange rate quotes and bond price-yield relationships. Questions often include small calculations on cross rates, index levels or bond yields, and definitions such as impact cost and free float.

points.heading: Equity indices
points.text: An index tracks a basket of stocks. Most Indian indices, including Nifty 50 and Sensex, are free-float market-capitalisation weighted: only shares readily available for trading count. If a company has ₹2 lakh crore market cap but promoters hold 60%, its free-float market cap is ₹80,000 crore, which determines its weight.

points.heading: Index qualities
points.text: A good index is diversified, liquid and representative. Impact cost measures liquidity: the percentage price movement caused by executing a given order size compared with the ideal price. Lower impact cost means more liquid. Index levels are adjusted for corporate actions so that a split or bonus does not change the index value.

points.heading: Foreign exchange market basics
points.text: The forex market is OTC, dominated by banks. In a direct quote like USD/INR 84.00, the base currency (USD) is quoted in terms of the price currency (INR). Bid is the rate at which the dealer buys the base currency, ask is the rate at which it sells. Spread = ask minus bid.

points.heading: Spot, forward and cross rates
points.text: Spot settles two business days after the trade. Forward rates differ from spot because of interest rate differentials. Cross rates derive a third rate: if USD/INR is 84 and EUR/USD is 1.10, then EUR/INR is about 84 x 1.10 = 92.40. Questions often test this multiplication.

points.heading: Reference rate
points.text: Exchange-traded USD/INR futures and options are cash settled in rupees using the reference rate published by FBIL (Financial Benchmarks India Ltd) on the expiry date. Other currency pairs use rates specified by exchanges. Know that the settlement is in INR, not USD.

points.heading: Government securities
points.text: G-secs are issued by RBI on behalf of the Government through auctions. T-bills are short-term discount instruments (91, 182, 364 days); dated securities carry a fixed or floating coupon. Trading happens on NDS-OM and OTC, and settlement is through CCIL. Stock exchanges also offer retail access.

points.heading: Price and yield
points.text: Bond prices and yields move inversely. A bond with ₹100 face value and 7% coupon trading at ₹98 has a yield to maturity above 7%. When market yields rise, prices of existing bonds fall, and longer-duration bonds fall more. Duration measures this sensitivity.

points.heading: Benchmark interest rates
points.text: Short-term benchmarks include MIBOR and the overnight rates in the call and TREPS markets, administered or published by FBIL and CCIL. Interest rate futures in India are mainly on G-sec bonds and T-bills. These rates also drive pricing of currency forwards through interest rate differentials.

formulas: Cross rate: EUR/INR = EUR/USD x USD/INR.
Free-float market cap = total market cap x (1 - promoter and locked-in holding %).
Current yield = annual coupon / market price.
traps: Index weights use free-float market cap, not full market cap.
Bid is where the dealer buys the base currency; the customer selling USD gets the bid.
USD/INR exchange-traded derivatives settle in rupees using the FBIL reference rate, without delivery of dollars.
If yields rise, bond prices fall; a question showing both rising is wrong.
items.recap: Indices like Nifty and Sensex are free-float market-cap weighted; impact cost measures liquidity. Forex: direct quotes, bid below ask, spot T+2, cross rates by multiplication, FBIL reference rate for settlement. G-secs via RBI auctions, traded on NDS-OM, settled by CCIL. Bond prices and yields move inversely; duration measures sensitivity. MIBOR and TREPS rates are short-term benchmarks.

items.title: Forwards and Futures Pricing: NISM XIII Revision Notes
items.description: Cost of carry pricing, basis, contango and backwardation, interest rate parity for currency futures, mark to market and contract specs, with worked numbers.
items.intro: This chapter explains how forwards and futures work and how they are priced across equity, currency and interest rate markets. It is one of the heaviest chapters in NISM XIII, with calculation questions on fair value, basis, mark-to-market and currency forward premium. Practise the cost of carry and interest rate parity formulas until they are automatic.

points.heading: Futures versus forwards
points.text: Futures are standardised, exchange-traded and centrally cleared; forwards are bilateral and customised. Futures settle gains and losses daily through mark to market, while forwards settle once at maturity. Futures can be squared off before expiry; forwards normally need the counterparty's agreement to cancel.

points.heading: Cost of carry model
points.text: The fair futures price equals spot plus the cost of carrying the asset till expiry, minus income received. For Nifty at 24,000, interest of 7% a year and 30 days to expiry, fair value is about 24,000 x (1 + 0.07 x 30/365) = 24,138, less the value of dividends expected in the period.

points.heading: Basis and convergence
points.text: Basis is spot minus futures (some texts use futures minus spot; read each question carefully). As expiry approaches, the futures price converges to the spot price and basis narrows to zero. On the expiry day, index futures settle at the closing index value.

points.heading: Contango and backwardation
points.text: When futures trade above spot, the market is in contango, the usual state when carry costs exceed income. When futures trade below spot, it is backwardation, which can happen with large expected dividends, high demand for the underlying, or strong bearish sentiment.

points.heading: Currency futures pricing
points.text: Interest rate parity links forward and spot rates: the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount. With USD/INR spot at 84.00, Indian rate 7% and US rate 5%, the one-year forward is about 84 x 1.07/1.05 = 85.60. So USD trades at a forward premium against INR.

points.heading: Interest rate futures
points.text: Indian IRFs are mainly on 10-year and other G-secs (cash settled based on a weighted average price) and on T-bills. If interest rates rise, bond prices fall, so a long IRF position loses. An investor expecting rates to rise would sell IRF to hedge a bond portfolio.

points.heading: Mark to market
points.text: Every day, open positions are revalued at the daily settlement price and the difference is paid or received. If you bought one Nifty futures lot of 75 units at 24,000 and it settles at 23,900, you pay 100 x 75 = ₹7,500 that day. Lot sizes are revised by exchanges, so always use the lot given in the question.

points.heading: Contract specifications
points.text: Every futures contract specifies underlying, lot size, tick size, expiry day, settlement method and price bands. Equity index futures are cash settled; stock futures are physically settled at expiry. USD/INR futures have a lot size of USD 1,000, are quoted in rupees per dollar to four decimals and settle in cash.

formulas: Fair futures price F = S x (1 + r x t) - dividends (or S x e^(rt) with continuous compounding).
Currency forward F = S x (1 + r_domestic x t) / (1 + r_foreign x t).
Annualised forward premium % = (F - S)/S x 12/months x 100.
Daily MTM = (today's settlement price - previous settlement or trade price) x lot size x number of lots.
traps: Contango means futures above spot; backwardation means futures below spot. Students often mix the terms.
In currency futures, the higher-interest currency trades at a forward discount, not a premium.
Stock futures in India are physically settled at expiry; index futures are cash settled.
Basis can be defined either way; check whether the question uses spot minus futures or futures minus spot.
items.recap: Futures are standardised, cleared, marked to market forwards. Fair value = spot plus carry minus income. Futures converge to spot at expiry. Contango: futures above spot; backwardation: below. Interest rate parity prices currency forwards; higher-rate currency is at a forward discount. Long IRF loses when rates rise. Index futures cash settle; stock futures settle physically; USD/INR lot is USD 1,000.

items.title: Hedging and Arbitrage with Futures: NISM XIII Notes
items.description: Long and short hedges, beta-based hedge ratios, cash-futures arbitrage, currency hedges for importers and exporters, and IRF hedging worked step by step.
items.intro: Once pricing is clear, the next question is how to use futures. This chapter covers hedging equity portfolios with index futures, hedging single stocks, cash-and-carry arbitrage, currency hedges for importers and exporters, and hedging bond portfolios with interest rate futures. Expect calculation questions on the number of contracts and on arbitrage profit.

points.heading: Short hedge
points.text: A short hedge sells futures to protect an asset already held or to be sold. A mutual fund holding ₹10 crore of large-cap stocks that fears a fall over the next month can sell Nifty futures. Losses on the portfolio are offset by gains on the short futures, though basis risk remains.

points.heading: Long hedge
points.text: A long hedge buys futures to lock in the price of something to be bought later. An investor expecting ₹50 lakh of bonus in two months, who wants to invest in the index at today's level, can buy index futures now. If the market rises, futures gains compensate for the higher purchase price.

points.heading: Beta-based hedge ratio
points.text: Portfolios move with the market according to beta. Number of contracts = beta x portfolio value / (futures price x lot size). For a ₹12 crore portfolio with beta 1.25, Nifty futures at 24,000 and an assumed lot of 75: 1.25 x 12,00,00,000 / (24,000 x 75) = about 83 lots.

points.heading: Changing portfolio beta
points.text: Futures can also raise or lower beta without trading the underlying shares. To reduce beta from 1.2 to 0.8, sell futures equal to (1.2 - 0.8) x portfolio value / futures contract value. Buying futures increases beta. This is cheaper and faster than selling shares.

points.heading: Cash and carry arbitrage
points.text: If futures trade above fair value, buy the stock in cash and sell futures; hold till expiry and deliver or square off. Example: stock at ₹1,000, futures ₹1,020 for one month, carry cost ₹6. Arbitrage profit is about ₹14 per share before costs. Reverse arbitrage (sell cash, buy futures) works when futures are below fair value.

points.heading: Exporters and importers
points.text: An exporter expecting USD receipts fears a fall in USD/INR, so sells USD/INR futures. An importer with USD payables fears a rise, so buys USD/INR futures. Example: importer buys 100 lots (USD 1,00,000) at 84.30; if spot rises to 85.00 at maturity, the futures gain of ₹70,000 offsets the higher rupee cost.

points.heading: Hedging with interest rate futures
points.text: A bank holding G-secs fears rising yields, which cut bond prices. It sells IRF so that gains on futures offset losses on bonds. The number of contracts is based on matching modified duration or PV01 of the portfolio with that of the futures contract.

points.heading: Basis risk and limits of hedging
points.text: A hedge is rarely perfect. If the portfolio is not identical to the index, or expiry does not match the exposure period, the gain on futures will not exactly offset the loss. Hedging also gives up upside: a short hedge loses on futures when markets rise.

formulas: Number of index futures contracts = beta x portfolio value / (futures price x lot size).
Contracts to change beta = (target beta - current beta) x portfolio value / (futures price x lot size); negative means sell.
Arbitrage profit = futures price - spot price - cost of carry (before transaction costs).
traps: Exporters sell USD/INR futures; importers buy them. Reversing this is a frequent wrong option.
Hedging removes upside as well as downside; it is not free insurance.
A long hedge protects against a price rise; a short hedge protects against a fall.
For a beta hedge, multiply portfolio value by beta before dividing by contract value.
items.recap: Short hedge protects holdings against a fall; long hedge locks in purchase price. Contracts = beta x portfolio value / (futures price x lot size). Futures can raise or lower beta cheaply. Cash-and-carry when futures are rich, reverse when cheap. Exporters sell, importers buy USD/INR futures. IRF hedges use duration or PV01 matching. Basis risk means hedges are imperfect.

items.title: Options Basics and Greeks: NISM XIII Revision Notes
items.description: Calls and puts, moneyness, intrinsic and time value, premium drivers, put-call parity, Greeks and Indian option settlement rules, with quick worked examples.
items.intro: Options make up a large share of NISM XIII questions. This chapter covers terminology, payoffs, moneyness, factors that affect premium, option Greeks, put-call parity and contract specifications in equity and currency options. Calculation questions on intrinsic value, breakeven and payoff appear regularly, as do conceptual questions on which way premium moves when a factor changes.

points.heading: Calls and puts
points.text: A call gives the buyer the right to buy at the strike; a put gives the right to sell. The buyer pays a premium upfront; the seller receives it and must perform if exercised. A long call profits when prices rise above strike plus premium; a long put profits when prices fall below strike minus premium.

points.heading: Moneyness
points.text: A call is in the money when spot is above strike, at the money when equal, and out of the money when below. For puts it is the reverse. With Nifty at 24,000, a 23,800 call is ITM by 200 points, while a 23,800 put is OTM.

points.heading: Intrinsic and time value
points.text: Premium = intrinsic value + time value. If a 23,800 call trades at 350 with Nifty at 24,000, intrinsic value is 200 and time value 150. OTM options have only time value. Time value decays to zero at expiry, and the decay speeds up in the final weeks.

points.heading: Premium drivers
points.text: Call premium rises with higher spot, lower strike, longer time, higher volatility and higher interest rates; it falls with expected dividends. Put premium rises with lower spot, higher strike, longer time and higher volatility; it falls with higher interest rates and rises with dividends. Volatility increases both calls and puts.

points.heading: Option pricing models
points.text: The Black-Scholes model prices European options using spot, strike, time, volatility and the risk-free rate. The binomial model breaks time into steps and also handles American options. Implied volatility is the volatility that makes the model price equal the market premium; India VIX is built from Nifty option implied volatility.

points.heading: Greeks
points.text: Delta measures change in premium for a one-unit change in the underlying (call 0 to 1, put -1 to 0; ATM about 0.5). Gamma measures change in delta. Theta is time decay, usually negative for buyers. Vega measures sensitivity to volatility. Rho measures sensitivity to interest rates. Option buyers are long gamma and vega, short theta.

points.heading: Put-call parity
points.text: For European options on the same underlying, strike and expiry: call premium + present value of strike = put premium + spot. If it does not hold, arbitrage is possible. Example: with S = K = 100 and PV(K) = 98, C minus P should be 2; a call at 6 and put at 4 satisfies parity, while a call at 8 would not.

points.heading: Indian contract rules
points.text: Index and stock options on NSE and BSE are European style, exercisable only at expiry. Stock options in-the-money at expiry are physically settled; index options are cash settled. Currency options on USD/INR are European and cash settled in rupees. Exchanges set strikes, lot sizes and expiry days, which SEBI has revised in recent years.

formulas: Call intrinsic value = max(0, S - K); put intrinsic value = max(0, K - S).
Breakeven: long call = K + premium; long put = K - premium.
Put-call parity: C + K/(1+r)^t = P + S.
traps: Higher interest rates raise call premiums and lower put premiums.
Higher volatility increases both call and put premiums.
Indian stock options are European, not American, since 2011.
Time value is highest for at-the-money options, not deep ITM ones.
Delta of a put is negative; a delta of 0.4 for a put is impossible.
items.recap: Calls = right to buy, puts = right to sell; buyers pay premium, sellers take obligation. Premium = intrinsic + time value; ATM has most time value. Volatility raises all premiums; rates raise calls and lower puts. Greeks: delta, gamma, theta, vega, rho. Put-call parity: C + PV(K) = P + S. Indian equity and currency options are European; stock options settle physically.

items.title: Option Trading Strategies: NISM XIII Revision Notes
items.description: Payoffs, maximum profit, maximum loss and breakevens for covered calls, protective puts, spreads, straddles, strangles, butterflies and collars, worked out.
items.intro: This chapter builds strategies from single options and futures, and NISM XIII tests them through payoff questions: what is the maximum loss, where is the breakeven, which view does a strategy express. Work through each with simple numbers. Most strategies fall into three groups: directional (spreads), volatility (straddles, strangles) and protective (covered call, protective put, collar).

points.heading: Protective put
points.text: Own the stock and buy a put. It works like insurance: the put caps the downside at strike minus premium paid. Example: hold shares at ₹500, buy a 480 put for ₹10. Maximum loss is 500 - 480 + 10 = ₹30 per share, while upside stays open less the premium.

points.heading: Covered call
points.text: Own the stock and sell a call. The premium earns extra income, but gains above the strike are given up. Suitable when the view is neutral to mildly bullish. Maximum profit = strike - purchase price + premium; the downside is that of the stock less the premium received.

points.heading: Bull call spread
points.text: Buy a lower-strike call and sell a higher-strike call, same expiry. Cost is lower than a naked call, but profit is capped. With a 24,000 call bought at 300 and 24,300 call sold at 150: net debit 150, maximum profit 300 - 150 = 150 points, breakeven 24,150.

points.heading: Bear put spread
points.text: Buy a higher-strike put and sell a lower-strike put. Used for a moderately bearish view. Maximum profit is the difference in strikes minus net debit; maximum loss is the net debit. A bear call spread (sell lower call, buy higher call) is the credit version of the same view.

points.heading: Long straddle
points.text: Buy a call and a put at the same strike and expiry. It profits from a large move in either direction, for example before a major result or policy announcement. Maximum loss is the total premium if the price ends at the strike. Breakevens are strike plus and minus total premium.

points.heading: Long strangle
points.text: Buy an OTM call and an OTM put. Cheaper than a straddle but needs a bigger move. A short straddle or short strangle is the reverse view: the seller expects low volatility, collects premium and faces large losses if the market moves sharply.

points.heading: Butterfly spread
points.text: A long call butterfly buys one lower strike, sells two middle strikes and buys one higher strike. It profits if the price stays near the middle strike at expiry, with limited risk and limited reward. It is a low-cost, low-volatility view.

points.heading: Collar
points.text: Own the stock, buy a protective put and sell a call to fund it. Both downside and upside are capped. If both premiums are equal, it is a zero-cost collar. Useful for a promoter or investor who wants to protect gains without selling.

points.heading: Synthetic positions
points.text: Long call plus short put at the same strike behaves like long futures. Long stock plus long put behaves like a long call. These equivalences, based on put-call parity, appear as matching questions.

formulas: Bull call spread: max profit = (higher strike - lower strike) - net debit; breakeven = lower strike + net debit.
Long straddle breakevens = strike +/- (call premium + put premium).
Long strangle breakevens = call strike + total premium and put strike - total premium.
traps: A long straddle needs volatility, not direction; a short straddle loses on big moves either way.
Covered call caps upside but does not protect much downside; the protective put protects downside.
In a bull call spread the maximum loss is the net premium paid, not the full premium of the bought call.
Long call plus short put is synthetic long futures, not a straddle.
items.recap: Protective put = stock plus put (insurance). Covered call = stock plus short call (income, capped upside). Bull call and bear put spreads are cheaper directional bets with capped profit. Long straddle and strangle profit from big moves; short versions bet on calm markets with large risk. Butterfly bets on staying near the middle strike. Collar caps both sides.

items.title: Derivatives Clearing, Margins and Settlement: XIII Notes
items.description: Order types, novation, SPAN and exposure margins, mark to market, position limits, settlement of futures and options, and the settlement guarantee fund.
items.intro: This chapter explains how derivatives trades move from order entry to final settlement and how exchanges and clearing corporations control risk. Margin types, daily settlement, final settlement and position limits are favourite topics. Expect questions on who pays which margin, how option premiums and exercise are settled, and the purpose of the core settlement guarantee fund.

points.heading: Trading system
points.text: Derivatives trade on screen-based, order-driven systems matched on price-time priority. Orders can be limit, market, stop-loss or immediate-or-cancel, and can be day orders. Each trade carries the client's UCC. Price bands and dynamic circuit filters prevent erroneous orders from executing at absurd prices.

points.heading: Clearing and novation
points.text: After a trade, the clearing corporation becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer through novation. This removes counterparty risk between trading members. Clearing members are responsible to the clearing corporation for their own trades and those of the trading members they clear for.

points.heading: Initial margin
points.text: Initial margin is collected upfront to cover the potential one-day loss on a portfolio. Indian clearing corporations historically used SPAN, which simulates price and volatility scenarios to find the worst likely loss for the whole portfolio. Hedged positions get margin benefit because losses on one leg are offset by gains on the other.

points.heading: Exposure and other margins
points.text: Exposure margin or extreme loss margin is charged on top of initial margin to cover moves beyond the SPAN scenarios. Premium margin is collected from option buyers until the premium is paid; assignment margin on exercised positions; delivery margin for physically settled stock derivatives near expiry. Clients must pay margins upfront.

points.heading: Daily settlement
points.text: Futures are marked to market daily at the settlement price, with profits paid and losses collected in cash the next day. Option premium is paid by buyers and received by sellers on T+1. Options are not marked to market for the buyer, but sellers' margins are revalued daily.

points.heading: Final settlement
points.text: Index futures and options settle in cash at the final settlement price (the closing value of the index on expiry). ITM stock futures and options positions at expiry are physically settled through delivery of shares. Currency derivatives settle in cash in rupees at the reference rate.

points.heading: Position limits
points.text: Exchanges set market-wide, trading member and client-level position limits to prevent concentration. When open interest in a stock crosses 95% of the market-wide position limit, the stock enters a ban period: no fresh positions can be taken, only reduction of existing positions, until it falls below 80%.

points.heading: Settlement guarantee fund and defaults
points.text: Each clearing corporation keeps a core settlement guarantee fund contributed by itself, exchanges and clearing members to complete settlement if a member defaults. The default waterfall uses the defaulter's margins first, then its SGF contribution, then the clearing corporation's resources and others' contributions in a defined order.

traps: Option buyers pay premium, not SPAN margin; sellers pay margin.
The F&O ban period starts above 95% of market-wide position limit and ends when it falls below 80%.
Novation makes the clearing corporation the counterparty; exchanges do not guarantee trades directly.
Stock derivatives are physically settled at expiry; index derivatives are cash settled.
items.recap: Order-driven screen trading with UCC and price bands. Clearing corporation becomes central counterparty through novation. Margins: SPAN-type initial margin, exposure or ELM, premium, assignment and delivery margins, all upfront. Futures MTM daily; option premium T+1. Index and currency derivatives cash settle; stock derivatives physically settle. Ban at 95% of MWPL, exit below 80%. Core SGF backs defaults.

items.title: Derivatives Regulation in India: NISM XIII Notes
items.description: SCRA and SEBI Act provisions, RBI's role in currency and interest rate derivatives, committee recommendations, eligibility of stocks and position limits.
items.intro: Exchange-traded derivatives in India sit under several laws and regulators. Equity derivatives are governed by SEBI under SCRA and the SEBI Act, while currency and interest rate derivatives involve RBI because they touch FEMA and monetary policy. Questions test which regulator decides what, the committees that shaped the market and the eligibility criteria for derivatives on stocks.

points.heading: Legal basis
points.text: SCRA's definition of securities was amended in 1999 to include derivatives, allowing exchange trading. Section 18A says derivative contracts are legal and valid if traded on a recognised stock exchange and settled through its clearing house. The SEBI Act gives SEBI power to regulate these exchanges and intermediaries.

points.heading: Committees
points.text: The L.C. Gupta Committee (1998) recommended the regulatory framework for equity derivatives and a phased introduction starting with index futures. The J.R. Varma Committee recommended risk containment measures, including margining based on value at risk. Later committees on currency and interest rate futures were set up jointly by RBI and SEBI.

points.heading: Joint regulation of currency and IRF
points.text: Currency and interest rate derivatives on exchanges are permitted by RBI under FEMA and RBI Act provisions, while SEBI regulates exchange operations, membership and surveillance. Changes such as permitted currency pairs, participant eligibility and exposure requirements are announced through joint or coordinated circulars.

points.heading: Exchange requirements
points.text: A derivatives exchange or segment needs separate approval, a separate clearing corporation or clearing segment, adequate net worth for members, online surveillance and risk management systems, and investor protection measures. Members of the derivatives segment need specific registration.

points.heading: Eligibility of stocks for F&O
points.text: SEBI sets criteria for including stocks in the derivatives segment based on market capitalisation, average daily traded value, and median quarter-sigma order size and market-wide position limits. Stocks that no longer meet criteria are phased out. These criteria are revised periodically, so learn the factors rather than exact numbers.

points.heading: Position limits for participants
points.text: Position limits are prescribed for clients, trading members, FPIs and mutual funds at index and stock level. For currency derivatives, participants who take positions must have an underlying exposure as per RBI's rules. Hedging positions by institutions may receive higher limits.

points.heading: Recent investor protection measures
points.text: SEBI introduced measures in 2024 to curb speculative excess in index derivatives: higher minimum contract size, upfront collection of option premium, intraday monitoring of position limits, removal of calendar spread benefit on expiry day and fewer weekly expiries. Check the latest circulars for exact values.

points.heading: Surveillance and enforcement
points.text: Exchanges run real-time surveillance for manipulation, spoofing, synchronised trades and position limit breaches. Violations attract penalties under exchange bye-laws and action by SEBI under the SEBI Act and PFUTP Regulations.

traps: Section 18A of SCRA validates exchange-traded derivatives; OTC equity derivatives are not covered by it.
L.C. Gupta was about the framework; J.R. Varma was about risk containment and margins.
RBI and SEBI jointly govern exchange-traded currency and interest rate derivatives; SEBI alone does not decide currency pairs.
Stock eligibility for F&O is reviewed periodically; a stock can be removed from the segment.
items.recap: Derivatives became securities under SCRA in 1999; Section 18A validates exchange-traded contracts. L.C. Gupta Committee designed the framework, J.R. Varma Committee the risk management. SEBI regulates equity derivatives; RBI and SEBI jointly regulate currency and interest rate derivatives. Stocks must meet SEBI eligibility criteria. Position limits apply to clients, members, FPIs and MFs.

items.title: Accounting and Tax for Derivatives: NISM XIII Notes
items.description: Accounting entries for futures margins, MTM and option premium, tax treatment of F&O income as business income, STT and tax audit turnover, revised clearly.
items.intro: This short chapter covers how derivative transactions are recorded in books and taxed in India. Questions test where margin and MTM entries go, how option premium is treated, why F&O income is non-speculative business income, and how turnover is computed for tax audit. Tax rates change, so remember the principle and check the current rate from the income tax department.

points.heading: Accounting for futures margin
points.text: Initial margin paid to the broker or clearing member is recorded as a current asset (deposit), not an expense. When margin is in the form of bank guarantee or securities, it is disclosed rather than booked as cash. The margin returns when positions are closed.

points.heading: Accounting for daily MTM
points.text: MTM received or paid is credited or debited to a separate MTM account, a current asset or liability. On final settlement or squaring off, the net balance is transferred to profit and loss. Unrealised losses on open positions at the balance sheet date are provided for under prudent accounting.

points.heading: Accounting for options
points.text: Premium paid by the buyer is shown as a current asset until expiry or exercise; premium received by the seller is a current liability. On expiry or exercise, the premium is transferred to profit and loss. Companies following Ind AS treat derivatives as financial instruments measured at fair value.

points.heading: Tax nature of F&O income
points.text: Under Section 43(5) of the Income-tax Act, derivative transactions on a recognised exchange are excluded from 'speculative transactions'. So income or loss from F&O trading is taxed as non-speculative business income. Losses can be set off against other business income and carried forward for eight years.

points.heading: Intraday equity is different
points.text: Intraday equity cash trades (no delivery) are speculative business, while F&O is non-speculative. Confusing the two is a common error. Investors using F&O for hedging also report results as business income.

points.heading: Securities transaction tax
points.text: STT is charged on the sale of futures (on traded value) and on the sale of options (on premium) as well as on exercised options (on settlement value). Rates were increased in 2024; as of 2026 check the current rates on the income tax department website. STT paid on business transactions is allowed as a deduction from business income.

points.heading: Turnover for tax audit
points.text: For F&O, turnover is the aggregate of absolute profits and losses on each trade (positive and negative differences), plus premium received on sale of options where included in profit computation, as per ICAI guidance. Tax audit applicability depends on this turnover and on profit levels under Section 44AB.

points.heading: Currency and interest rate derivatives
points.text: Exchange-traded currency and interest rate derivatives are also excluded from speculative transactions and taxed as business income. STT does not apply to them, but stamp duty and exchange charges do.

traps: F&O income is non-speculative business income, not capital gains and not speculative income.
Initial margin is a deposit (asset), not an expense.
STT on options is charged on premium for sale, but on settlement value when exercised.
F&O turnover for tax audit is the sum of absolute profits and losses, not total contract value traded.
items.recap: Margins are assets; MTM goes to a separate account and to P&L on settlement; option premium is a current asset for buyers and a liability for sellers until expiry. F&O on recognised exchanges is non-speculative business income under Section 43(5); losses carry forward eight years. STT applies to equity derivatives, not currency or IRF. Turnover equals absolute profits plus losses.

items.chapter: Sales Practices, Code of Conduct & Investor Protection
items.title: Derivatives Sales Practices and Investor Protection
items.description: Know your client, suitability, risk disclosures, conflicts, code of conduct, grievance redressal and investor protection funds for derivatives sales staff.
items.intro: Derivatives can cause losses larger than an investor expects, so NISM XIII ends with how intermediaries should sell and service them. The chapter covers KYC, suitability, risk disclosure, the code of conduct for brokers and staff, investor grievance mechanisms and investor protection funds. Questions are scenario-based: pick the most ethical or compliant action.

points.heading: Know your client
points.text: Before activating derivatives trading, the broker must complete KYC and collect financial details. SEBI requires proof of financial capacity, such as bank statements, ITR or net worth certificate, for the derivatives segment. A student with no income asking to trade options should prompt closer review.

points.heading: Suitability
points.text: Staff should match products to the client's knowledge, objectives and risk capacity. Recommending option selling to a retiree who needs stable income is unsuitable even if the client is willing. Documenting the assessment protects both client and firm.

points.heading: Risk disclosure
points.text: Clients must receive the risk disclosure document explaining leverage, possibility of losing more than the margin, liquidity risk and the effect of margin calls. SEBI also requires brokers to display a risk disclosure about F&O losses on login, based on SEBI's study showing that a large majority of individual F&O traders made net losses.

points.heading: No assured returns
points.text: Sales staff must never promise profits, guaranteed income or 'sure-shot' tips. Advertising past profits of other clients or showing back-tested results as if achieved is misleading. Stock tips through messaging groups by unregistered persons are a regulatory concern.

points.heading: Code of conduct for brokers
points.text: Brokers must act with integrity, due skill and care, avoid conflicts, not churn client accounts for brokerage, execute orders promptly at the best available price, maintain confidentiality, and issue contract notes and statements on time. Employees should follow the firm's personal trading policy.

points.heading: Handling client funds
points.text: Client funds must be kept in client accounts and used only for that client's obligations. Brokers should not lend client securities or use them for their own margin without authorisation through the prescribed mechanism. Running accounts must be settled periodically.

points.heading: Grievance redressal
points.text: Clients should first complain to the broker. Unresolved issues can go to the exchange investor services cell, to SEBI's SCORES portal, and then to the online dispute resolution platform (conciliation and arbitration) set up through MIIs. Each step has defined timelines.

points.heading: Investor protection funds
points.text: Exchanges and depositories maintain investor protection funds to compensate investors when a broker is declared a defaulter, within limits per investor. The funds also support investor awareness programmes. Compensation covers genuine claims against defaulting members, not trading losses.

traps: Investor protection funds compensate for a broker's default, not for market losses on trades.
A client's consent does not make an unsuitable recommendation acceptable.
Financial proof is needed to enable derivatives trading, not merely a PAN and address.
Escalation starts with the broker; SCORES comes after the intermediary has had a chance to resolve the complaint.
items.recap: Complete KYC and financial proof before enabling F&O. Recommend only suitable products and document it. Give the risk disclosure document and never promise returns. Follow the broker code: integrity, no churning, best execution, timely contract notes, segregated client funds. Complaints: broker, exchange, SCORES, ODR. IPFs compensate for broker default, not trading losses.

items.title: Commodity Markets in India: NISM XVI Revision Notes
items.description: Types of commodities, spot and derivatives markets, history from FCRA to SEBI, exchanges, warehousing and participants in Indian commodity markets, revised.
items.intro: The first chapter of NISM Series XVI introduces commodities as an asset class and traces how Indian commodity markets evolved. It covers spot and derivatives markets, the shift of regulation from the Forward Markets Commission to SEBI, the national exchanges, and the role of warehousing. Questions are mostly factual: dates, institutions, classifications and the reasons commodity derivatives exist.

points.heading: What makes a commodity
points.text: A commodity is a basic good that is broadly interchangeable with other units of the same grade, such as wheat of a defined quality, gold of 995 purity or crude oil of a stated grade. Standardisation of grade and quantity is what allows commodities to be traded on exchanges.

points.heading: Classification
points.text: Commodities are usually grouped as agricultural (cereals, pulses, oilseeds, spices, cotton, guar), metals (precious such as gold and silver; base metals such as copper, zinc, aluminium) and energy (crude oil, natural gas). Agricultural commodities are seasonal and perishable, so storage and quality matter more.

points.heading: Spot markets
points.text: Physical commodities trade in mandis regulated under state APMC laws, through traders and commission agents, and increasingly through electronic platforms like e-NAM. Spot prices vary by location and quality. Fragmented spot markets are one reason futures prices provide a useful national reference.

points.heading: Evolution of regulation
points.text: Commodity futures were regulated under the Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952 by the Forward Markets Commission. In 2003 national multi-commodity exchanges were set up. In September 2015 the FMC merged with SEBI and the FCRA was repealed; commodity derivatives became securities under SCRA.

points.heading: Exchanges
points.text: MCX is the largest exchange for metals and energy; NCDEX focuses on agricultural commodities. NSE and BSE also offer commodity derivatives after SEBI allowed universal exchanges in 2018. Each exchange works with a clearing corporation, such as MCXCCL for MCX.

points.heading: Why commodity derivatives
points.text: They let farmers, traders, processors, jewellers and importers hedge price risk, support price discovery across the country, and give investors exposure to commodities. A dal mill can lock in the price of tur months ahead, and a jeweller can hedge gold inventory.

points.heading: Participants
points.text: Hedgers (producers, processors, exporters, importers), speculators, arbitrageurs, and institutional participants such as mutual funds, AIFs, portfolio managers and eligible foreign entities with exposure to Indian commodities. Farmer producer organisations (FPOs) aggregate small farmers to use exchanges.

points.heading: Warehousing
points.text: Delivery-based commodity contracts need accredited warehouses, assayers to certify quality and electronic warehouse receipts. The Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (WDRA), under the 2007 Act, regulates warehouses issuing negotiable warehouse receipts, which can be used as collateral for loans.

traps: FMC merged into SEBI in September 2015; FCRA was repealed then, and SCRA now governs commodity derivatives.
NCDEX is agri-focused; MCX dominates metals and energy.
WDRA regulates warehouses and receipts; it does not regulate commodity exchanges.
Standardised grade and quantity are essential for exchange trading; unique goods cannot be commoditised.
items.recap: Commodities are standardised, interchangeable goods: agri, metals, energy. Spot trade happens in APMC mandis and e-NAM. FCRA 1952 and FMC regulated futures until the 2015 merger with SEBI; SCRA now applies. MCX leads metals and energy, NCDEX agri; NSE and BSE also trade. Participants include hedgers, speculators, arbitrageurs, FPOs and institutions. WDRA regulates warehouse receipts.

items.title: Commodity Indices and Index Futures: NISM XVI Notes
items.description: Why commodity indices exist, how weights are set, roll yield, sector indices, MCX iCOMDEX and cash-settled bullion index futures, explained for revision.
items.intro: Commodity indices summarise price movements across a basket of commodities and can be traded through index futures. This short chapter covers why indices exist, how they are constructed, the effect of rolling futures, and examples from Indian exchanges. Questions test construction choices, the difference between spot and futures-based indices, and features of index futures such as cash settlement.

points.heading: Purpose
points.text: Indices show broad commodity price trends, serve as benchmarks for funds, help measure inflation pressures and provide an underlying for index derivatives. A rising composite commodity index can signal input cost pressure for manufacturers before it shows in retail inflation.

points.heading: Futures-based construction
points.text: Most investable commodity indices are built from futures prices rather than spot, because futures are traded, transparent and easy to replicate. The index rolls from the near-month contract to the next before expiry, according to a published schedule.

points.heading: Weighting methods
points.text: Weights can be based on production value, trading liquidity, or a combination, with caps to prevent one commodity or sector from dominating. For example, a composite index may cap energy so that a crude oil spike does not swamp agricultural signals.

points.heading: Roll yield
points.text: When the index rolls, it sells the expiring contract and buys the next one. In backwardation (next contract cheaper), rolling adds return; in contango (next contract dearer), rolling reduces return. This is why index returns can differ from spot price changes.

points.heading: Indian examples
points.text: MCX publishes the iCOMDEX family, including a composite index and sectoral indices for bullion, base metals and energy. NCDEX has had agricultural indices. MCX launched bullion index futures (BULLDEX) and later other index futures, which are cash settled.

points.heading: Index futures features
points.text: Commodity index futures are cash settled because delivering a basket is impractical. They allow a trader to take a view on a whole sector, such as bullion, with one contract. Margins and position limits are set by the exchange and clearing corporation.

points.heading: Uses for investors and hedgers
points.text: A jewellery company can hedge broad bullion exposure with a bullion index contract; a fund can gain diversified commodity exposure. Since indices may not match a specific hedger's input exactly, basis risk remains.

points.heading: Rebalancing and governance
points.text: Index providers periodically review constituents and weights, publish methodology documents and have index committees. Changes are announced in advance so that users can adjust positions.

traps: Roll yield is positive in backwardation and negative in contango.
Commodity index futures are cash settled, not delivery based.
Most investable commodity indices use futures prices, not mandi spot prices.
Capping weights is a design choice to avoid concentration, not a regulatory requirement for all indices.
items.recap: Commodity indices track baskets for benchmarking, inflation signals and trading. Investable indices use futures, roll according to a schedule and are weighted by production or liquidity with caps. Roll yield helps in backwardation, hurts in contango. MCX iCOMDEX includes composite and sector indices; index futures like BULLDEX are cash settled. Basis risk remains for hedgers.

items.title: Commodity Futures Pricing and Contracts: XVI Notes
items.description: Contract specifications, delivery types, cost of carry with storage and convenience yield, basis and backwardation in commodity futures, with examples.
items.intro: Commodity futures are the core product in NISM XVI and carry the most questions. The chapter covers contract specifications, settlement types, pricing through the cost of carry including storage and insurance, convenience yield, basis and the behaviour of futures prices near expiry. Practise a few fair value calculations and memorise the meaning of each specification field.

points.heading: Contract specifications
points.text: Each contract specifies the commodity and its quality, trading unit, delivery unit, price quote basis (for example ₹ per 10 grams for gold, ₹ per quintal for many agri goods), tick size, daily price limits, delivery centres and expiry date. A gold mini contract and a gold contract differ in lot size, not quality.

points.heading: Settlement types
points.text: Contracts can be compulsory delivery (all open positions at expiry must deliver or take delivery), both-option delivery (delivery only when both buyer and seller choose it) or cash settled. Many agricultural contracts on NCDEX are compulsory delivery; some metals and energy contracts on MCX are cash settled against international benchmarks.

points.heading: Cost of carry
points.text: Fair futures price = spot + interest cost + storage + insurance - convenience yield. If chana spot is ₹5,500 per quintal, interest is 9% a year, and storage and insurance cost ₹40 for three months: fair futures is about 5,500 + 124 + 40 = ₹5,664, ignoring convenience yield.

points.heading: Convenience yield
points.text: Holding the physical commodity gives benefits, such as keeping a factory running during shortages. This convenience yield lowers the futures price relative to spot. When stocks are tight, convenience yield can exceed carry costs and push futures below spot (backwardation).

points.heading: Basis
points.text: Basis is spot minus futures. It reflects carry costs, local supply and demand, and quality and location differences. A strong local harvest can widen negative basis at a mandi far from the delivery centre. At expiry, basis for delivery-centre spot converges toward zero.

points.heading: Seasonality
points.text: Agricultural prices are influenced by sowing, monsoon and harvest. Futures for months after harvest often trade lower than those before harvest. Traders and hedgers watch crop estimates, MSP announcements and import duty changes.

points.heading: Tender and delivery period
points.text: Before expiry, compulsory-delivery contracts enter a tender or staggered delivery period when sellers can give intention to deliver. Additional delivery period margins apply. Buyers receive goods through accredited warehouses with quality certified by assayers.

points.heading: Price limits
points.text: Daily price limits (DPL) cap how far prices can move in a day, with relaxation after a cooling-off period if the limit is hit. International-linked contracts like gold and crude have wider or flexible bands that follow global prices.

formulas: Fair futures price = spot x (1 + r x t) + storage + insurance - convenience yield.
Basis = spot price - futures price.
traps: Convenience yield reduces the fair futures price; storage and insurance increase it.
Both-option delivery requires both buyer and seller to opt for delivery; otherwise it cash settles.
Mini contracts differ in size, not in the grade of the commodity.
Backwardation in commodities is common during shortages because of high convenience yield.
items.recap: Commodity futures specify quality, unit, quote, tick, DPL, delivery centre and expiry. Settlement: compulsory delivery, both-option or cash. Fair value = spot + interest + storage + insurance - convenience yield. Basis = spot minus futures and converges at expiry. Seasonality drives agri prices. Delivery via accredited warehouses and assayers, with tender period and delivery margins.

items.title: Commodity Options on Futures and Goods: XVI Notes
items.description: Options on commodity futures and on goods, devolvement into futures, moneyness, Black-76 pricing, Greeks and settlement rules in Indian commodity options.
items.intro: SEBI allowed commodity options in 2017, starting with options on gold futures on MCX, and later permitted options on goods that settle directly by delivery. This chapter covers how these options work, how they settle at expiry, pricing factors and Greeks. Questions often test devolvement, the difference between options on futures and options on goods, and payoff basics.

points.heading: Options on futures
points.text: In an option on futures, the underlying is a futures contract of the same commodity. On exercise, the option devolves into a futures position: a long call becomes a long futures position at the strike, and the counterparty gets the short futures position. The futures then follow their own settlement rules.

points.heading: Options on goods
points.text: In options on goods (introduced later), the underlying is the physical commodity itself. ITM options at expiry result in delivery of the goods, giving hedgers a direct route to physical settlement without first going through futures.

points.heading: Style and exercise
points.text: Commodity options in India are European style: they can be exercised only on expiry day. In-the-money options are exercised automatically unless the holder gives a contrary instruction within the window allowed by the exchange, which is useful for near-the-money strikes where costs may exceed value.

points.heading: Moneyness and payoff
points.text: A gold call option with strike ₹72,000 per 10 g is ITM when gold futures trade at ₹72,800. Intrinsic value is ₹800 per 10 g. Buyer's maximum loss is the premium; seller's loss can be large. Payoff logic is the same as in equity options.

points.heading: Pricing
points.text: Options on futures are typically priced using the Black-76 model, a variant of Black-Scholes using the futures price instead of spot and no separate carry term. Inputs: futures price, strike, time, volatility and interest rate. Higher volatility raises both call and put premiums.

points.heading: Greeks
points.text: Delta shows change in premium per unit change in the futures price; gamma shows how fast delta changes; theta shows time decay; vega shows sensitivity to volatility. A farmer who buys puts is long vega: if volatility rises during a monsoon scare, the puts gain value.

points.heading: Uses for hedgers
points.text: A producer can buy puts to set a floor price while keeping upside; a processor can buy calls to cap input costs. Options cost a premium upfront but avoid margin calls that futures hedgers face, which suits small hedgers with limited working capital.

points.heading: Margins and settlement
points.text: Buyers pay the full premium upfront; sellers pay initial and exposure margins. Near expiry, sellers and ITM buyers may face additional margins because positions may devolve into futures or delivery. Premium is settled on T+1.

traps: Options on futures devolve into futures positions; they do not directly deliver the commodity.
Indian commodity options are European, exercisable only on expiry.
