Option buyers pay premium, not margin; sellers pay margin.
Black-76 uses the futures price as the underlying, not the spot price.
items.recap: Commodity options began in 2017 with options on gold futures. Options on futures devolve into futures; options on goods settle in the physical commodity. European style with auto-exercise of ITM options unless contrary instruction. Priced with Black-76; Greeks as in equity. Hedgers buy puts for a floor or calls for a cap. Buyers pay premium; sellers pay margins.

items.chapter: Strategies using Commodity Futures and Options
items.title: Commodity Hedging and Spread Strategies: XVI Notes
items.description: Short and long hedges, hedge ratios, basis risk, calendar and inter-commodity spreads, arbitrage and option strategies for farmers, processors and traders.
items.intro: This chapter applies futures and options to real business problems: a farmer protecting harvest prices, a mill fixing raw material cost, a jeweller managing inventory and traders exploiting spreads. Questions are scenario-based and often include a small calculation of the effective price after hedging. Think through who is exposed to rising or falling prices before choosing a position.

points.heading: Short hedge for producers
points.text: A soybean farmer or a stockist holding inventory fears falling prices and sells futures. If spot falls from ₹4,800 to ₹4,500 per quintal and futures fall by a similar amount, the futures gain offsets the lower spot sale, giving an effective price close to the original level.

points.heading: Long hedge for consumers
points.text: A refinery, mill or jeweller that must buy later fears rising prices and buys futures. A cotton mill buying cotton futures in March for October requirements locks in an input cost; if prices rise, futures gains offset the higher purchase price.

points.heading: Basis risk
points.text: Hedges are imperfect when the local spot price moves differently from the futures price because of location, quality or timing. A farmer in a region with a bumper crop may see local prices fall more than futures. The effective price = futures price at hedge + basis at close.

points.heading: Hedge ratio
points.text: The hedge ratio is the number of futures units per unit of exposure. A simple hedge uses a ratio of one. When the hedged item differs from the contract commodity, the optimal ratio is based on correlation and relative volatility of price changes.

points.heading: Calendar spreads
points.text: Buy one month and sell another month of the same commodity to profit from changes in the price difference. If the June-August gold spread is unusually wide relative to carry cost, a trader can sell August and buy June. Spreads have lower margins because the legs offset.

points.heading: Inter-commodity spreads
points.text: Trade related commodities, such as the soybean crush spread (soybean versus soy oil and soymeal) or the crack spread (crude versus refined products). A processor's margin depends on these spreads, so spreads can hedge processing margins.

points.heading: Arbitrage
points.text: Cash and carry arbitrage: buy spot and sell futures when futures exceed fair value including storage and insurance, then deliver at expiry. Inter-exchange arbitrage exploits price differences of the same commodity on two exchanges or between Indian and international prices adjusted for duty and currency.

points.heading: Option strategies
points.text: Farmers can buy puts to set a minimum price while keeping upside. Processors can buy calls to cap costs. A collar (buy put, sell call) reduces premium cost but limits upside. Covered call writing by stockists earns premium on inventory.

formulas: Effective price for a short hedger = initial futures price + basis at the time of closing (basis = spot - futures).
Minimum variance hedge ratio = correlation x (standard deviation of spot changes / standard deviation of futures changes).
traps: Producers and stockists hedge by selling futures; consumers and processors hedge by buying.
A perfect hedge exists only when basis does not change; basis risk is the residual risk.
Spread positions usually have lower margins than outright positions because the legs offset.
Buying puts gives a floor price without margin calls, but costs premium upfront.
items.recap: Producers and stockists sell futures (short hedge); consumers and processors buy (long hedge). Basis risk remains: effective price = initial futures + closing basis. Hedge ratio may differ from one when commodities differ. Calendar and inter-commodity spreads (crush, crack) trade price differences. Arbitrage compares futures with full carry cost. Puts give floors, calls give caps, collars reduce cost.

items.title: Commodity Derivatives Trading Mechanism: XVI Notes
items.description: Trading sessions, order types, UCC, price limits, position limits, contract launch calendar and member structure on Indian commodity exchanges, in brief.
items.intro: This chapter describes how commodity derivatives are actually traded: the membership structure, trading hours, order types, client codes, price limits and position limits. Questions are practical and procedural, asking which order type fits a need, what happens when a daily price limit is hit, or why agricultural and international commodities have different trading hours.

points.heading: Membership
points.text: Trading members execute trades for themselves and clients; clearing members clear and settle trades. Members are registered with SEBI as stock brokers in the commodity derivatives segment. Clients deal through members who must complete KYC and provide rights and obligations and risk disclosure documents.

points.heading: Trading hours
points.text: Agricultural commodities usually trade during Indian daytime hours, close to physical market activity. Metals and energy, which are linked to global prices, trade till late night to overlap with international markets such as London and New York. Exact timings are set by exchanges and change with daylight saving in the US.

points.heading: Order-driven matching
points.text: Exchanges run anonymous order-driven electronic platforms matched on price-time priority. The best buy and best sell orders are shown in the order book. Each order carries a Unique Client Code so trades can be traced to the client.

points.heading: Order types
points.text: Limit orders specify the maximum buy or minimum sell price; market orders execute at the best available price; stop-loss orders trigger when price reaches a set level; immediate-or-cancel orders execute what is possible immediately and cancel the rest. Good-till-cancelled or good-till-date orders stay until executed or expiry where offered.

points.heading: Daily price limits
points.text: Each contract has a DPL, for example a few percent around the previous close. When a limit is hit, trading may pause for a cooling-off period and the limit may then be relaxed by a further amount. Internationally linked contracts may have dynamic limits that track global prices.

points.heading: Position limits
points.text: Exchanges and SEBI set client-level and member-level position limits, often as a percentage of market-wide open interest or a fixed quantity, whichever is higher. Agri commodities have tighter limits to prevent hoarding-type speculation. Hedgers can seek higher limits with proof of exposure.

points.heading: Contract launch and expiry
points.text: Exchanges publish a calendar of contracts with launch and expiry dates. Several months are available at once; the near month is usually most liquid. Before expiry, positions in delivery contracts enter the tender or staggered delivery period.

points.heading: Surveillance
points.text: Exchanges monitor price and volume patterns, concentrated positions and synchronised trades. They can impose special margins, restrict new positions or suspend contracts in extreme cases, such as sharp unexplained price spikes in a thinly traded agri commodity.

traps: International-linked commodities trade late into the night; agri contracts mostly trade during the day.
An IOC order cancels any unexecuted portion immediately; it does not wait in the book.
Hitting the daily price limit triggers a cooling-off and possible relaxation, not automatic closure for the day in every case.
Hedgers can get higher position limits only with documented underlying exposure.
items.recap: Members registered with SEBI trade and clear for clients with KYC and UCC. Agri contracts trade daytime; metals and energy till late night. Price-time priority matching; limit, market, stop-loss and IOC orders. Daily price limits with cooling-off and relaxation. Client and member position limits, tighter for agri, with hedger exemptions. Exchanges publish contract calendars and run surveillance.

items.title: Commodity Clearing, Margins and Delivery: NISM XVI
items.description: Clearing corporations, initial, extreme loss and delivery margins, MTM, warehouse delivery, assaying and settlement guarantee funds in commodities.
items.intro: Clearing and settlement in commodities includes everything seen in equity derivatives plus physical delivery through warehouses. This chapter covers the clearing corporation's role, margin types peculiar to commodities, mark-to-market, the delivery process with accredited warehouses and assayers, and default protection. Questions often test margin names, delivery steps and who certifies quality.

points.heading: Clearing corporation
points.text: Each commodity exchange settles through a recognised clearing corporation that becomes the counterparty to every trade by novation. It computes obligations, collects margins and settles funds and goods. Clearing members are responsible for the trades of their clients and trading members.

points.heading: Initial and extreme loss margin
points.text: Initial margin covers the likely one-day loss, computed through a portfolio-based risk model at a high confidence level. Extreme loss margin covers losses beyond that. Both must be collected upfront from clients. Margins rise when volatility rises.

points.heading: Additional and special margins
points.text: Exchanges can levy additional or special margins when prices move sharply or when a contract shows concentration, for example during a sudden surge in guar or cotton prices. These are temporary measures to curb excessive speculation.

points.heading: Pre-expiry and delivery margins
points.text: As expiry approaches, delivery contracts carry staggered pre-expiry margins that rise each day. During the tender or delivery period, delivery period margins apply to positions that will result in delivery, so that a defaulting buyer or seller does not disrupt settlement.

points.heading: Mark to market
points.text: Futures positions are marked to market daily at the settlement price. Profits are paid and losses collected in cash on the next working day. Failure to pay MTM leads to the member being restricted from trading and positions being closed.

points.heading: Delivery process
points.text: Sellers deposit goods in exchange-accredited warehouses, where assayers check quality against contract specifications. Electronic negotiable warehouse receipts are created in a repository. On settlement, the buyer pays funds and receives the warehouse receipt, then can lift the goods or keep them stored.

points.heading: Quality and penalties
points.text: Goods within an allowed range of quality may be accepted with premiums or discounts. Goods below the minimum grade are rejected. Sellers who fail to deliver face penalties, and the buyer receives compensation according to exchange rules.

points.heading: Settlement guarantee fund
points.text: The clearing corporation maintains a core settlement guarantee fund to complete settlement if a member defaults. The default waterfall uses the defaulter's margins and contributions first, then the clearing corporation's own resources and other contributions in order.

traps: Assayers certify quality; warehouses store goods; the clearing corporation settles. Each role is separate.
Delivery period margins are charged on positions headed for delivery, in addition to normal margins.
MTM is settled in cash daily, even in delivery-based contracts.
Goods slightly off-grade may be accepted at a discount; only below minimum grade are rejected.
items.recap: Clearing corporation novates every trade and settles funds and goods. Margins: initial, extreme loss, additional or special, pre-expiry staggered and delivery period margins, all upfront. Daily cash MTM. Delivery through accredited warehouses with assayers and electronic warehouse receipts; quality premiums and discounts apply. Core SGF and default waterfall protect settlement.

items.title: Commodity Derivatives Regulation: NISM XVI Notes
items.description: Repeal of FCRA, SEBI as regulator under SCRA, WDRA, institutional participants, position limits and product approval for Indian commodity derivatives.
items.intro: Commodity derivatives moved from a separate regulatory world into the securities framework in 2015. This chapter covers the legal foundation, SEBI's powers, related regulators such as WDRA, and rules on who may participate. Exam questions test dates, the legal status of commodity derivatives, institutional participation and the role of exchanges in surveillance.

points.heading: From FCRA to SCRA
points.text: The Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952 and the Forward Markets Commission regulated commodity futures for decades. The Finance Act, 2015 repealed FCRA and merged FMC with SEBI from 28 September 2015. Commodity derivatives were added to the definition of securities under SCRA.

points.heading: SEBI's powers
points.text: SEBI now recognises commodity exchanges, registers members as stock brokers, approves new contracts, sets margin and position limit frameworks, and enforces rules against manipulation using the SEBI Act and PFUTP Regulations. Its commodity derivatives department handles policy.

points.heading: Product approval
points.text: Exchanges must obtain SEBI approval to launch a commodity contract. SEBI looks at the commodity's market size, spot price transparency, deliverability and susceptibility to manipulation. Some sensitive agri commodities have had trading suspended in the interest of controlling food inflation.

points.heading: WDRA and warehouses
points.text: The Warehousing (Development and Regulation) Act, 2007 created WDRA, which registers warehouses and regulates negotiable warehouse receipts. SEBI requires exchanges to use WDRA-registered or accredited warehouses for delivery of agri commodities.

points.heading: Institutional participation
points.text: Since 2018-19 SEBI has allowed category III AIFs, portfolio managers and mutual funds (through specified schemes) to participate, with limits. Eligible foreign entities with actual exposure to Indian commodities can participate in specified non-agri contracts. Banks have limited participation subject to RBI rules.

points.heading: Position limits and hedge exemption
points.text: SEBI prescribes client-level and member-level position limits for agri and non-agri commodities. Hedgers can obtain hedge limits from exchanges based on underlying exposure, verified by documents such as stock statements or contracts.

points.heading: Universal exchange
points.text: In 2018 SEBI allowed exchanges to offer equity and commodity derivatives under one roof. So NSE and BSE introduced commodities and MCX introduced other products, increasing competition.

points.heading: Investor protection
points.text: Commodity brokers are subject to the same KYC, client fund segregation, grievance redressal, SCORES and ODR framework as equity brokers. Exchanges maintain investor protection funds for commodity segments.

traps: The FMC-SEBI merger took effect in September 2015, not 2003 (when national commodity exchanges began).
Commodity derivatives are now securities under SCRA; FCRA no longer applies.
WDRA regulates warehouses and receipts, not the exchanges or brokers.
SEBI approval is required before an exchange launches a new commodity contract.
items.recap: FCRA was repealed and FMC merged with SEBI on 28 September 2015; commodity derivatives became securities under SCRA. SEBI recognises exchanges, registers brokers, approves contracts and enforces anti-manipulation rules. WDRA regulates warehouses under the 2007 Act. Category III AIFs, PMS, MFs and eligible foreign entities may participate within limits. Universal exchanges allowed from 2018.

items.title: Tax and Accounting for Commodity Derivatives: XVI
items.description: Commodity transaction tax, non-speculative status of exchange commodity derivatives, accounting for margins, MTM and options, and GST on delivery, simplified.
items.intro: This short chapter explains how commodity derivative transactions are recorded and taxed. Key points are the commodity transaction tax, the treatment of exchange-traded commodity derivatives as non-speculative business income, accounting entries for margin and mark-to-market, and the GST implications when contracts end in physical delivery. Rates change, so focus on principles.

points.heading: Commodity transaction tax
points.text: CTT, introduced through the Finance Act 2013, is levied on the sale of non-agricultural commodity derivatives traded on recognised exchanges, such as gold, crude oil and copper futures. Specified agricultural commodities are exempt. Check current rates on the income tax department website.

points.heading: Non-speculative business income
points.text: Section 43(5) treats eligible transactions in commodity derivatives on recognised exchanges, on which CTT is chargeable, as non-speculative. Agri commodity derivatives exempt from CTT were also brought within non-speculative treatment by later amendments. Income or loss is taxed as business income.

points.heading: Set-off and carry forward
points.text: Non-speculative business losses from commodity derivatives can be set off against other business income (and, in the same year, against other heads except salary) and carried forward for eight years against business income. CTT paid is deductible when computing business income.

points.heading: Accounting for margins
points.text: Initial and additional margins paid are recorded as current assets in a margin deposit account. Margins in the form of securities or bank guarantees are disclosed but not booked as cash.

points.heading: Accounting for MTM
points.text: Daily MTM is passed through a mark-to-market account. At the reporting date, net debit balances on open positions are provided for as losses, while net credit balances are usually ignored under prudence. On final settlement, the balance is taken to profit and loss.

points.heading: Accounting for options
points.text: Premium paid is carried as an asset and premium received as a liability until expiry, exercise or squaring off. On exercise of options on futures, the premium is adjusted against the resulting futures position as per applicable guidance.

points.heading: GST on delivery
points.text: When a contract results in delivery of goods, GST applies on the supply at the rate applicable to that commodity. The seller must be GST-registered where required, and the exchange and clearing corporation handle invoicing through prescribed procedures. Cash-settled contracts involve no supply of goods.

points.heading: Hedging accounting
points.text: Companies that hedge raw material or inventory may use hedge accounting under Ind AS 109 if documentation and effectiveness tests are met, so that gains and losses on the hedge are matched with the hedged item.

traps: CTT applies to non-agricultural commodity derivatives; specified agri commodities are exempt.
Exchange-traded commodity derivative income is non-speculative business income, not capital gains.
Net unrealised MTM losses are provided for; unrealised gains are generally not recognised under prudence.
GST arises only when there is physical delivery, not on cash-settled positions.
items.recap: CTT is charged on sale of non-agri commodity derivatives; specified agri ones are exempt. Exchange commodity derivatives are non-speculative business income under Section 43(5); losses carry forward eight years and CTT is deductible. Margins are assets; MTM via separate account with provision for net losses. Premiums are assets or liabilities till settlement. GST applies on delivery.

items.chapter: Codes of Conduct and Investor Protection
items.title: Commodity Broker Conduct and Investor Protection
items.description: KYC, suitability, risk disclosure, broker code of conduct, client fund rules, SCORES, ODR and investor protection funds for commodity derivatives clients.
items.intro: The final chapter of NISM XVI sets out how commodity derivatives brokers and their staff must treat clients. It covers client onboarding, risk disclosure, the broker code of conduct, handling of client funds, grievance redressal and investor protection funds. Questions are mostly scenario-based ethics questions: identify the correct conduct or the right escalation route.

points.heading: Client onboarding
points.text: Brokers must complete KYC, collect the account opening form and financial information, provide rights and obligations, the risk disclosure document and the tariff sheet, and allot a UCC. Financial proof is required before activating derivatives trading.

points.heading: Hedger versus speculator profile
points.text: Understanding whether a client is a hedger (farmer, trader, processor) or a speculator helps the broker explain products and margin needs properly. A farmer producer organisation hedging soybean needs explanation of delivery rules, not leveraged trading tips.

points.heading: Risk disclosure
points.text: Clients must be told that leverage can cause losses beyond the initial margin, that prices can hit limits and become illiquid, that delivery obligations may arise at expiry, and that international events can move prices overnight.

points.heading: Broker code of conduct
points.text: Brokers must act with integrity, due skill and care, avoid misleading statements, not promise returns, avoid churning, execute orders at the best available price, keep client information confidential and maintain adequate infrastructure and qualified staff.

points.heading: Client funds and margins
points.text: Client funds must be kept separate from the broker's own and used only for that client's obligations. Margins must be collected upfront and reported accurately. Running account settlement returns idle funds periodically.

points.heading: Contract notes and statements
points.text: Contract notes must be sent within 24 hours of trades, and periodic statements of funds and positions must be provided, so clients can verify every transaction.

points.heading: Grievance redressal
points.text: Complaints go first to the broker, then to the exchange's investor services, then to SEBI's SCORES portal, and disputes can be taken to the online dispute resolution platform for conciliation and arbitration.

points.heading: Unregistered tips and advice
points.text: Staff should not forward commodity tips from unregistered sources or run paid advisory groups. Giving recommendations for a fee needs SEBI registration as an investment adviser or research analyst. Exchanges also warn investors against dummy or 'dabba' trading platforms that operate outside the exchange system and offer no protection.

points.heading: Investor protection fund
points.text: Commodity exchanges maintain investor protection funds to compensate clients of defaulting members for genuine claims, within prescribed limits, and to finance investor education such as farmer awareness programmes.

traps: IPF compensation covers member default, not trading losses or price movements.
Promising assured returns on commodity trading violates the code of conduct.
Delivery obligations must be explained to clients holding positions in compulsory-delivery contracts near expiry.
Complaints must normally go to the broker first before SCORES.
items.recap: Onboard with KYC, financial proof, UCC, rights and obligations and risk disclosure. Understand whether the client hedges or speculates. Never promise returns or churn. Segregate client funds, collect margins upfront, send contract notes within 24 hours. Escalate complaints from broker to exchange to SCORES to ODR. IPFs compensate for broker default only.

items.title: Retirement Planning Overview: NISM XVII Revision Notes
items.description: Why retirement planning matters in India, longevity and inflation risk, life stages, and inflating today's expenses into the future, with worked numbers.
items.intro: NISM Series XVII (Retirement Adviser) opens with why individuals in India must plan for retirement themselves and what makes it different from other goals. The chapter covers demographic and social trends, the main risks retirees face and the accumulation and distribution phases. Expect conceptual questions plus a simple future-value calculation of expenses under inflation.

points.heading: Why planning matters now
points.text: Indians are living longer, joint families are giving way to nuclear households, and most private-sector and self-employed workers have no defined-benefit pension. Rising healthcare costs add pressure. The result is that an individual's own savings must fund 20 to 30 years of retired life.

points.heading: Longevity risk
points.text: Longevity risk is the risk of outliving one's savings. Planning to age 85 when a client lives to 95 can leave ten unfunded years. Advisers usually plan for a life expectancy well above the average, especially for the younger spouse in a couple.

points.heading: Inflation risk
points.text: Inflation erodes purchasing power over long retirements. At 6% inflation, prices roughly double every 12 years. Monthly expenses of ₹40,000 today will be about ₹40,000 x (1.06)^20 = ₹1.28 lakh in 20 years. Fixed-income-only portfolios struggle against this.

points.heading: Other risks
points.text: Retirees also face interest rate risk (falling FD rates reduce income), market risk, sequence-of-returns risk (poor returns early in retirement hurt more), health risk, and the risk of financial dependence or fraud. A plan must address each, not just accumulate a large number.

points.heading: Phases of retirement planning
points.text: Accumulation is the working-life phase of saving and growing the corpus. Transition is the few years before retirement when risk is reduced and plans are finalised. Distribution is the phase of drawing income. Different products and asset mixes suit each phase.

points.heading: Start early: power of compounding
points.text: A 25-year-old investing ₹5,000 a month at 10% a year accumulates far more by 60 than a 40-year-old investing ₹15,000 a month at the same rate, despite contributing less in total. Delay is the costliest mistake in retirement planning.

points.heading: Expenses after retirement
points.text: Some expenses fall (commuting, children's education, EMIs), while others rise (healthcare, travel, help at home). A replacement ratio of 70% to 80% of pre-retirement expenses is a rough starting point, but a line-by-line budget is better.

points.heading: Role of the retirement adviser
points.text: The adviser assesses needs, estimates the corpus, recommends suitable products such as NPS, EPF, PPF, mutual funds and annuities, monitors progress and helps convert savings into income. PFRDA registers retirement advisers who must pass NISM XVII.

formulas: Future expense = current expense x (1 + inflation)^years.
Rule of 72: years to double = 72 / rate (at 6% inflation, about 12 years).
traps: Longevity risk is outliving savings, not dying early.
Sequence-of-returns risk matters most just before and just after retirement, not early in the career.
Expenses do not simply fall to zero after retirement; healthcare usually rises.
Starting early beats contributing more later because of compounding.
items.recap: Longer lives, nuclear families and lack of pensions make self-funded retirement essential. Main risks: longevity, inflation, interest rate, market, sequence of returns, health. Phases: accumulation, transition, distribution. Inflate expenses: E x (1+i)^n; ₹40,000 at 6% for 20 years is about ₹1.28 lakh. Start early. Advisers register with PFRDA after NISM XVII.

items.title: Pension Systems and PFRDA: NISM XVII Revision Notes
items.description: Defined benefit vs defined contribution, India's pension pillars, the move from old pension to NPS and UPS, and PFRDA's powers and intermediaries, in brief.
items.intro: This chapter explains the types of pension systems, how India's pension landscape evolved and how the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority regulates NPS and related schemes. Questions test the difference between defined benefit and defined contribution, key dates in NPS history, PFRDA's role and the functions of intermediaries such as Points of Presence.

points.heading: Defined benefit versus defined contribution
points.text: In a defined benefit plan the pension is fixed by a formula, such as 50% of last drawn pay, and the employer bears investment and longevity risk. In a defined contribution plan, contributions are fixed and the pension depends on accumulated corpus and returns, so the member bears the risk. NPS is defined contribution.

points.heading: Funded and unfunded
points.text: An unfunded (pay-as-you-go) scheme pays current pensions from current revenues, as with the old government pension scheme. A funded scheme invests contributions to pay future pensions. Rising pension bills of governments were a key reason for moving to funded schemes.

points.heading: Pillars of pension
points.text: The World Bank multi-pillar model is often used: a non-contributory social pension (pillar zero), mandatory contributory schemes, voluntary savings, and informal family support. In India, examples include old-age social assistance, EPF and EPS, NPS, APY and personal savings.

points.heading: Evolution in India
points.text: Central government employees joining from 1 January 2004 (except armed forces) moved to the National Pension System; most states followed. NPS was opened to all citizens in 2009. From April 2025, central government NPS employees can opt for the Unified Pension Scheme, which assures a pension linked to average basic pay for qualifying service.

points.heading: PFRDA
points.text: PFRDA was set up in 2003 by executive order and became statutory under the PFRDA Act, 2013 (effective 2014). It regulates NPS, Atal Pension Yojana administration and pension funds, registers intermediaries, protects subscribers and promotes old-age income security.

points.heading: NPS intermediaries
points.text: Points of Presence (banks and others) are the first point of contact for subscribers, handling registration and contributions. Central Recordkeeping Agencies maintain accounts and issue the PRAN. Pension funds invest the money. The NPS Trust oversees assets in subscribers' interest. A trustee bank handles fund flows, a custodian holds securities, and annuity service providers (life insurers) pay annuities.

points.heading: Retirement advisers under PFRDA
points.text: PFRDA's Retirement Adviser Regulations allow registered advisers to guide subscribers on NPS and retirement planning. They must hold the NISM XVII certification and follow a code of conduct covering suitability, disclosure and fair dealing.

points.heading: Subscriber protection
points.text: PFRDA prescribes caps on charges, disclosure of scheme returns and portfolios, grievance redressal through the CRA's central grievance system and escalation to the NPS Trust and an ombudsman. Investment guidelines limit concentration and credit risk.

traps: NPS is defined contribution; the old government pension was defined benefit and unfunded.
NPS began for central government employees on 1 January 2004 and for all citizens in 2009.
Points of Presence collect contributions and register subscribers; CRAs keep records; pension funds invest.
PFRDA became statutory under the 2013 Act, though the authority existed from 2003.
items.recap: Defined benefit fixes the pension; defined contribution fixes contributions and shifts risk to the member. India moved government employees from an unfunded DB pension to NPS from 2004, opened NPS to all in 2009 and added UPS in 2025. PFRDA (statutory from 2014) regulates NPS and APY. Intermediaries: POP, CRA, pension funds, NPS Trust, trustee bank, custodian, ASPs.

items.title: NPS Architecture: Tiers, PRAN and Models (XVII)
items.description: NPS Tier I and Tier II, PRAN, all-citizen and corporate models, NPS Vatsalya, entry age, contributions and tax deductions, revised for NISM Series XVII.
items.intro: This chapter explains how NPS is structured for different subscriber groups and how an account works day to day. You need to know the account tiers, subscriber models, eligibility, minimum contributions and the tax benefits linked to contributions. Several limits have changed in recent years, so wherever a number appears, treat it as current as of 2026 and verify with PFRDA.

points.heading: PRAN
points.text: Each subscriber receives a unique Permanent Retirement Account Number from the CRA. It stays the same across jobs, cities and POPs, so a subscriber moving from a corporate job to self-employment keeps the same NPS account. Portability is a key advantage over older schemes.

points.heading: Tier I and Tier II
points.text: Tier I is the pension account with restrictions on withdrawal and tax benefits on contributions. Tier II is a voluntary savings account that can be opened only with an active Tier I, allows free withdrawals and generally carries no tax benefit (except a special Tier II tax-saver for government employees).

points.heading: Subscriber models
points.text: NPS works through several models: central government, state government, corporate (employers enrol staff, often with employer contributions), all-citizen (individuals through POPs or eNPS online), and NPS Lite/Swavalamban (now largely replaced by APY). Each model has slightly different default choices.

points.heading: Eligibility
points.text: Indian citizens, including NRIs, aged 18 to 70 years can open an all-citizen NPS account. OCI cardholders are also eligible. Contributions can continue till exit, and PFRDA has allowed deferment of exit and continuation beyond 60 subject to its rules.

points.heading: NPS Vatsalya
points.text: Launched in 2024, NPS Vatsalya lets parents or guardians open an NPS account for a minor. On attaining 18, the account converts into a regular all-citizen Tier I account after fresh KYC of the subscriber. It helps start compounding very early.

points.heading: Contributions
points.text: There is a small minimum contribution per year for Tier I to keep the account active, and no maximum. Contributions can be made online through eNPS, through POPs or by employers. Employer contributions in the corporate model go directly to the employee's PRAN.

points.heading: Tax on contributions
points.text: Own contributions qualify under Section 80CCD(1) within the overall ₹1.5 lakh limit with 80C, plus an extra ₹50,000 under Section 80CCD(1B) in the old tax regime. Employer contributions qualify under 80CCD(2) up to a percentage of salary, also available in the new regime. Check current limits for 2026.

points.heading: Charges
points.text: NPS has among the lowest charges of any retirement product: pension fund management fees, CRA charges and POP charges are capped by PFRDA. Low costs make a big difference over 30-year horizons.

traps: Tier II requires an active Tier I account; it cannot exist alone.
PRAN does not change when a subscriber changes job or POP.
80CCD(1B) gives ₹50,000 over and above the ₹1.5 lakh 80C limit, only in the old regime.
NPS Vatsalya converts into a normal Tier I account at 18; it is not closed and paid out.
items.recap: Every subscriber gets a portable PRAN. Tier I is the locked-in pension account with tax benefits; Tier II is optional, liquid and needs Tier I. Models: government, corporate, all-citizen, Lite. Citizens and NRIs aged 18 to 70 can join; OCIs too. NPS Vatsalya for minors converts at 18. Tax: 80CCD(1), extra ₹50,000 under 80CCD(1B), employer 80CCD(2). Charges are capped.

items.title: NPS Investment Choices and Pension Funds: XVII Notes
items.description: Active choice limits, auto choice lifecycle funds, asset classes E, C, G and A, pension fund managers and switching rules in NPS, revised simply.
items.intro: This chapter covers how NPS money is invested: the asset classes, the active and auto choice options, lifecycle funds, pension fund managers and rules for switching. Questions test equity limits by age, what each asset class holds, who decides allocation under each choice, and what happens for government employees. Treat specific percentage caps as as of 2026.

points.heading: Asset classes
points.text: E is equity (mainly large-cap index stocks), C is corporate debt, G is government securities, and A is alternative assets such as REITs, InvITs and AIFs, with a small cap on allocation. Each pension fund manages separate schemes for each asset class.

points.heading: Active choice
points.text: Under active choice the subscriber decides the allocation across E, C, G and A. Equity is capped at 75% up to a certain age, after which the cap tapers each year, and asset class A has a low maximum. A 35-year-old could choose 75% E, 15% C and 10% G.

points.heading: Auto choice: lifecycle funds
points.text: Under auto choice the allocation is set by age through lifecycle funds. LC75 (aggressive), LC50 (moderate) and LC25 (conservative) start with maximum equity of 75%, 50% and 25% respectively and reduce equity as the subscriber ages, shifting to G. A balanced lifecycle option was added later. LC50 is the default if no choice is made.

points.heading: Why taper equity
points.text: Equity has higher expected returns but higher volatility. As retirement approaches, a sharp fall could permanently hurt the corpus because there is little time to recover. Lifecycle funds reduce this sequence risk automatically, without the subscriber having to rebalance.

points.heading: Pension fund managers
points.text: Subscribers choose one pension fund manager from those registered with PFRDA, such as funds sponsored by SBI, LIC, UTI, HDFC, ICICI Prudential, Kotak, Aditya Birla, Axis, Tata and others. The PFM invests within PFRDA's investment guidelines. Fees are capped and returns are published regularly.

points.heading: Switching
points.text: Subscribers can change their pension fund manager and their scheme preference or allocation a limited number of times a year, as permitted by PFRDA (for example, PFM change once a year and allocation changes a few times a year). Switching does not attract tax.

points.heading: Government subscribers
points.text: Government employees were traditionally invested in a default scheme split among government-sponsored pension funds with a conservative mix. They now have the option to choose active or auto choice and private PFMs, subject to conditions.

points.heading: Returns and risk
points.text: NPS returns are market linked and not guaranteed. Equity schemes have delivered higher long-term returns than G and C schemes but with greater volatility. Advisers should match choice to risk profile and time horizon rather than chasing last year's best fund.

traps: Under active choice the subscriber decides allocation; under auto choice the lifecycle fund decides by age.
LC75 is aggressive, LC25 conservative; LC50 is the default auto choice.
Asset class A has a very low cap and is not a large equity alternative.
NPS returns are not guaranteed, even though costs are low.
items.recap: NPS invests in E (equity), C (corporate debt), G (government securities) and A (alternatives, small cap). Active choice: subscriber decides, equity capped at 75% with age-based taper. Auto choice: lifecycle funds LC75, LC50 (default), LC25 and a balanced option reduce equity with age. Choose one PFM; limited annual switches allowed without tax. Returns are market linked.

items.title: NPS Exit, Withdrawal and Annuity Rules: XVII Notes
items.description: Normal exit, premature exit, death, partial withdrawals, systematic lump sum withdrawal and the mandatory annuity rule under NPS, with tax points and traps.
items.intro: Exit rules decide how much of an NPS corpus becomes cash and how much must buy a pension. This chapter is frequently tested because the rules differ for normal exit, premature exit and death, and PFRDA has amended them several times, including changes for non-government subscribers in 2025. Learn the logic and the traditional numbers, and confirm current limits with PFRDA before advising.

points.heading: Normal exit
points.text: Normal exit happens on superannuation or at 60. Traditionally, at least 40% of the corpus had to buy an annuity and up to 60% could be withdrawn as lump sum. PFRDA's 2025 amendments allow non-government subscribers a larger lump sum share; check the current split before advising.

points.heading: Small corpus
points.text: If the total corpus at normal exit is at or below a threshold set by PFRDA (raised over time), the subscriber can withdraw the entire amount without buying an annuity. This avoids forcing tiny annuities that would pay negligible monthly income.

points.heading: Premature exit
points.text: Exit before 60 (after a minimum period in NPS) is treated as premature. Traditionally at least 80% of the corpus had to be annuitised and at most 20% taken as lump sum, again with full withdrawal allowed for small corpuses. The rule discourages using NPS as a short-term saving.

points.heading: Death of subscriber
points.text: On death, the entire corpus is paid to the nominee or legal heirs, who may also choose to buy an annuity. For government employees covered by additional relief rules, family pension options may apply instead.

points.heading: Partial withdrawal
points.text: After a minimum period of subscription, Tier I subscribers can withdraw up to 25% of their own contributions (not employer contributions or returns) for specified purposes: children's higher education or marriage, buying or building a first house, treatment of specified illnesses, starting a business or skill development. The number of withdrawals is limited.

points.heading: Deferment and systematic withdrawal
points.text: Subscribers can defer the lump sum and annuity purchase to a later age, staying invested. They can also take the lump sum in instalments through systematic lump sum withdrawal, giving a mutual-fund-SWP-like income while the balance stays invested.

points.heading: Annuity purchase
points.text: The annuity must be bought from an empanelled annuity service provider, which are life insurance companies. The subscriber chooses the annuity type (life, with return of purchase price, joint life and so on). The annuity rate is fixed at purchase and annuity income is taxable as income.

points.heading: Tax at exit
points.text: The lump sum withdrawn at normal exit, up to 60% of the corpus, is tax exempt. Partial withdrawals within the rules are exempt. The amount used to buy an annuity is not taxed at purchase, but the annuity received later is taxable in the year of receipt.

traps: Partial withdrawal is up to 25% of the subscriber's own contributions, not 25% of the total corpus.
Annuities must be bought from empanelled life insurers (ASPs), not from pension fund managers.
Annuity income is taxable even though the commuted lump sum is tax free.
Premature exit forces a much larger annuity share than normal exit.
items.recap: Normal exit at 60: traditionally 60% lump sum (tax free) and 40% annuity; 2025 changes give non-government subscribers more flexibility. Small corpuses can be fully withdrawn. Premature exit: traditionally 80% annuity. Death: full corpus to nominee. Partial withdrawal up to 25% of own contributions for listed needs. Annuity from empanelled insurers; annuity income is taxable.

items.chapter: Other Retirement Products (EPF, PPF, SCSS, APY, MFs)
items.title: EPF, PPF, SCSS, APY and Mutual Funds for Retirement
items.description: EPF and EPS split, PPF lock-in, SCSS limits, Atal Pension Yojana pensions and retirement-oriented mutual funds compared, with tax notes for NISM Series XVII.
items.intro: Besides NPS, Indian retirement planning uses employer schemes, small savings schemes, social security schemes and mutual funds. This chapter compares EPF and EPS, PPF, the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme, Atal Pension Yojana and retirement-oriented mutual funds. Questions test contribution splits, lock-ins, eligibility ages and tax status. Rates on small savings change quarterly.

points.heading: EPF and EPS
points.text: Under the EPF scheme, the employee contributes 12% of basic pay plus DA. Of the employer's 12%, 8.33% (on wages up to the ceiling of ₹15,000 a month, so up to ₹1,250) goes to the Employees' Pension Scheme and the rest to EPF. EPFO declares the EPF interest rate each year.

points.heading: EPS pension
points.text: EPS is a defined benefit pension: monthly pension = pensionable salary x pensionable service / 70, payable from 58 with at least 10 years of service. Example: pensionable salary ₹15,000 and 30 years' service gives ₹15,000 x 30 / 70 = about ₹6,429 a month.

points.heading: EPF withdrawals and tax
points.text: EPF can be withdrawn on retirement or after two months of unemployment, with partial withdrawals for housing, illness and education. Withdrawal is tax free after five years of continuous service. Interest on employee contributions above ₹2.5 lakh a year is taxable.

points.heading: PPF
points.text: PPF has a 15-year lock-in, extendable in blocks of five years, a minimum deposit of ₹500 and maximum of ₹1.5 lakh a year. It is EEE (exempt contribution under 80C, exempt interest, exempt maturity). Loans are allowed from the third to sixth year and partial withdrawals from the seventh year.

points.heading: SCSS
points.text: The Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme is open to those aged 60 and above (with relaxations for certain retirees), with a five-year tenure extendable by three years and a maximum investment of ₹30 lakh. Interest is paid quarterly and is taxable; the deposit qualifies for 80C. Rate is set quarterly by government.

points.heading: Atal Pension Yojana
points.text: APY is a government-backed pension for unorganised-sector workers aged 18 to 40, giving a guaranteed monthly pension of ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 from 60, depending on contribution and joining age. On death, the spouse gets the same pension and the nominee gets the corpus. Income taxpayers are not eligible to join since October 2022.

points.heading: Mutual funds for retirement
points.text: Retirement solution-oriented funds have a five-year lock-in or until retirement, whichever is earlier. Diversified equity funds suit long accumulation through SIPs; hybrid and debt funds suit the transition and distribution phases. SWPs give regular income with tax only on the gains portion.

points.heading: Comparing products
points.text: EPF, PPF and SCSS offer government-backed safety but limited flexibility; NPS and mutual funds offer market-linked growth with low cost; APY gives a guaranteed small pension. A combination usually works better than any single product.

formulas: EPS monthly pension = pensionable salary x pensionable service / 70.
Employer EPS share = 8.33% x min(wage, ₹15,000).
traps: Of the employer's 12%, only 8.33% (capped at ₹1,250 a month) goes to EPS; the rest goes to EPF.
SCSS interest is taxable even though the deposit qualifies for 80C.
APY entry age is 18 to 40, not up to 60; the pension starts at 60.
PPF partial withdrawal starts in the seventh year; loans are in years three to six.
items.recap: EPF: 12% plus 12%, with 8.33% of employer share (up to ₹1,250) to EPS; EPS pension = salary x service / 70. PPF: 15 years, ₹1.5 lakh cap, EEE. SCSS: 60+, ₹30 lakh max, five years, quarterly taxable interest. APY: join 18 to 40, guaranteed ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 from 60, spouse continues. Mutual funds: SIPs to accumulate, SWPs to draw.

items.title: Retirement Corpus Calculation: NISM XVII Revision Notes
items.description: Retirement planning steps, inflation-adjusted expenses, real rate of return, corpus as a growing annuity and the savings shortfall, with worked sums.
items.intro: This is the most calculation-heavy chapter of NISM XVII and carries many marks. It walks through the planning process and the maths of estimating the corpus needed at retirement, then working out how much more must be saved. Practise inflating expenses, computing the real rate, valuing a growing annuity and finding the shortfall until each step takes under two minutes.

points.heading: The planning process
points.text: Gather data (age, income, expenses, assets, liabilities, goals, health), set the retirement age and life expectancy, estimate expenses at retirement, compute the corpus required, value existing savings at retirement, find the shortfall, design a savings and investment plan, implement it and review at least yearly.

points.heading: Expenses at retirement
points.text: Start with today's annual expenses that will continue in retirement, adjust for items that will fall or rise, and inflate to the retirement year. ₹6 lakh a year today at 6% inflation becomes about ₹6 lakh x (1.06)^15 = ₹14.4 lakh in 15 years.

points.heading: Real rate of return
points.text: During retirement the corpus earns a return while withdrawals grow with inflation. The inflation-adjusted (real) rate is (1 + return)/(1 + inflation) - 1, not simply return minus inflation. With 8% return and 6% inflation, real rate = 1.08/1.06 - 1 = 1.89%.

points.heading: Corpus as growing annuity
points.text: The corpus needed is the present value, at retirement, of withdrawals that grow with inflation for the retirement period, discounted at the real rate. For first-year need of ₹8 lakh, 20 years, withdrawals at the start of each year, at a real rate of 1.89%, the corpus is about ₹8 lakh x 16.84 = ₹1.35 crore.

points.heading: Value of existing savings
points.text: Project current retirement investments to the retirement date at their expected return. ₹20 lakh growing at 9% for 20 years becomes 20 x (1.09)^20 = about ₹1.12 crore. Include EPF, PPF, NPS and dedicated mutual funds; exclude assets earmarked for other goals.

points.heading: Shortfall and savings required
points.text: Shortfall = corpus required - projected value of existing savings. If ₹2.5 crore is needed and existing savings will grow to ₹1.12 crore, the gap is ₹1.38 crore. At 9% for 20 years, the annual saving needed is 1.38 crore / 51.16 = about ₹2.7 lakh a year, or a monthly SIP computed similarly.

points.heading: Assumptions drive results
points.text: Small changes in inflation, return or life expectancy change the corpus a lot. Use conservative returns, realistic inflation (including higher medical inflation) and a long life expectancy. Show clients a range of outcomes rather than one precise number.

points.heading: Review and adjust
points.text: Plans must be reviewed annually and after life events such as job change, inheritance or illness. Step-up SIPs that increase contributions with salary can close the gap faster than a flat SIP.

formulas: Expense at retirement = current expense x (1 + i)^n.
Real rate = (1 + r)/(1 + i) - 1.
Corpus (withdrawals at start of year) = E1 x [1 - (1 + real)^-N] / real x (1 + real).
FV of existing savings = PV x (1 + r)^n; annual saving = shortfall x r / [(1 + r)^n - 1].
traps: Real rate is (1+r)/(1+i) - 1, not r - i; the difference matters in exam options.
Withdrawals at the beginning of the year need an annuity-due factor, which gives a larger corpus.
Use the expense at retirement, not today's expense, as the first withdrawal.
Existing savings must be grown to the retirement date before subtracting from the corpus.
items.recap: Process: gather data, estimate expenses at retirement, compute corpus, project existing savings, find shortfall, plan savings, review. Inflate expenses with (1+i)^n. Real rate = (1+r)/(1+i) - 1. Corpus = PV of inflation-growing withdrawals at the real rate. Shortfall = corpus minus future value of existing savings; divide by the FV annuity factor to get yearly saving.

items.title: Retirement Asset Allocation and Glide Paths: XVII
items.description: Asset allocation by life stage, glide paths, bucket strategy, sequence-of-returns risk, rebalancing and product choice for accumulation and drawdown.
items.intro: This chapter turns the retirement number into an investment plan. It covers asset allocation across life stages, glide paths that reduce risk with age, the bucket approach for retirees, rebalancing, and the role of SIPs and SWPs. Questions are conceptual and scenario-based: pick the best allocation for a client or explain why a strategy reduces a specific risk.

points.heading: Asset allocation drives outcomes
points.text: The split between equity, debt, gold and cash explains most of the variation in a portfolio's long-term return and risk. For long accumulation periods, a meaningful equity share is needed to beat inflation. For a 30-year-old, 70% to 80% equity may be reasonable; for someone at 58, much less.

points.heading: Glide path
points.text: A glide path is a pre-set schedule for reducing equity and increasing debt as retirement approaches. NPS lifecycle funds and target-date funds follow one automatically. It protects the corpus from a large equity fall just before retirement, when there is little time to recover.

points.heading: Rules of thumb
points.text: The '100 minus age' rule suggests equity percentage; at 40, about 60% equity. It is a starting point, not a prescription, and should be adjusted for risk tolerance, other income such as pensions, and health. Some advisers use 110 or 120 minus age given longer lives.

points.heading: Sequence-of-returns risk
points.text: Two retirees with the same average return can end with very different outcomes if one suffers losses early in retirement while withdrawing money. Selling units in a falling market locks in losses. Keeping two to three years of expenses in safe assets reduces forced selling.

points.heading: Bucket strategy
points.text: Divide the retirement corpus into buckets: short-term (one to three years of expenses in liquid or short-term debt funds and deposits), medium-term (hybrid or debt funds for years four to ten), and long-term (equity for growth beyond ten years). Refill the short bucket from the others periodically.

points.heading: Rebalancing
points.text: Market moves change the allocation over time. If equity rises from 50% to 62%, sell some equity and buy debt to return to target. Rebalancing annually or at set bands enforces 'buy low, sell high' discipline. Tax and exit loads should be considered.

points.heading: Products by phase
points.text: Accumulation: equity mutual funds via SIPs, NPS with higher equity, EPF and PPF as debt anchors. Transition: shift gradually to hybrid and debt funds, lock in gains. Distribution: SCSS, annuities, debt funds with SWPs, and a smaller equity portion to fight inflation.

points.heading: Behavioural pitfalls
points.text: Panic selling in crashes, chasing recent winners, holding too much cash, and keeping all money in fixed deposits out of fear are common mistakes. An adviser's job includes keeping clients disciplined during volatility.

traps: A glide path reduces equity as retirement nears; it does not eliminate equity entirely at retirement.
Sequence risk depends on the order of returns, not the average return.
In a bucket strategy the short-term bucket holds safe, liquid assets, not equities.
'100 minus age' is a rough guide, not a regulatory rule.
items.recap: Asset allocation drives retirement outcomes. Glide paths reduce equity with age; NPS lifecycle funds do this automatically. '100 minus age' is a starting rule of thumb. Sequence-of-returns risk is highest around retirement; keep two to three years of expenses safe. Bucket strategy: short (safe), medium (hybrid/debt), long (equity). Rebalance periodically and manage behaviour.

items.title: Retirement Income and Annuity Options: NISM XVII Notes
items.description: Annuity types, how annuity income is computed, SWP from mutual funds, reverse mortgage and withdrawal rates for retirees, with examples and common exam traps.
items.intro: The distribution phase is about turning a corpus into reliable income for life. This chapter covers annuities in detail, systematic withdrawal plans from mutual funds, reverse mortgage and sustainable withdrawal rates. Questions include simple annuity income calculations, matching annuity types to needs, and comparing annuities with SWPs for flexibility, tax and longevity protection.

points.heading: What an annuity does
points.text: An annuity converts a lump sum into regular income, usually for life, from a life insurer. It transfers longevity risk to the insurer. ₹50 lakh at an annuity rate of 7% gives ₹3.5 lakh a year, or about ₹29,167 a month before tax.

points.heading: Immediate and deferred
points.text: An immediate annuity starts paying soon after purchase, typically at retirement. A deferred annuity accumulates for some years before payments begin. NPS annuities on exit are immediate annuities purchased from empanelled insurers.

points.heading: Annuity options
points.text: Life annuity (highest income, stops on death), life annuity with return of purchase price (lower income, corpus returned to nominee), joint life last survivor (continues to spouse), increasing annuity (rises by a fixed rate each year), and annuity certain for a fixed period then life. More features mean lower income.

points.heading: Choosing an option
points.text: A married client wanting to protect a spouse should consider joint life last survivor. A client wanting to leave money to children may choose return of purchase price. A client with no dependants and high longevity concern may prefer plain life annuity for maximum income.

points.heading: Limitations of annuities
points.text: Annuity rates are fixed at purchase and do not rise with inflation unless an increasing option is chosen. The corpus is usually irrevocable. Annuity income is fully taxable as income. Many advisers suggest annuitising only part of the corpus.

points.heading: Systematic withdrawal plans
points.text: An SWP redeems a fixed amount from a mutual fund at regular intervals. Only the gains portion of each redemption is taxed, which can make post-tax income higher than an annuity. The corpus stays invested and accessible, but there is no guarantee and it can run out if returns are poor.

points.heading: Withdrawal rates
points.text: A sustainable withdrawal rate is the percentage of the initial corpus that can be withdrawn each year, adjusted for inflation, without exhausting it. The US '4% rule' is often cited; with higher Indian inflation, advisers often use more conservative rates or flexible withdrawals.

points.heading: Reverse mortgage
points.text: Senior citizens owning a house can borrow against it from banks and receive periodic payments while continuing to live there. The loan is repaid from sale of the house after death or by heirs. Payments received under an approved reverse mortgage are not taxable as income.

formulas: Annual annuity income = purchase price x annuity rate; monthly = annual / 12.
Withdrawal rate = first-year withdrawal / initial corpus.
traps: Return of purchase price gives lower income than plain life annuity because the capital is returned.
Annuity income is taxable; only the gains portion of an SWP redemption is taxable.
Annuities transfer longevity risk; SWPs do not.
Reverse mortgage payments are loan receipts, not taxable income.
items.recap: Annuities turn a lump sum into lifelong income from insurers: ₹50 lakh at 7% gives about ₹29,167 a month. Options: life, return of purchase price, joint life last survivor, increasing. More features mean less income. Annuity income is fully taxable; SWPs are taxed only on gains but carry market and longevity risk. Reverse mortgage unlocks home value tax-free.

items.title: Tax on Gratuity, Pension and PF: NISM XVII Notes
items.description: Tax rules for gratuity, leave encashment, commuted and uncommuted pension, EPF, NPS withdrawals and senior citizen benefits, revised with 2026 check flags.
items.intro: Retirees receive several types of payments, each taxed differently. This chapter covers gratuity, leave encashment, pension (commuted and uncommuted), provident fund, NPS and annuity income, and benefits for senior citizens. Questions test which amounts are exempt and what limits apply. Tax limits change through Finance Acts, so treat every figure here as as of 2026 and verify with the income tax department.

points.heading: Gratuity
points.text: For employees covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act, gratuity = 15/26 x last drawn salary (basic plus DA) x completed years of service. The exemption is the least of the formula amount, the statutory ceiling (₹20 lakh) and the actual gratuity. Government employees' gratuity is fully exempt.

points.heading: Leave encashment
points.text: Leave encashment on retirement is fully exempt for government employees. For non-government employees it is exempt up to the least of specified limits, with the overall cap raised to ₹25 lakh from April 2023. Encashment during service is fully taxable.

points.heading: Uncommuted and commuted pension
points.text: Uncommuted (monthly) pension is taxed as salary, and the standard deduction applies. Commuted pension (lump sum) is fully exempt for government employees. For others, one-third of the full commuted value is exempt if gratuity is also received, and one-half if not.

points.heading: Family pension
points.text: Family pension received by heirs is taxed under 'income from other sources' with a deduction of one-third or a fixed amount, whichever is lower (the fixed amount is higher in the new regime).

points.heading: Provident fund
points.text: EPF withdrawal after five years of continuous service is exempt. Withdrawal before five years is taxable unless due to specified reasons. Interest on employee contributions above ₹2.5 lakh a year is taxable. PPF is fully exempt.

points.heading: NPS and annuity
points.text: At exit, up to 60% of the NPS corpus withdrawn as lump sum is exempt, and partial withdrawals within rules are exempt. Annuity income is taxable in the year received. Employer contributions under 80CCD(2) are deductible, with an overall cap on tax-free employer retirement contributions.

points.heading: Senior citizen benefits
points.text: Seniors (60+) enjoy a higher basic exemption in the old regime, Section 80TTB deduction on interest up to ₹50,000, higher 80D limits for health insurance, and higher TDS thresholds on interest. Those aged 75+ with only pension and interest from the same bank can be exempt from filing returns under Section 194P conditions.

points.heading: Old versus new regime
points.text: Many deductions (80C, 80CCD(1B), 80TTB, 80D) are available only in the old regime, while the new regime offers lower slab rates and a higher standard deduction. Retirees should compare both each year; the better choice depends on deductions and income mix.

formulas: Gratuity (covered employees) = 15/26 x last drawn monthly salary x completed years of service.
Exempt commuted pension (non-government) = 1/3 of full value if gratuity received, else 1/2.
traps: Monthly pension is taxed as salary, not as income from other sources; family pension is other sources.
Commuted pension exemption for non-government employees depends on whether gratuity is received.
EPF interest is taxable on employee contributions above ₹2.5 lakh a year even before withdrawal.
80TTB applies only to senior citizens and only in the old regime.
items.recap: Gratuity: 15/26 x salary x years, exempt up to ₹20 lakh; government fully exempt. Leave encashment cap ₹25 lakh for non-government. Monthly pension = salary income; commuted pension exempt fully (government) or 1/3 or 1/2 (others). Family pension: other sources with deduction. EPF exempt after five years. NPS 60% lump sum exempt; annuity taxable. Compare old and new regimes yearly.

items.chapter: Health, Insurance & Estate Aspects in Retirement
items.title: Health Cover and Estate Planning in Retirement: XVII
items.description: Health insurance for seniors, group cover gaps, top-ups, PM-JAY, life insurance needs, wills, nomination, joint holdings and succession for retirees in India.
items.intro: A retirement plan can fail because of one hospital bill or a messy inheritance. This chapter covers health insurance for retirees, the gap left by employer group cover, life insurance needs after retirement, and estate planning tools such as wills and nominations. Questions are mostly scenario-based: choose the most suitable advice for a client approaching retirement.

points.heading: Medical inflation
points.text: Healthcare costs in India have historically risen faster than general inflation, and older people need care more often. A retirement budget must include health insurance premiums, out-of-pocket costs and long-term care, not just routine expenses.

points.heading: Group cover gap
points.text: Employer group health cover usually ends at retirement. A 55-year-old relying only on group cover should buy an individual or family floater policy well before retirement, so that waiting periods for pre-existing diseases are served while still employed and premiums are lower.

points.heading: Senior citizen policies
points.text: Policies for seniors often have co-payment (the insured pays a share of each claim), room rent limits and disease-wise sub-limits. Read these carefully. IRDAI removed the upper age limit for buying health insurance in 2024 and capped waiting periods for pre-existing conditions.

points.heading: Top-up and super top-up
points.text: A top-up pays above a deductible for each claim; a super top-up pays when aggregate claims in a year exceed the deductible. A base cover of ₹5 lakh plus a super top-up of ₹20 lakh is often cheaper than a single ₹25 lakh base policy.

points.heading: Government schemes
points.text: PM-JAY (Ayushman Bharat) was extended in 2024 to all citizens aged 70 and above regardless of income, with cover per family per year. CGHS covers central government pensioners. These complement, not replace, private cover for most middle-class retirees.

points.heading: Life insurance after retirement
points.text: Once children are independent and loans repaid, the need for life cover usually falls. Term cover may still be useful if a spouse depends on the retiree's pension that will stop on death, or to cover outstanding liabilities.

points.heading: Wills and succession
points.text: A will directs how assets pass after death and can appoint an executor. Without a will, assets pass under succession laws such as the Hindu Succession Act or the Indian Succession Act, which may not match the person's wishes. A will can be changed any time; the latest valid will prevails.

points.heading: Nomination and joint holding
points.text: Nomination makes transfer easier for bank accounts, demat accounts, mutual funds, insurance and NPS. Courts have generally held that a nominee may receive assets as a trustee for legal heirs, so nomination does not replace a will. Joint holding with 'either or survivor' helps the spouse access funds quickly.

points.heading: Power of attorney and other tools
points.text: A power of attorney helps someone manage finances if the retiree becomes unable to; it ends on death. Private trusts can manage assets for dependants with special needs. The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 allows seniors to claim maintenance from children.

traps: Nomination is not a substitute for a will; a nominee may hold assets for legal heirs.
Group health cover usually ends at retirement; buy individual cover before, not after.
A super top-up looks at aggregate yearly claims; a top-up looks at each claim separately.
A power of attorney ends on the death of the person who granted it.
items.recap: Plan for medical inflation. Buy individual health cover before group cover ends, mind co-pays and sub-limits, use super top-ups for cheap extra cover. PM-JAY covers all 70+. Life cover need falls but may protect a dependent spouse. Write a will; nomination eases transfer but nominees may be trustees for heirs. Use joint holdings, POA and trusts sensibly.

items.chapter: Ethics, Code of Conduct & Grievance Redressal
items.title: Retirement Adviser Ethics and NPS Grievances: XVII
items.description: Code of conduct for PFRDA retirement advisers, suitability, disclosure, conflicts, and NPS grievance routes via CGMS, NPS Trust and ombudsman.
items.intro: Retirement advice affects a client's income for decades, so NISM XVII ends with ethics and grievance handling. The chapter covers the conduct expected of PFRDA-registered retirement advisers, suitability and disclosure duties, conflicts of interest, and the grievance redressal system for NPS subscribers. Questions are mostly scenarios: identify the ethical action or the right grievance route.

points.heading: Registration and certification
points.text: Retirement advisers are registered with PFRDA under its Retirement Adviser Regulations and must pass NISM Series XVII. They must renew certification as required and display registration details in communications with clients.

points.heading: Fiduciary approach
points.text: An adviser must place the client's interest first. Recommending a product because it pays a higher commission, when a cheaper suitable option exists, breaches this duty. Advice should be based on the client's goals, risk profile, tax position and existing assets.

points.heading: Know your client and suitability
points.text: Collect full information on income, expenses, liabilities, dependants, health and risk tolerance. A 58-year-old with no other pension who wants to move 90% of the corpus into small-cap funds should be counselled on risk; suitability documentation protects both sides.

points.heading: Disclosure
points.text: Advisers must disclose fees, commissions, conflicts of interest and the limits of their services in writing. They must explain product features, risks, charges, lock-ins and exit rules clearly, especially NPS annuity requirements and withdrawal restrictions.

points.heading: Prohibited conduct
points.text: Advisers must not promise assured returns, misrepresent product features, pressure clients, handle client money in cash beyond permitted modes, or share client data without consent. Advertising must be fair and not misleading.

points.heading: NPS grievance channels
points.text: NPS subscribers can lodge grievances through the CRA's Central Grievance Management System (CGMS) online, by phone or through the POP. The CRA routes complaints to the relevant entity: POP, pension fund, nodal office or annuity service provider.

points.heading: Escalation
points.text: If the grievance is not resolved within the prescribed time or the subscriber is unhappy, it can be escalated to the NPS Trust and then to the ombudsman appointed under PFRDA's grievance redressal regulations. Annuity complaints against insurers may also go to the insurance ombudsman.

points.heading: Record keeping
points.text: Advisers should keep records of client information, risk profiles, advice and the reasons for it, disclosures and communications. Good records help resolve disputes and demonstrate compliance during PFRDA inspections.

traps: NPS grievances are lodged through the CRA's CGMS, not directly with PFRDA as a first step.
A client's insistence does not remove the adviser's duty to warn about unsuitable choices.
Promising a fixed return on NPS is prohibited because returns are market linked.
Commission and fee disclosure must be in writing, before the advice is acted on.
items.recap: Retirement advisers register with PFRDA and hold NISM XVII. Put the client first, know the client, give suitable advice, disclose fees and conflicts in writing, never promise assured returns or mislead. NPS grievances: CGMS via CRA (or POP), then NPS Trust, then ombudsman. Keep records of advice and rationale for inspections and disputes.

items.title: Introduction to Insurance: IC-38 Revision Notes
items.description: How insurance pools risk, history of insurance in India, risk management methods, peril vs hazard and the role of reinsurance, revised for IRDAI IC-38.
items.intro: The opening chapter of the IC-38 syllabus explains what insurance is, how it works through pooling of risk, and how the industry developed in India. Questions test basic definitions, key historical milestones, methods of managing risk and terms like peril, hazard and reinsurance. Most questions are direct and quick, so clarity on vocabulary earns easy marks in the 50-question paper.

points.heading: Pooling of risk
points.text: Insurance collects small premiums from many people exposed to similar risks and pays the few who suffer a loss. If 1,000 houses worth ₹20 lakh each face a 1 in 1,000 chance of fire in a year, a premium of a little over ₹2,000 each can fund one total loss. The law of large numbers makes losses predictable for the group.

points.heading: Peril and hazard
points.text: A peril is the cause of loss, such as fire, flood, theft or death. A hazard increases the chance or severity of loss. Physical hazards are tangible (storing fuel near a kitchen); moral hazard comes from dishonesty or carelessness of the insured, such as overinsuring and then causing a loss.

points.heading: Managing risk
points.text: Risks can be avoided (not doing the activity), retained (bearing small losses yourself), reduced (fire extinguishers, safe driving), or transferred (insurance). Insurance suits risks with low probability but high severity. Small, frequent losses are usually better retained.

points.heading: Insurable risks
points.text: An insurable risk involves a large number of similar exposures, an accidental and measurable loss, a premium that is affordable, and a loss that is not catastrophic for the insurer as a whole. Speculative risks, where gain is possible (like betting), are not insurable; only pure risks are.

points.heading: History in India
points.text: Oriental Life Insurance Company was set up in Kolkata in 1818. Life insurance was nationalised in 1956, forming LIC. General insurance was nationalised in 1972 under GIC and four subsidiaries. The Malhotra Committee (1993) recommended opening the sector, and the IRDA Act, 1999 created the regulator and allowed private insurers.

points.heading: Role of IRDAI
points.text: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India registers insurers and intermediaries, protects policyholders' interests, frames regulations on products, solvency and conduct, and promotes orderly growth of the industry. It is a statutory body under the IRDA Act, 1999.

points.heading: Reinsurance
points.text: Reinsurance is insurance for insurers: an insurer passes part of a large risk to a reinsurer to protect its own solvency. GIC Re is India's national reinsurer, and foreign reinsurers operate through branches. Policyholders deal only with the original insurer.

points.heading: Insurance as a social good
points.text: Insurance protects families from financial ruin, supports lending (banks need collateral insured), encourages enterprise, and channels long-term savings into infrastructure and government securities. Life insurers are among the largest investors in Indian government bonds.

traps: Peril is the cause of loss; hazard is a condition that increases it. Fire is a peril; storing petrol is a hazard.
Only pure risks (loss or no loss) are insurable, not speculative risks.
Insurance transfers risk; it does not prevent the loss from happening.
LIC was formed in 1956; general insurance was nationalised later, in 1972.
items.recap: Insurance pools premiums from many to pay the few who suffer losses, relying on the law of large numbers. Peril causes loss; hazard increases it; moral hazard comes from behaviour. Manage risk by avoiding, retaining, reducing or transferring it. Only pure risks are insurable. Key dates: 1818 Oriental Life, 1956 LIC, 1972 GIC, 1999 IRDA Act. Reinsurance protects insurers.

items.title: Insurance Customer Service and Grievances: IC-38 Notes
items.description: Free-look period, policyholder protection, insurer grievance cells, Bima Bharosa, ombudsman limits and consumer commissions explained for IC-38.
items.intro: An insurance agent is the face of the insurer for most customers, so IC-38 tests service standards and the grievance redressal system closely. This chapter covers the importance of customer service, communication, the free-look period, policyholder protection rules and the escalation route from the insurer to the ombudsman and consumer commissions. Limits and timelines are revised by IRDAI from time to time.

points.heading: Why service matters
points.text: Insurance is a promise to pay in the future, so trust built through service decides renewals and referrals. A customer who gets a timely reminder before a premium due date and quick help with a claim is far more likely to renew and recommend. Lifetime value of a satisfied customer is high.

points.heading: Communication skills
points.text: Agents should listen actively, explain clearly without jargon, avoid exaggeration, and confirm understanding. Non-verbal cues and punctuality matter. Explaining exclusions honestly at the sale prevents disputes at claim time.

points.heading: Free-look period
points.text: After receiving the policy document, the policyholder can review it and return it if not satisfied, during the free-look period. The insurer refunds the premium after deducting proportionate risk premium, medical examination costs and stamp duty (and unit value changes for ULIPs). IRDAI extended the free-look period to 30 days in 2024 for life and health policies; check current rules.

points.heading: Policyholder protection rules
points.text: IRDAI regulations require insurers to give clear proposal forms, benefit illustrations and key features documents, respond to service requests within set timelines, and disclose the grievance process. Agents must give prospects correct information about all material terms.

points.heading: Insurer's grievance system
points.text: Every insurer has a grievance redressal officer and a grievance cell. A complaint should first be lodged with the insurer, which must acknowledge it promptly and resolve it within the time IRDAI specifies (typically two weeks).

points.heading: Bima Bharosa
points.text: IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal (successor to IGMS) lets policyholders register and track complaints against insurers online. It acts as a central repository and monitors whether insurers resolve complaints on time.

points.heading: Insurance ombudsman
points.text: If the insurer rejects the complaint, does not reply within the time allowed, or the policyholder is unhappy with the reply, a complaint can be filed with the insurance ombudsman within one year of the insurer's reply, for claims up to ₹50 lakh. The ombudsman's award is binding on the insurer, which must comply within 30 days; the policyholder can still go to court if unsatisfied.

points.heading: Consumer commissions
