points.text: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, complaints can go to the District Commission (up to ₹50 lakh), State Commission (₹50 lakh to ₹2 crore) and National Commission (above ₹2 crore), based on value of consideration paid, as revised in 2021.

traps: The ombudsman route is open only after first approaching the insurer.
The ombudsman's award binds the insurer, not the policyholder.
Free-look refund is not the full premium; proportionate risk premium, medical and stamp costs are deducted.
Consumer commission jurisdiction is based on consideration paid, not the claim amount alone.
items.recap: Service builds trust and renewals; communicate clearly and disclose exclusions. Free-look lets policyholders return a policy with partial deductions (now 30 days for life and health). Complain first to the insurer's GRO; track on Bima Bharosa; then go to the insurance ombudsman within one year, up to ₹50 lakh, award binding on insurer within 30 days. Consumer commissions are the other route.

items.title: Insurance Agent Regulations and Code: IC-38 Notes
items.description: Agent eligibility, training, IC-38 exam, appointment by insurers, Section 41 anti-rebating, commission rules and the IRDAI code of conduct for agents.
items.intro: This chapter explains the legal framework that governs insurance agents: who can become one, how they are appointed, what they may and may not do, and the penalties for violations. Questions test eligibility, training, the number of insurers an agent can represent, Section 41 on rebating, and the agent's code of conduct. IRDAI rules here are updated periodically.

points.heading: Who is an insurance agent
points.text: An insurance agent is a person appointed by an insurer to solicit and procure insurance business, including renewals, in return for commission. The agent represents the insurer, so the insurer is responsible for the agent's acts within authority.

points.heading: Eligibility
points.text: An individual must be at least 18 years old, have the minimum educational qualification prescribed by IRDAI (at least a 10th standard pass), complete the prescribed training from an approved institution and pass the IRDAI pre-recruitment examination (IC-38). The person must not be disqualified, for example for criminal breach of trust or being of unsound mind.

points.heading: Appointment by insurer
points.text: Since 2016 regulations, insurers themselves appoint individual agents after verifying eligibility, rather than IRDAI issuing licences. The insurer issues an appointment letter and identity card. The agent can work for a limited number of insurers across life, general and health as IRDAI permits; check current rules.

points.heading: Section 41: rebating prohibited
points.text: No person may offer any rebate of commission or premium as an inducement to take or renew a policy, except rebates allowed in the insurer's published prospectus. An agent offering a customer half of his commission to buy a policy violates Section 41 and faces a penalty.

points.heading: Commission
points.text: Commission is paid by the insurer, not by the policyholder directly, from the premium. IRDAI's expense of management regulations allow insurers to set commission through board-approved policies within overall expense limits. Agents must disclose commission if the customer asks.

points.heading: Code of conduct
points.text: Agents must identify themselves and the insurer, explain product features fully, help in filling the proposal form correctly, disclose all material facts to the insurer, not induce policyholders to drop existing policies for new ones (twisting), and assist in claims. They must not misrepresent or collect premium beyond authority.

points.heading: Cancellation of appointment
points.text: The insurer can cancel an appointment for violating the code of conduct, fraud, or disqualification. IRDAI can impose penalties on insurers and intermediaries for violations. A cancelled agent's details may be shared across the industry to prevent reappointment elsewhere.

points.heading: Other intermediaries
points.text: Corporate agents (including banks under bancassurance), insurance brokers (who represent the customer, not the insurer), insurance marketing firms, web aggregators and point-of-sales persons are other channels with their own regulations. Exams often contrast agents and brokers.

traps: An agent represents the insurer; a broker represents the customer.
Offering part of commission as a rebate violates Section 41 unless allowed in the prospectus.
Insurers, not IRDAI, now appoint individual agents after the IC-38 exam and training.
Persuading a customer to surrender an old policy to buy a new one (twisting) breaches the code of conduct.
items.recap: Agents are appointed by insurers to sell and service policies for commission. Eligibility: 18+, minimum 10th pass, prescribed training and IC-38. Section 41 bans rebates except those in the prospectus. Commission comes from the insurer within expense limits. Code: disclose fully, fill proposals honestly, no twisting, help with claims. Brokers represent customers, agents represent insurers.

items.title: Legal Principles of Insurance Contracts: IC-38
items.description: Valid contracts, utmost good faith, material facts, insurable interest, indemnity, subrogation, contribution, proximate cause and Section 45 explained.
items.intro: Insurance policies are legal contracts, and IC-38 tests the principles that govern them. This chapter covers the elements of a valid contract, the special principles of insurance such as utmost good faith and insurable interest, the indemnity principles used in general insurance, and Section 45 of the Insurance Act. Questions often describe a situation and ask which principle applies.

points.heading: Valid contract elements
points.text: Under the Indian Contract Act, a valid contract needs offer and acceptance, lawful consideration, competent parties (adult, sound mind, not disqualified), free consent (no coercion, fraud, misrepresentation) and a lawful object. In insurance, the proposal is the offer and the issue of the policy is acceptance; premium is consideration.

points.heading: Utmost good faith
points.text: Insurance contracts require uberrimae fidei: both parties must disclose all material facts voluntarily and truthfully. The proposer knows more about their health, habits and property, so non-disclosure of a heart condition or a previous fire can make the policy voidable.

points.heading: Material facts
points.text: A material fact is one that would influence the insurer's decision to accept the risk or fix the premium: health history, occupation, smoking, other policies, previous claims. Facts that reduce risk, or that the insurer already knows, need not be disclosed.

points.heading: Insurable interest
points.text: The insured must stand to suffer a financial loss from the event. A person has insurable interest in their own life and their spouse's; an employer in a key employee; a creditor in a debtor up to the debt. In life insurance it must exist at the start; in marine insurance at the time of loss; in other general insurance at both times.

points.heading: Indemnity
points.text: General insurance aims to restore the insured to the same financial position as before the loss, not to allow profit. If a ₹5 lakh car is damaged by ₹80,000, the insurer pays up to the loss (subject to deductibles), not the sum insured. Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity because life cannot be valued.

points.heading: Subrogation and contribution
points.text: Subrogation lets the insurer, after paying a claim, step into the insured's shoes and recover from a third party responsible for the loss. Contribution applies when the same property is insured with more than one insurer: each pays its rateable share, so the insured does not recover more than the loss.

points.heading: Proximate cause
points.text: The insurer pays only if the proximate cause, the dominant and effective cause, is an insured peril. If a fire (insured) causes a wall to collapse later, the fire is the proximate cause. If the main cause is an excluded peril, the claim may be rejected.

points.heading: Section 45
points.text: Under Section 45 of the Insurance Act, no life policy can be called in question on any ground after three years from the date of issue, risk commencement, revival or rider, whichever is later. Within three years, the insurer may repudiate for fraud or non-disclosure of material facts, with reasons in writing.

traps: Utmost good faith binds both parties, not only the proposer.
Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity; subrogation and contribution do not apply to it.
Insurable interest in marine insurance must exist at the time of loss, not necessarily at the start.
After three years, a life policy cannot be questioned even for fraud under Section 45.
items.recap: Valid contract: offer, acceptance, consideration, competent parties, free consent, lawful object. Insurance adds utmost good faith (disclose material facts), insurable interest (timing differs for life, marine, general), indemnity (no profit from loss), subrogation, contribution and proximate cause. Life insurance is not indemnity. Section 45: no questioning a life policy after three years.

items.title: Life Insurance and Financial Planning: IC-38 Notes
items.description: Why families need life cover, human life value and needs methods, life stages, financial planning steps and the agent's role, with simple examples.
items.intro: This chapter links life insurance to the broader task of financial planning. It explains why families need protection, how to estimate the right cover using human life value and needs-based methods, how needs change across life stages, and where insurance fits among savings and investments. Questions include a simple HLV calculation and matching life stages with suitable products.

points.heading: The core need
points.text: Life insurance protects dependants from the financial loss caused by the early death of an earning member. Without it, a family may have to sell assets, take loans or cut children's education. It also offers savings and retirement options, but protection is the primary purpose.

points.heading: Human life value
points.text: HLV estimates the economic value of a person to the family as the present value of future income used for the family. A simple method: annual income contributed to the family divided by a suitable interest rate. If a person contributes ₹6 lakh a year and the rate is 8%, HLV is about ₹75 lakh.

points.heading: Needs-based approach
points.text: Add up the family's needs on death: outstanding loans, an emergency fund, children's education and marriage, and an income stream for the spouse. Subtract existing assets and cover. The gap is the additional insurance needed. This is often more practical than HLV.

points.heading: Life stages
points.text: A young single person has low need for life cover but should start saving. A young married couple with a home loan needs high term cover. Parents with school-going children need protection and education funding. Empty nesters shift focus to retirement. Retirees need annuities and health cover.

points.heading: Financial planning process
points.text: Establish the relationship, gather data, analyse the current position, develop recommendations, implement and monitor. Goals should be specific, measurable and time-bound. Insurance comes first in the plan because protection must be in place before investing for growth.

points.heading: Risks across life
points.text: People face the risk of dying too early (family left without income), living too long (outliving savings) and disability or illness (loss of income plus extra costs). Term insurance, annuities and health or disability covers respectively address these.

points.heading: Savings and investment
points.text: Insurance-linked savings such as endowment or ULIPs combine protection and saving but usually give lower cover per rupee than term plans. Financial planning compares them with alternatives such as PPF, mutual funds and deposits based on goals and risk.

points.heading: Agent's role
points.text: An agent should first understand the family's situation and recommend adequate cover, not just sell the product with the best commission. A ₹10 lakh endowment policy for a 30-year-old breadwinner with a ₹40 lakh home loan leaves the family exposed.

formulas: Simple HLV = annual income contributed to the family / interest rate (for example ₹6 lakh / 0.08 = ₹75 lakh).
traps: Protection is the primary purpose of life insurance; savings is secondary.
HLV uses income contributed to the family, not total gross income.
Retirees mainly need health cover and annuities, not large life cover.
Needs-based cover subtracts existing assets and insurance from total needs.
items.recap: Life insurance protects dependants against loss of income. Estimate cover by human life value (income for family divided by interest rate) or by needs (liabilities plus goals minus assets). Needs change by life stage. Financial planning: gather data, analyse, recommend, implement, monitor. Protection first, then savings. Risks: dying early, living long, disability.

items.title: Life Insurance Products and Riders: IC-38 Revision
items.description: Term, endowment, money back, whole life, ULIPs, pension plans, riders, par vs non-par policies and government schemes like PMJJBY, compared for IC-38.
items.intro: IC-38 expects agents to know each life insurance product's purpose, benefits and limitations. This chapter covers traditional plans (term, endowment, whole life, money back), unit linked plans, pension products, riders and group and government schemes. Questions ask which product suits a customer's need or what a specific feature means, such as a surrender value or a lock-in period.

points.heading: Term insurance
points.text: Term insurance pays the sum assured only if the insured dies during the term; nothing is paid on survival in a pure term plan. It gives the highest cover per rupee of premium. A 30-year-old can often get ₹1 crore of cover for a modest annual premium. Return-of-premium variants cost more.

points.heading: Endowment
points.text: An endowment plan pays the sum assured plus bonuses either on death during the term or on survival to maturity. It combines protection and savings but cover per rupee is much lower than term. Suitable for disciplined savers wanting guaranteed or bonus-linked maturity.

points.heading: Money back
points.text: Money back plans pay a part of the sum assured at intervals during the term (survival benefits), with the full sum assured payable on death regardless of earlier payouts. Useful for planned expenses like education milestones.

points.heading: Whole life
points.text: Whole life plans cover the insured for life (or till an advanced age such as 99 or 100), paying on death whenever it happens. They are used for estate planning or leaving a legacy.

points.heading: ULIPs
points.text: Unit linked insurance plans invest the premium, after charges, in funds chosen by the policyholder (equity, debt, balanced). Investment risk lies with the policyholder. ULIPs have a five-year lock-in, allow switches between funds, and must disclose charges. NAV-based value is paid on maturity or death.

points.heading: Pension and annuity plans
points.text: Deferred pension plans accumulate money until vesting, after which an annuity is bought. Immediate annuities start paying soon after a lump sum is paid. Options include life annuity, joint life and return of purchase price.

points.heading: Participating and non-participating
points.text: Participating (with-profit) policies share in the insurer's surplus through bonuses; non-participating policies have fixed benefits without bonuses. Bonuses, once declared as reversionary bonuses, are added to the policy and paid with the claim.

points.heading: Riders
points.text: Riders are add-ons that extend cover for an extra premium: accidental death benefit, critical illness, waiver of premium, and accidental disability. IRDAI caps rider premiums relative to the base policy so the base cover remains the main contract.

points.heading: Group and government schemes
points.text: Group term insurance covers employees or members under one master policy. PMJJBY offers ₹2 lakh life cover for an annual premium for people aged 18 to 50 with a bank account; PMSBY offers accident cover for those aged 18 to 70. Premiums are revised periodically.

traps: Pure term plans pay nothing on survival.
In money back plans, the full sum assured is paid on death even after survival benefits.
ULIP investment risk is borne by the policyholder, not the insurer.
Non-participating policies do not receive bonuses.
items.recap: Term: pure protection, cheapest cover. Endowment: death or maturity benefit with savings. Money back: periodic payouts plus full cover on death. Whole life: cover for life. ULIPs: market-linked, five-year lock-in, policyholder bears risk. Pension plans build corpus then annuity. Par policies earn bonuses. Riders add cover. PMJJBY (life, 18 to 50) and PMSBY (accident, 18 to 70).

items.title: Life Insurance Premium and Bonus Basics: IC-38 Notes
items.description: How life premiums are built from mortality, interest and expenses, office vs net premium, rebates, surplus, bonuses and actuarial valuation for IC-38.
items.intro: This chapter explains, without heavy maths, how life insurers set premiums and value their liabilities. It covers the elements of premium, the difference between net and office premium, rebates and loadings, how surplus arises and is shared as bonuses, and the role of the appointed actuary. Questions are conceptual: identify which factor raises or lowers premium, or what a bonus type means.

points.heading: Elements of premium
points.text: A life insurance premium is built from mortality (the expected cost of claims based on the probability of death at each age), interest (premiums are invested, so expected investment earnings reduce the premium), expenses (commission, administration, medicals) and a margin for contingencies and, in participating plans, bonus loading.

points.heading: Mortality tables
points.text: Insurers use mortality tables showing the probability of death at each age, based on the experience of insured lives in India (for example the IALM tables). Higher age means higher mortality and so higher premium for the same cover. Women are often charged lower rates because of longer life expectancy.

points.heading: Interest assumption
points.text: If the insurer assumes a higher interest rate on invested premiums, the premium can be lower. Insurers use conservative interest assumptions so that they can meet guarantees even if returns fall.

points.heading: Net and office premium
points.text: Net premium covers only mortality and interest. Office (gross) premium adds loadings for expenses, contingencies and bonuses. The policyholder pays the office premium. A participating policy has a higher office premium than an equivalent non-participating one because of bonus loading.

points.heading: Rebates and loadings
points.text: Rebates are given for higher sum assured (lower expense per ₹1,000 of cover) and for annual or half-yearly modes instead of monthly. Extra premium is loaded for substandard lives such as those with health conditions or hazardous occupations. Online purchase may also carry a lower premium.

points.heading: Surplus
points.text: Surplus arises when actual experience is better than assumed: fewer deaths than expected, higher investment returns or lower expenses. The appointed actuary determines surplus through valuation, and a large share of surplus from participating business is distributed to participating policyholders.

points.heading: Types of bonus
points.text: Simple reversionary bonus is declared as a rate per ₹1,000 sum assured and added each year; compound reversionary bonus is calculated on the sum assured plus existing bonuses. Terminal bonus is paid once at maturity or death for long-held policies. Interim bonus covers the period between the last valuation and the claim.

points.heading: Valuation and solvency
points.text: The appointed actuary values liabilities periodically using prudent assumptions to check that assets are enough to meet future claims. IRDAI requires insurers to maintain a minimum solvency ratio (currently 150%), meaning available solvency margin must exceed the required margin with a buffer.

traps: A higher interest assumption lowers the premium; higher mortality or expense raises it.
Net premium excludes expense loading; office premium is what the customer pays.
Compound reversionary bonus is calculated on sum assured plus attached bonuses; simple is on sum assured only.
Surplus comes from experience better than assumptions, not from simply charging more.
items.recap: Premium elements: mortality, interest, expenses, contingency and bonus loading. Net premium = mortality and interest; office premium adds loadings. Rebates for high sum assured and annual mode; extra premium for substandard lives. Surplus arises from better-than-expected experience and funds bonuses: simple or compound reversionary, terminal, interim. Appointed actuary values liabilities; solvency ratio 150%.

items.title: Proposal Forms and Underwriting: IC-38 Revision Notes
items.description: Proposal form, prospectus, benefit illustration, KYC, first premium receipt, policy document, endorsements and underwriting decisions explained.
items.intro: This chapter carries a large share of IC-38 marks. It covers the documents used from prospecting to policy issue, and how insurers decide whether to accept a risk and on what terms. Questions test the purpose of each document, the agent's responsibilities, and underwriting outcomes such as standard acceptance, extra premium, postponement and decline.

points.heading: Prospectus and sales literature
points.text: The prospectus or product brochure describes the plan's benefits, conditions, exclusions and charges, and must be approved under IRDAI rules. Agents must not modify or make claims beyond it. A benefit illustration shows projected benefits at assumed rates, which are not guaranteed.

points.heading: Proposal form
points.text: The proposal form is the basis of the contract. It records personal details, occupation, income, health, habits, family history, other insurance and nominee details. The proposer must answer truthfully and sign. If the agent fills it, the agent must read it back to the proposer and record a declaration.

points.heading: KYC and age proof
points.text: Insurers verify identity, address and age through officially valid documents under PMLA requirements. Standard age proofs include birth certificates, school certificates and passports; non-standard proofs may lead to an extra premium or restrictions. Age misstatement can change benefits.

points.heading: First premium receipt
points.text: When the proposal is accepted and the first premium is received, the insurer issues a first premium receipt, which is evidence that the contract has commenced (subject to any conditions). Renewal premium receipts are issued for later premiums.

points.heading: Policy document
points.text: The policy document is evidence of the contract. It contains the policy schedule (names, dates, sum assured, premium, term, nominee), standard provisions, special conditions and exclusions. It must be read with the proposal form, which is part of the contract.

points.heading: Endorsements
points.text: Changes to a policy after issue, such as change of address, nominee, assignment or correction of age, are made by endorsement. The endorsement becomes part of the policy and overrides earlier terms where they conflict.

points.heading: Underwriting process
points.text: Underwriting assesses the risk to decide acceptance and terms. Field underwriting by agents provides first-hand information. Medical underwriting looks at health, tests and history; financial underwriting checks that cover is reasonable compared with income, to prevent over-insurance and moral hazard.

points.heading: Underwriting outcomes
points.text: A proposal can be accepted at standard rates, accepted with an extra premium, accepted with a lien (reduced benefit in early years), accepted with reduced sum assured or restricted terms, postponed (for example after recent surgery), or declined. Substandard lives are those with higher than normal risk.

points.heading: Non-medical underwriting
points.text: For lower sums assured and younger ages, insurers may issue policies without medical examination, relying on the declaration of good health. Higher sums and older ages trigger medical tests. Honest disclosure is crucial because claims can be contested within three years.

traps: The proposal form is part of the policy contract; misstatements in it affect claims.
Benefit illustrations show projections, not guaranteed amounts.
Postponement is a temporary decision, not a decline.
Financial underwriting guards against over-insurance relative to income, not just health risk.
items.recap: Prospectus and benefit illustration explain the product; the proposal form, signed by the proposer, is the basis of the contract. KYC and age proof are mandatory. First premium receipt evidences commencement; the policy document holds the schedule, conditions and exclusions; endorsements record later changes. Underwriting is medical, financial and field-based; outcomes include standard, extra premium, lien, postponement and decline.

items.title: Life Insurance Claims Process: IC-38 Revision Notes
items.description: Maturity, survival benefit and death claims, early claims, nomination and assignment, presumption of death and IRDAI claim timelines for IC-38.
items.intro: Claims are the moment of truth in insurance. This chapter covers the types of life insurance claims, the documents required, how nominees, assignees and legal heirs receive money, how early claims are investigated, and the timelines IRDAI sets. Questions often test who receives the claim, what an early claim is, and the role of nomination versus assignment.

points.heading: Types of claims
points.text: Survival benefit claims are periodic payments in money back plans. Maturity claims are paid when the policyholder survives to the end of the term. Death claims arise when the insured dies during the term. Rider claims, such as accidental death or critical illness, follow their own conditions.

points.heading: Maturity claims
points.text: Insurers send intimation in advance of maturity. The policyholder submits the discharge form, policy document (or indemnity if lost), and bank details. Payment is made on or before the maturity date if documents are in order. Assignees, if any, must sign the discharge.

points.heading: Death claim documents
points.text: Standard requirements include the claim form, death certificate, policy document, the claimant's identity and bank details, and for early claims, medical records, employer certificate and, for unnatural death, police FIR and post-mortem report. Insurers cannot ask for documents not needed for the claim.

points.heading: Early claims
points.text: A death claim within the first three years of the policy (or revival) is often called an early claim and may be investigated for non-disclosure of material facts. After three years, Section 45 prevents the insurer from questioning the policy on any ground.

points.heading: Nomination
points.text: Under Section 39, the policyholder can nominate persons to receive the policy money on death. Nomination can be changed any time by endorsement. A 'beneficial nominee' (spouse, children or parents) is entitled to the money absolutely; other nominees receive it on behalf of legal heirs. If there is no nominee, legal heirs need succession documents.

points.heading: Assignment
points.text: Under Section 38, the policyholder can transfer rights in the policy to another person by assignment, absolute (all rights) or conditional (rights revert in specified events). Assignment is commonly done to a bank as security for a loan. On absolute assignment, nomination is cancelled.

points.heading: Presumption of death
points.text: When a person has been missing for seven years and not heard of by those who would naturally have heard, the law presumes death. Premiums should be kept paid until the presumption can be raised through a court order, after which the claim can be settled.

points.heading: Timelines and interest
points.text: IRDAI regulations require insurers to settle death claims within a fixed period after receiving all documents, with a longer period where investigation is needed, and to pay interest for delay. These periods were shortened under the 2024 policyholder protection framework; check current timelines.

traps: Assignment transfers ownership rights; nomination only names who receives the money on death.
Absolute assignment cancels an existing nomination.
Presumption of death needs seven years of being unheard of; premiums should continue meanwhile.
Early claim generally means death within three years of commencement or revival.
items.recap: Claims: survival benefit, maturity, death and riders. Maturity needs discharge form and policy; death needs claim form, death certificate and supporting records, more for unnatural deaths. Early claims (within three years) may be investigated; after three years Section 45 protects. Section 39 nomination, Section 38 assignment. Presumption of death after seven years. IRDAI sets settlement timelines with interest for delay.

items.title: Health Insurance Basics for IC-38: Revision Notes
items.description: Hospitalisation cover, floaters, pre-existing disease waiting periods, cashless claims, top-ups, critical illness, portability and 80D for IC-38.
items.intro: Health insurance is a major part of IC-38 because agents of life, general and health insurers all deal with it. This chapter covers the types of health products, key policy terms, waiting periods, claim processes through TPAs and cashless networks, standard products and tax benefits. Questions often test definitions such as day care, co-payment, sub-limit and portability.

points.heading: Hospitalisation policy
points.text: The basic indemnity health policy pays medical expenses for hospitalisation of at least 24 hours, up to the sum insured. It typically covers room rent, ICU, doctors' fees, medicines and tests, plus pre-hospitalisation (often 30 days) and post-hospitalisation (often 60 days) expenses related to the illness.

points.heading: Day care and domiciliary
points.text: Day care procedures such as cataract surgery or chemotherapy need less than 24 hours of hospitalisation due to technology, and are covered as listed in the policy. Domiciliary treatment covers treatment at home when the patient cannot be moved or a hospital bed is unavailable, subject to conditions.

points.heading: Individual and floater
points.text: An individual policy has a separate sum insured for each person. A family floater shares one sum insured across family members, which is cheaper but can be exhausted by one member's large claim. Senior parents are often better on separate policies.

points.heading: Waiting periods
points.text: Most policies have an initial waiting period (often 30 days, except accidents), specific waiting periods for listed diseases, and a waiting period for pre-existing diseases. IRDAI capped the pre-existing disease waiting period at three years and the moratorium period at five years in 2024; after the moratorium, claims cannot be contested except for fraud.

points.heading: Co-payment and sub-limits
points.text: Co-payment means the insured pays a fixed percentage of each claim. Sub-limits cap amounts for room rent or specific procedures. A policy with a 1% room rent limit on ₹3 lakh cover allows ₹3,000 a day; a costlier room can lead to proportionate deduction of other charges.

points.heading: Benefit and other products
points.text: Critical illness policies pay a fixed lump sum on diagnosis of listed illnesses regardless of actual expenses. Hospital cash pays a daily amount. Top-up and super top-up policies pay above a deductible. Standard products such as Arogya Sanjeevani have uniform features across insurers.

points.heading: Claims, TPAs and cashless
points.text: Third party administrators process claims and manage hospital networks for insurers. In cashless claims, the hospital seeks pre-authorisation and the insurer pays directly. In reimbursement claims, the insured pays first and submits bills. IRDAI has pushed for faster cashless authorisation and discharge approval.

points.heading: Portability and tax
points.text: Portability lets a policyholder move to another insurer with credit for waiting periods already served, if applied for before renewal. Premiums qualify for deduction under Section 80D within limits that are higher for senior citizens (old tax regime). Preventive health check-ups are included within the limit.

traps: Critical illness is a benefit policy paying a fixed sum; hospitalisation policies are indemnity.
Day care procedures are covered even though hospitalisation is under 24 hours.
A floater shares one sum insured; one large claim reduces cover for all members.
Portability transfers waiting period credit, not unused sum insured.
items.recap: Basic health policies indemnify hospitalisation of 24+ hours plus pre and post expenses; day care and domiciliary are special cases. Individual vs floater sum insured. Waiting periods: initial, specific, pre-existing (max three years); five-year moratorium. Co-pay and sub-limits reduce claims. Critical illness pays a lump sum. TPAs handle cashless and reimbursement. Portability keeps waiting credit; 80D gives tax benefit.

items.title: General Insurance Products: IC-38 Revision Notes
items.description: Fire, marine, motor, engineering, liability and accident covers, average clause, deductibles, IDV and no claim bonus, with examples for IC-38.
items.intro: General insurance covers property, liability and personal accident risks. For IC-38, you need a working knowledge of the main classes, how sums insured and claims are calculated, and key terms such as average clause, deductible, IDV and no claim bonus. Questions often include a quick under-insurance calculation or ask which policy covers a described loss.

points.heading: Fire insurance
points.text: Property policies cover buildings, plant, stocks and contents against fire and allied perils such as lightning, explosion, storm, flood, riot and malicious damage. For businesses, standard products such as Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha (small units) and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha are used; Bharat Griha Raksha covers homes.

points.heading: Average clause
points.text: If property is under-insured, claims are reduced proportionately. A building worth ₹50 lakh insured for ₹40 lakh suffers a ₹10 lakh loss: claim = 10 lakh x 40/50 = ₹8 lakh. This encourages insuring for full value. Some standard home and small business policies waive average within limits.

points.heading: Marine insurance
points.text: Marine cargo insurance covers goods in transit by sea, air, rail or road, using Institute Cargo Clauses A (widest, all risks subject to exclusions), B and C (narrowest, named perils). Marine hull insurance covers ships. Insurable interest must exist at the time of loss.

points.heading: Motor insurance
points.text: Third-party liability insurance is compulsory under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, covering death, injury and property damage to others. Own damage cover protects the insured vehicle. A comprehensive (package) policy combines both. Standalone own damage policies are available for vehicles with separate TP cover.

points.heading: IDV and no claim bonus
points.text: Insured Declared Value is the sum insured for own damage, based on the manufacturer's listed price less depreciation by age. No claim bonus is a discount on the own damage premium for claim-free years, rising in steps from 20% to 50%, and belongs to the insured, so it can transfer to a new vehicle.

points.heading: Engineering and liability
points.text: Engineering covers include contractor's all risk, erection all risk, machinery breakdown and electronic equipment insurance. Liability covers include public liability, product liability, professional indemnity and directors and officers liability, protecting against legal claims by third parties.

points.heading: Personal accident and others
points.text: Personal accident policies pay fixed benefits for accidental death or disability and may reimburse medical expenses. Other covers include burglary, money in transit, fidelity guarantee, travel, crop insurance (PMFBY), shopkeeper's and householder's packages.

points.heading: Deductibles and claims
points.text: A deductible (excess) is the first part of each claim borne by the insured, reducing small claims and premium. On a claim, the insured notifies the insurer promptly, takes steps to minimise loss, and a surveyor may assess losses above a threshold. Subrogation and contribution apply in general insurance.

formulas: Claim under average clause = loss x (sum insured / value at risk).
IDV = manufacturer's listed selling price less age-based depreciation (plus accessories similarly adjusted).
traps: Third-party motor cover is compulsory; own damage cover is optional.
No claim bonus belongs to the insured, not the vehicle.
Institute Cargo Clause A is the widest; C is the narrowest.
Average clause applies when sum insured is less than value at risk, reducing the claim proportionately.
items.recap: General insurance covers property, liability and accident risks. Fire policies (Bharat Sookshma, Laghu, Griha Raksha) cover fire and allied perils; average clause cuts claims for under-insurance. Marine cargo uses ICC A, B, C. Motor third-party is compulsory; own damage is optional; IDV is sum insured; NCB 20% to 50% stays with the insured. Engineering, liability and PA round off products.

items.title: JAIIB Indian Economy and Financial System Notes
items.description: JAIIB IE&IFS revision: national income, inflation, monetary and fiscal policy tools, RBI functions, financial markets, BoP and financial inclusion in brief.
items.intro: Paper 1 of JAIIB, Indian Economy and Indian Financial System, tests whether a banker understands the economic environment in which banks work. It spans macroeconomics, monetary and fiscal policy, the structure of financial markets, regulators and recent reforms. Questions are mostly conceptual with some current-affairs flavour, so learn the mechanisms and check current policy rates from RBI before the exam.

points.heading: National income concepts
points.text: GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced within India in a year; GNP adds net factor income from abroad. Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP uses constant base-year prices, removing inflation. GDP at factor cost plus net indirect taxes gives GDP at market prices. India's GDP base year is periodically revised by MoSPI.

points.heading: Sectors of the economy
points.text: The primary sector covers agriculture and allied activities, secondary covers manufacturing, construction and utilities, and tertiary covers services. Services contribute the largest share of India's GDP, while agriculture still employs a large share of the workforce, a contrast examiners like.

points.heading: Inflation and its measures
points.text: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. CPI (Combined) measures retail prices and is the target for RBI's monetary policy under flexible inflation targeting: 4% with a band of 2% to 6%. WPI measures wholesale prices. Demand-pull and cost-push are the two broad causes.

points.heading: Monetary policy framework
points.text: The six-member Monetary Policy Committee sets the repo rate. The liquidity adjustment facility corridor has the Standing Deposit Facility at the floor and the Marginal Standing Facility at the ceiling, with the repo rate in between. RBI also uses CRR, SLR, open market operations and variable rate repos and reverse repos.

points.heading: Quantitative tools
points.text: CRR is the share of net demand and time liabilities banks keep as cash balances with RBI, earning no interest. SLR is the share kept in liquid assets such as government securities. Raising CRR or SLR reduces lendable funds; OMO purchases inject liquidity and sales absorb it.

points.heading: Fiscal policy
points.text: Fiscal policy covers government taxation, spending and borrowing. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments. The FRBM framework sets deficit targets.

points.heading: Balance of payments
points.text: The current account records trade in goods and services, income and transfers (including remittances, where India is the world's largest recipient). The capital account records FDI, FPI, loans and banking capital. India usually runs a trade deficit partly offset by services exports and remittances. RBI manages forex reserves.

points.heading: Structure of the financial system
points.text: The system comprises institutions (banks, NBFCs, insurers, mutual funds, pension funds), markets (money, capital, forex, government securities, derivatives), instruments and services. Regulators include RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA and IFSCA for GIFT City.

points.heading: RBI's functions
points.text: RBI is the monetary authority, issuer of currency, banker to the government, banker's bank and lender of last resort, regulator and supervisor of banks and NBFCs, manager of foreign exchange under FEMA, and overseer of payment systems.

points.heading: Money market
points.text: The money market deals in funds up to one year: call money (overnight), notice money (2 to 14 days), term money, treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit and repo/TREPS. It helps banks manage daily liquidity and transmits policy rate changes.

points.heading: Banking sector reforms
points.text: Key milestones: bank nationalisation in 1969 and 1980; Narasimham Committee reforms in 1991 and 1998 (prudential norms, deregulation of interest rates); entry of new private banks; payments banks and small finance banks from 2015; recapitalisation and mergers of public sector banks around 2019-20.

points.heading: Financial inclusion and digital payments
points.text: PMJDY opened accounts for the unbanked with RuPay cards and overdraft facility; DBT routes subsidies directly. UPI, operated by NPCI, has made India a leader in real-time retail payments. Business correspondents extend banking to villages without branches.

formulas: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure - (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts).
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest payments.
Real GDP growth is approximately nominal GDP growth - inflation (GDP deflator).
traps: SDF is the floor and MSF the ceiling of the LAF corridor; the old fixed reverse repo is no longer the floor.
RBI targets CPI inflation, not WPI.
CRR earns no interest; SLR assets do.
Primary deficit excludes interest payments; revenue deficit compares revenue items only.
items.recap: GDP vs GNP, nominal vs real. CPI targeting at 4% (2% to 6%) by the six-member MPC. LAF corridor: SDF floor, repo, MSF ceiling; CRR and SLR as quantitative tools; OMOs manage liquidity. Fiscal, revenue and primary deficits. BoP: current and capital accounts. RBI: monetary authority, currency, government banker, regulator, forex manager. Reforms and inclusion through PMJDY and UPI.

items.title: JAIIB Principles and Practices of Banking Notes
items.description: JAIIB PPB revision: banker-customer relations, KYC, negotiable instruments, cheque dishonour, payment systems, charges, NPAs and priority sector.
items.intro: Principles and Practices of Banking is the core operational paper of JAIIB. It covers the banker-customer relationship, accounts and KYC, negotiable instruments, payment systems, lending principles, securities and charges, asset classification and customer service. Many questions are section-based, especially from the Negotiable Instruments Act. Limits and thresholds change, so check current RBI circulars.

points.heading: Banker-customer relationship
points.text: The primary relationship is debtor-creditor: for deposits the bank is the debtor, for loans the creditor. Other relationships arise by function: trustee (for funds given for a specific purpose), agent (collecting cheques, paying bills), bailee (safe custody) and lessor-lessee (safe deposit lockers).

points.heading: Types of accounts and KYC
points.text: Savings, current, recurring and fixed deposit accounts serve different needs. Special customers include minors, joint holders, partnerships, companies, trusts and HUFs, each needing specific documents and mandates. KYC under the RBI Master Direction requires identification, address verification, beneficial ownership checks and risk categorisation with periodic updation.

points.heading: Negotiable instruments
points.text: The NI Act, 1881 covers promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques. A cheque is a bill drawn on a specified banker payable on demand. A holder in due course takes the instrument for value, in good faith, before maturity, and gets a better title than the transferor.

points.heading: Crossing and endorsement
points.text: General crossing (two parallel lines) means payment only through a bank account. Special crossing names a bank. 'Account payee' crossing directs collection only into the payee's account. Endorsements can be in blank, special, restrictive or conditional.

points.heading: Section 138: cheque dishonour
points.text: Dishonour for insufficient funds is a criminal offence if the cheque was presented within its validity (three months), the payee sends a demand notice within 30 days of learning of dishonour, and the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving notice. The complaint must be filed within one month of the cause of action. Punishment can be up to two years or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both.

points.heading: Payment systems
points.text: NEFT settles in half-hourly batches round the clock; RTGS is real-time gross settlement for high-value payments (minimum ₹2 lakh); IMPS and UPI are instant. CTS clears cheques using images. NACH handles bulk debits and credits like EMIs and salaries. RBI's Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 governs them.

points.heading: Lending principles
points.text: Safety, liquidity, profitability, purpose, diversification and security guide lending. Credit appraisal looks at the borrower's character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions (the five Cs). Loan documentation must be complete and enforceable.

points.heading: Modes of creating charge
points.text: Pledge transfers possession of movable goods to the lender. Hypothecation creates a charge without possession, common for vehicles and stocks. Mortgage creates an interest in immovable property; equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds is common. Lien is a right to retain goods until dues are paid; assignment transfers actionable claims such as book debts or policies.

points.heading: Asset classification
points.text: A loan becomes a non-performing asset when interest or instalment remains overdue for more than 90 days. Sub-standard assets have been NPAs for up to 12 months; doubtful assets beyond that; loss assets are identified as uncollectible. Provisioning increases with each category and the age of doubtful assets.

points.heading: Priority sector lending
points.text: Domestic scheduled commercial banks must lend 40% of adjusted net bank credit or credit equivalent of off-balance sheet exposure, whichever is higher, to priority sectors such as agriculture, MSMEs, export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure and renewable energy, with sub-targets for agriculture and weaker sections.

points.heading: Deposit insurance and grievance
points.text: DICGC insures deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, covering principal and interest. Customers with complaints first approach the bank, then the RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021, which provides a single window for complaints against banks, NBFCs and payment system participants.

points.heading: Banker's obligations
points.text: Banks must honour cheques when funds are sufficient and the cheque is in order, maintain secrecy of customer accounts except as permitted by law, and act on stop payment instructions. Wrongful dishonour can make the bank liable for damages to the customer's reputation.

traps: In a deposit, the bank is the debtor and the customer the creditor.
Hypothecation involves no transfer of possession; pledge does.
An NPA arises after more than 90 days overdue, not 90 days from disbursement.
Section 138 notice must be sent within 30 days of learning of dishonour; the drawer then gets 15 days to pay.
DICGC cover is ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, combining principal and interest.
items.recap: Relationship: debtor-creditor plus trustee, agent, bailee, lessor. KYC with risk categorisation. NI Act: promissory note, bill, cheque; holder in due course; crossings. Section 138: 3-month validity, 30-day notice, 15 days to pay, complaint within a month. Payment systems: NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, UPI, CTS, NACH. Charges: pledge, hypothecation, mortgage, lien, assignment. NPA after 90 days. PSL 40%. DICGC ₹5 lakh.

items.title: JAIIB Accounting and Financial Management Notes
items.description: JAIIB AFM revision: double entry, final accounts, depreciation, bank statements, ratios, time value of money, capital budgeting and break-even.
items.intro: Accounting and Financial Management for Bankers is the most numerical JAIIB paper. It covers accounting principles and final accounts, depreciation, bank-specific accounts, ratio analysis, time value of money, capital budgeting, costing and working capital, and taxation basics. Expect around half the questions to involve calculations, so practise formulas with small numbers until you can do each in a minute.

points.heading: Accounting basics
points.text: Accounting follows concepts such as going concern, accrual, consistency, prudence and matching. Under double entry every transaction has equal debit and credit. Golden rules: personal accounts, debit the receiver and credit the giver; real accounts, debit what comes in and credit what goes out; nominal accounts, debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains.

points.heading: From journal to final accounts
points.text: Transactions are recorded in the journal, posted to ledgers, summarised in a trial balance, and adjusted for accruals, prepayments and depreciation to prepare the profit and loss account and balance sheet. A trial balance that agrees does not prove absence of errors, such as errors of omission or compensating errors.

points.heading: Depreciation
points.text: Straight line method charges equal depreciation each year: (cost - residual value) / useful life. Written down value method applies a fixed rate to the opening book value, giving higher charges in early years. A ₹10 lakh asset at 20% WDV is depreciated by ₹2 lakh in year one and ₹1.6 lakh in year two.

points.heading: Bank financial statements
points.text: Banks prepare accounts in formats prescribed under the Third Schedule of the Banking Regulation Act: Form A for the balance sheet and Form B for the profit and loss account, with schedules for capital, deposits, advances and investments. Interest income on NPAs is recognised only on realisation.

points.heading: Ratio analysis
points.text: Liquidity: current ratio (current assets / current liabilities), quick ratio. Leverage: debt-equity ratio, interest coverage. Profitability: net profit margin, return on assets, return on equity. Turnover: inventory turnover, debtors turnover. Bankers use these to judge borrowers' credit quality.

points.heading: Time value of money
points.text: Money today is worth more than the same money tomorrow. FV = PV x (1 + r)^n; PV = FV / (1 + r)^n. Annuity formulas value equal periodic flows. ₹1 lakh at 8% for 3 years grows to about ₹1.26 lakh. Effective annual rate rises with more frequent compounding.

points.heading: EMI calculation
points.text: EMI = P x r x (1 + r)^n / [(1 + r)^n - 1], where r is the monthly rate and n the number of months. In early EMIs, interest forms a larger part; principal share rises over time. Banks use this for retail loans.

points.heading: Capital budgeting
points.text: Payback period counts years to recover the investment. NPV discounts all cash flows at the cost of capital; accept if NPV is positive. IRR is the rate at which NPV is zero; accept if IRR exceeds cost of capital. Profitability index = PV of inflows / initial outlay. NPV is preferred when methods conflict.

points.heading: Costing and break-even
points.text: Costs are fixed or variable. Contribution = sales - variable cost. Break-even point in units = fixed costs / contribution per unit. With fixed cost ₹6 lakh, price ₹100 and variable cost ₹60, break-even is 15,000 units. Margin of safety = actual sales - break-even sales.

points.heading: Working capital
points.text: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities. The operating cycle runs from cash to raw materials, work in progress, finished goods, debtors and back to cash. Banks finance part of the working capital gap, with the borrower bringing a margin.

points.heading: Taxation basics
points.text: Bankers deduct TDS on interest above thresholds, report high-value transactions and handle GST on fees and charges. Banks must understand the tax treatment of interest income, provisions and depreciation in their own accounts.

formulas: SLM depreciation = (cost - residual value) / life; WDV depreciation = rate x opening book value.
Break-even units = fixed cost / (price - variable cost per unit).
NPV = sum of CF_t / (1+k)^t - initial investment.
traps: A balanced trial balance does not guarantee error-free accounts.
WDV gives higher depreciation in early years than SLM for the same asset.
Accept a project if IRR exceeds the cost of capital, not if IRR is merely positive.
Break-even uses contribution per unit, not selling price per unit.
items.recap: Double entry and golden rules; journal to ledger to trial balance to final accounts. Depreciation: SLM equal, WDV declining. Bank accounts in Third Schedule Forms A and B. Ratios: liquidity, leverage, profitability, turnover. TVM: FV and PV formulas, EMI. Capital budgeting: payback, NPV, IRR, PI. Break-even = fixed cost / contribution per unit. Working capital and operating cycle.

items.title: JAIIB Retail Banking and Wealth Management Notes
items.description: JAIIB RBWM revision: retail loans, EBLR pricing, home loan LTV caps, FOIR, credit cards, digital channels, CRM and wealth management basics.
items.intro: Retail Banking and Wealth Management covers the products and processes that serve individual customers: deposits, retail loans, cards, digital banking, marketing and relationship management, and wealth management including third-party products. Questions mix product rules, pricing, regulatory caps and selling ethics. Several limits come from RBI circulars that are updated, so verify current values.

points.heading: Retail banking scope
points.text: Retail banking serves individuals and small businesses with deposits, loans, cards, remittances and investment products through branches and digital channels. It offers stable low-cost deposits, diversified credit risk and cross-selling opportunities, but needs strong technology and processes to handle high volumes.

points.heading: Retail loan products
points.text: Home loans, vehicle loans, personal loans, education loans, gold loans and loans against property are the main products. Each has its own eligibility, margin, tenure and security. Education loans follow the Indian Banks' Association model scheme with moratorium during the course.

points.heading: Loan pricing
points.text: Floating-rate retail loans to individuals and MSMEs must be linked to an external benchmark such as the RBI repo rate or a government security yield (EBLR), with a spread fixed for the loan unless credit risk changes. Rates must be reset at least once every three months. This improves transmission of policy rate changes.

points.heading: Home loan LTV
points.text: RBI caps loan-to-value ratios for housing loans by loan size: up to 90% for smaller loans, 80% for middle bands and 75% for larger loans (as of 2026 — check RBI). Stamp duty, registration and documentation charges are normally excluded from the property cost for LTV, though they may be included for low-value homes costing up to ₹10 lakh.

points.heading: Repayment capacity
points.text: Banks assess fixed obligation to income ratio (FOIR): total EMIs as a share of monthly income, often capped at 50% to 60% depending on income. If a borrower earns ₹1 lakh a month and has existing EMIs of ₹15,000, a 50% FOIR leaves room for a new EMI of ₹35,000.

points.heading: Credit and debit cards
points.text: Credit cards offer revolving credit with interest-free periods; debit cards draw from the account. RBI's directions on cards require consent before issuing or upgrading cards, transparent charges, and closure requests to be honoured within set days. Card tokenisation protects card details online.

points.heading: Digital channels
points.text: Internet banking, mobile banking, UPI, ATMs and cash recyclers, and video KYC have moved most retail transactions out of branches. Banks must manage cyber risk, customer authentication and fraud monitoring, and educate customers on not sharing OTPs.

points.heading: Marketing and CRM
points.text: Retail banks segment customers by income, age and behaviour, use data analytics to offer the right product, and track customer lifetime value. Customer relationship management systems help in cross-selling and retention. Mis-selling damages trust and attracts regulatory action.

points.heading: Wealth management
points.text: Wealth management offers financial planning, investment advice, portfolio management, insurance and estate planning to affluent customers. Banks distribute mutual funds (as AMFI-registered distributors), insurance (as corporate agents) and other third-party products, and must follow suitability and disclosure norms.

points.heading: Financial planning basics
points.text: Planning involves understanding goals, risk profile and time horizon, allocating assets, and reviewing regularly. Emergency fund, adequate insurance and debt management come before investing. Tax planning uses provisions such as 80C and NPS within the chosen regime.

points.heading: Selling third-party products ethically
points.text: RBI requires banks to keep investment and insurance selling separate from compulsion: no tying products to loans, proper risk profiling, disclosure of commissions and avoiding mis-selling to senior citizens or unsophisticated customers.

formulas: FOIR = (existing EMIs + proposed EMI) / gross or net monthly income.
LTV = loan amount / property value x 100.
traps: EBLR loans must reset at least every three months; the spread cannot be changed arbitrarily.
LTV caps fall as loan size rises, not the other way round.
Banks must not force customers to buy insurance or investments as a condition for a loan.
Card upgrades or new cards need explicit customer consent.
items.recap: Retail banking serves individuals with deposits, loans, cards and digital services. Floating retail loans are priced over an external benchmark with quarterly resets. Home loan LTV caps fall with size. FOIR measures repayment capacity. Cards need consent and transparent charges. Digital channels need fraud controls. Wealth management covers planning, MFs, insurance and suitability, without tying or mis-selling.

items.title: CAIIB Advanced Bank Management Revision Notes
items.description: CAIIB ABM revision: statistics for bankers, normal distribution, time series, working capital assessment, Nayak and Tandon methods, HRM and governance.
items.intro: Advanced Bank Management is a compulsory CAIIB paper with four broad areas: statistics, human resource management, credit management and compliance with corporate governance. The statistics and credit modules carry most calculation questions: mean and variance, normal distribution, correlation, time series and working capital assessment. The HRM and governance modules are conceptual. Practise numerical items with small data sets.

points.heading: Measures of central tendency
points.text: Mean is the arithmetic average, median is the middle value when data are ordered, and mode is the most frequent value. For skewed data such as incomes, the median represents the typical value better than the mean. For 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, mean and median are both 6.

points.heading: Dispersion
points.text: Variance measures average squared deviation from the mean; standard deviation is its square root. For 2, 4, 6, 8, 10: deviations squared are 16, 4, 0, 4, 16, total 40, so population variance = 40/5 = 8 and SD is about 2.83. Sample variance divides by n - 1. Coefficient of variation = SD / mean.

points.heading: Normal distribution
points.text: The normal curve is symmetric and bell-shaped, with mean, median and mode equal. About 68% of observations lie within one SD of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. Banks use this logic in value at risk and credit scoring models.

points.heading: Correlation and regression
points.text: Correlation (from -1 to +1) measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship. Regression estimates one variable from another, for example deposits from income. Correlation does not prove causation, a favourite trap.

points.heading: Time series
points.text: A time series has four components: trend (long-term movement), seasonal (regular within-year patterns like festival deposits each October), cyclical (business cycles over several years) and irregular (random shocks such as a pandemic). Forecasting separates these components.

points.heading: Probability and sampling
points.text: Probability ranges from 0 to 1. Independent events multiply probabilities. Sampling methods include simple random, stratified, systematic and cluster sampling. Larger samples reduce sampling error. Banks use sampling in audits and customer surveys.

points.heading: Working capital assessment: turnover method
points.text: Under the Nayak Committee approach for MSME borrowers, working capital requirement is taken as 25% of projected annual turnover, of which at least 20% of turnover is financed by the bank and 5% is the borrower's margin. For projected turnover of ₹2 crore, bank finance is at least ₹40 lakh.

points.heading: MPBF methods
points.text: The Tandon Committee's first method sets maximum permissible bank finance at 75% of the working capital gap (current assets minus current liabilities other than bank borrowings). The second method sets it at 75% of current assets minus current liabilities, giving a lower figure because the borrower funds 25% of all current assets.

points.heading: Cash budget and other methods
points.text: For seasonal industries or borrowers with uneven cash flows, banks use the cash budget method, financing the peak deficit. Large borrowers are assessed on projected balance sheets, with loan component and cash credit split as per RBI's guidelines.

points.heading: Credit monitoring and NPA management
points.text: Monitoring uses stock statements, unit visits, account conduct, financial covenants and early warning signals. Stressed accounts are classified as SMA-0, SMA-1 and SMA-2 based on overdue days before becoming NPAs. Resolution options include restructuring, compromise settlements, SARFAESI and IBC.

points.heading: Human resource management
points.text: HRM covers manpower planning, recruitment, training, performance appraisal, compensation and employee relations. Motivation theories: Maslow's hierarchy of needs and Herzberg's hygiene and motivator factors. Banks increasingly use competency-based appraisal and digital learning.

points.heading: Compliance and governance
points.text: Banks have an independent chief compliance officer, risk-based compliance testing and board committees such as audit, risk management and nomination and remuneration. RBI guidelines govern board composition, tenure of CEOs and directors, and the fit and proper status of directors.

formulas: Population variance = sum of (x - mean)^2 / N; sample variance divides by n - 1.
Coefficient of variation = SD / mean x 100.
Turnover method: bank finance = 20% of projected turnover; total requirement = 25%.
MPBF Method II = 0.75 x current assets - current liabilities (excluding bank borrowings).
traps: Population variance divides by N; sample variance divides by n - 1.
Recurring festival-time deposit peaks are seasonal, not cyclical.
In the turnover method, the 5% margin is from the borrower; bank finance is 20% of turnover.
Tandon Method II gives lower MPBF than Method I because the borrower funds 25% of all current assets.
items.recap: Statistics: mean, median, mode; variance and SD (2,4,6,8,10 gives variance 8); normal curve 68-95-99.7; correlation is not causation; time series has trend, seasonal, cyclical, irregular parts. Credit: turnover method gives 20% bank finance plus 5% margin; Tandon Methods I and II; cash budget for seasonal units; SMA categories before NPA. HRM theories and governance structures.

items.title: CAIIB Bank Financial Management Revision Notes
items.description: CAIIB BFM revision: forex quotes and forward premium, ALM gaps, duration, Basel III capital, leverage ratio, LCR, NSFR, VaR and treasury basics for bankers.
items.intro: Bank Financial Management, a compulsory CAIIB paper, covers international banking and forex, risk management, treasury management and balance sheet management. Numerical questions are frequent: exchange rate arithmetic, forward premiums, gap analysis and capital ratios. Conceptual questions test Basel III components and liquidity standards. RBI's capital and liquidity numbers are stable but verify any recent changes.

points.heading: Exchange rate quotations
points.text: A direct quote states the price of one unit of foreign currency in home currency (USD/INR 83.00). Banks quote two-way rates: buying (bid) and selling (ask). For merchant transactions, TT rates apply when no delay in funds, and bill rates when there is a delay. Rupee has been on a market-determined exchange rate since 1993.

points.heading: Forward premium
points.text: Forward rates reflect interest rate differentials. Annualised forward premium = (forward - spot) / spot x 12 / months x 100. With spot 83.00 and three-month forward 83.50: 0.50/83 x 4 x 100 = about 2.41% a year. A currency at a premium is costlier in the forward market.

points.heading: Trade finance
points.text: Letters of credit under UCP 600 make the issuing bank liable to pay against compliant documents. Pre-shipment finance (packing credit) funds production; post-shipment finance funds the period until export proceeds arrive. ECGC provides credit insurance to exporters and banks. Nostro accounts are a bank's accounts with foreign banks in foreign currency.

points.heading: FEMA framework
points.text: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 classifies transactions as current account (largely free, with some restrictions) or capital account (permitted as specified). Authorised dealer banks handle forex transactions under RBI's directions, including the Liberalised Remittance Scheme for individuals.

points.heading: Risk types
points.text: Credit risk is the risk of borrower default; market risk arises from changes in interest rates, exchange rates and equity prices; operational risk from failed processes, people, systems or external events; liquidity risk from inability to meet obligations. Banks manage each with limits, models and capital.

points.heading: Basel III capital
points.text: Under RBI's Basel III rules, minimum Common Equity Tier 1 is 5.5% of risk-weighted assets, Tier 1 7% and total capital 9%. A capital conservation buffer of 2.5% in CET1 takes CET1 to 8% and total capital to 11.5%. D-SIBs hold an additional surcharge, and a countercyclical buffer can be activated.

points.heading: Leverage and liquidity ratios
points.text: The leverage ratio (Tier 1 capital / total exposure) must be at least 4% for D-SIBs and 3.5% for other banks under RBI norms. The Liquidity Coverage Ratio requires high-quality liquid assets at least equal to net cash outflows over 30 days of stress (100%). The Net Stable Funding Ratio requires available stable funding at least equal to required stable funding.

points.heading: ALM and gap analysis
points.text: Asset-liability management matches maturities and rate sensitivities. Liquidity gap = assets minus liabilities in each time bucket. Interest rate sensitivity gap = rate-sensitive assets minus rate-sensitive liabilities. A positive gap gains when rates rise; a negative gap gains when rates fall. Change in NII is roughly gap x change in rate.

points.heading: Duration
points.text: Duration measures the price sensitivity of a bond or portfolio to interest rate changes. Modified duration = Macaulay duration / (1 + yield). Duration gap = duration of assets - (liabilities/assets) x duration of liabilities. A positive duration gap means equity value falls when rates rise.

points.heading: Value at risk
points.text: VaR estimates the maximum loss over a given period at a given confidence level under normal conditions. A one-day 99% VaR of ₹5 crore means losses should exceed ₹5 crore on only about 1 in 100 days. VaR does not show how large losses can be beyond that threshold.

points.heading: Treasury management
points.text: Bank treasuries manage liquidity (CRR, SLR, call money, repos), investments in government securities, forex dealing and derivatives. Front office deals, mid office measures risk and limits, back office settles and accounts. Separation of these functions prevents fraud.

formulas: Annualised forward premium % = (F - S)/S x 12/n x 100.
Rate sensitivity gap = RSA - RSL; change in NII = gap x change in interest rate.
Duration gap = D_A - (L/A) x D_L.
Leverage ratio = Tier 1 capital / total exposure.
traps: CET1 minimum is 5.5%, but with the 2.5% conservation buffer it becomes 8%.
A negative interest rate gap benefits from falling rates, not rising.
LCR covers a 30-day stress period; NSFR is about one-year funding stability.
VaR does not measure the size of losses in the tail beyond the confidence level.
In a direct quote the foreign currency is the base; buying rate is lower than selling rate for the bank.
items.recap: Forex: direct quotes, bid and ask, TT and bill rates; forward premium = (F-S)/S x 12/n. Trade finance via LCs (UCP 600), packing credit, ECGC. FEMA current vs capital account. Basel III: CET1 5.5% + 2.5% CCB, total 11.5%; leverage ratio 4% D-SIBs, 3.5% others; LCR and NSFR 100%. ALM: gap = RSA - RSL; duration gap. VaR and treasury front, mid, back office.

items.title: CAIIB Advanced Business and Financial Management
items.description: CAIIB ABFM revision: strategy tools like SWOT and Porter, DuPont ROE, cost of capital, leverage, capital structure, dividend policy, valuation and M&A types.
items.intro: Advanced Business and Financial Management combines strategic management with corporate finance and valuation. Bankers need it to understand borrowers' business models, evaluate projects and assess mergers. Questions include strategy concepts, ratio and cost of capital calculations, leverage measures, valuation methods and merger classification. Formula-based items are common, so practise DuPont, WACC and leverage computations.

points.heading: Strategic analysis tools
points.text: SWOT separates internal factors (strengths, weaknesses) from external ones (opportunities, threats). PESTLE scans political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors. Porter's five forces assess industry attractiveness: rivalry, threat of new entrants, substitutes, bargaining power of buyers and of suppliers.

points.heading: Portfolio and growth strategy
points.text: The BCG matrix classifies businesses as stars (high growth, high share), cash cows (low growth, high share), question marks (high growth, low share) and dogs (low growth, low share). Ansoff's matrix covers market penetration, market development, product development and diversification.

points.heading: DuPont analysis
points.text: ROE = net profit margin x asset turnover x equity multiplier. A company with 5% margin, asset turnover of 2 and equity multiplier of 2 has ROE of 5% x 2 x 2 = 20%. DuPont shows whether ROE comes from profitability, efficiency or leverage.

points.heading: Cost of capital
points.text: Cost of equity can be estimated with CAPM: Ke = Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf). Cost of debt after tax = interest rate x (1 - tax rate). WACC weights each source by its market value proportion. Projects should earn more than WACC to create value.

points.heading: Leverage
points.text: Operating leverage (DOL = contribution / EBIT) measures how EBIT responds to sales changes. Financial leverage (DFL = EBIT / EBT) measures how EPS responds to EBIT changes. Combined leverage = DOL x DFL. High combined leverage means high risk for lenders.

points.heading: Capital structure
points.text: Capital structure theories include net income and net operating income approaches and Modigliani-Miller. With taxes, debt adds value through the interest tax shield, but bankruptcy costs limit how much debt is optimal. Bankers look at debt-equity and interest coverage limits.

points.heading: Dividend policy
points.text: Walter's model says retain earnings if return on investment exceeds cost of equity. Gordon's growth model values shares as D1 / (Ke - g). Modigliani-Miller argue dividend policy is irrelevant in perfect markets. In practice, stable dividends signal confidence.

points.heading: Business valuation
points.text: Valuation methods include discounted cash flow (present value of free cash flows), relative valuation using multiples (P/E, EV/EBITDA), and asset-based valuation (net asset value). DCF is sensitive to growth and discount rate assumptions.

points.heading: Mergers and acquisitions
points.text: A horizontal merger joins firms in the same line of business at the same stage, such as two banks offering similar services. Vertical mergers join different stages of a supply chain. Conglomerate mergers join unrelated businesses. Synergy, cost savings and market power are common motives; integration risk is the main danger.

points.heading: Working capital and project finance
points.text: Working capital management balances liquidity and profitability through inventory, receivables and payables policies. Project finance relies on project cash flows, with appraisal using NPV, IRR and DSCR. Debt service coverage ratio = cash available for debt service / debt service due.

points.heading: Emerging areas
points.text: Venture capital funds early-stage businesses in exchange for equity; private equity invests in more mature firms. Start-ups often use convertible instruments. Bankers increasingly lend to new-age businesses with cash-flow based assessment.

formulas: ROE = (net profit / sales) x (sales / assets) x (assets / equity).
CAPM: Ke = Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf); after-tax Kd = interest x (1 - t).
DOL = contribution / EBIT; DFL = EBIT / EBT; DCL = DOL x DFL.
Gordon: P0 = D1 / (Ke - g).
traps: In SWOT, strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external.
Two banks merging is horizontal, not conglomerate.
DFL uses EBIT / EBT, not EBIT / sales.
Cost of debt must be taken after tax when computing WACC.
items.recap: Strategy: SWOT (internal vs external), PESTLE, Porter's five forces, BCG and Ansoff matrices. Finance: DuPont ROE = margin x turnover x equity multiplier; WACC with CAPM and after-tax debt; DOL, DFL, DCL. Capital structure (MM with taxes) and dividend models (Walter, Gordon, MM). Valuation: DCF, multiples, NAV. M&A: horizontal, vertical, conglomerate. DSCR for project loans.

items.title: CAIIB Banking Regulations and Business Laws Notes
items.description: CAIIB BRBL revision: RBI Act, Banking Regulation Act sections, PMLA reporting, SARFAESI steps, IBC timelines and key business laws that bankers apply daily.
items.intro: Banking Regulations and Business Laws is the fourth compulsory CAIIB paper. It covers the RBI Act and Banking Regulation Act, anti-money laundering rules, recovery laws such as SARFAESI, DRT and IBC, and general business laws including contracts, companies and negotiable instruments. Questions are section and timeline based, so memorise key numbers and confirm any that have been amended recently.

points.heading: RBI Act, 1934
points.text: The RBI Act constitutes RBI and gives it powers over currency issue, monetary policy, and regulation of NBFCs (Chapter III-B). Section 42 requires scheduled banks to maintain CRR with RBI. Chapter IIIF (Sections 45Z onwards) sets the monetary policy framework, including the inflation target and the MPC.

points.heading: Banking Regulation Act, 1949
points.text: Section 5(b) defines banking as accepting deposits from the public for lending or investment, repayable on demand or otherwise and withdrawable by cheque or other means. Section 6 lists permitted businesses. Section 22 requires a licence from RBI to carry on banking business in India. Section 24 prescribes SLR.

points.heading: Supervisory powers
points.text: Section 35 empowers RBI to inspect banks; Section 35A to issue directions in public interest; Section 36ACA to supersede the board of a bank. Section 45 allows the central government, on RBI's application, to impose a moratorium and RBI to prepare a scheme of amalgamation or reconstruction.

points.heading: Other BR Act provisions
points.text: Section 17 requires banks to transfer at least 20% of profit to a reserve fund before dividends. Section 20 restricts loans to directors and their interested entities. Section 10B requires a managing director or whole-time chairman. Banks must also follow RBI rules on ownership and voting rights.

points.heading: PMLA obligations
points.text: Banks are reporting entities under PMLA. Cash transaction reports (above ₹10 lakh) are filed monthly, by the 15th of the next month; suspicious transaction reports within 7 days of the principal officer concluding suspicion; counterfeit currency reports and cross-border wire transfer reports as prescribed. Records are kept for five years.

points.heading: SARFAESI Act, 2002
points.text: Secured creditors can enforce security without court intervention when the account is an NPA. Section 13(2) requires a 60-day demand notice; if unpaid, the bank can take possession under Section 13(4) and sell the asset. The Act does not apply to loans below ₹1 lakh or where the outstanding is less than 20% of principal and interest. Borrowers can appeal to the DRT under Section 17 within 45 days.

points.heading: DRT and recovery
points.text: The Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 created Debt Recovery Tribunals for bank claims of ₹20 lakh and above, with appeals to the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal. Lok Adalats help settle smaller dues.

points.heading: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
points.text: A financial or operational creditor can initiate the corporate insolvency resolution process before the NCLT when default is at least ₹1 crore. CIRP must be completed within 180 days, extendable once by 90 days, and overall within 330 days including litigation. A resolution plan needs approval of at least 66% of the committee of creditors by voting share. A moratorium under Section 14 halts recovery actions.

points.heading: Contract and agency law
points.text: The Indian Contract Act governs loan agreements, guarantees (Sections 126 onwards: principal debtor, creditor, surety), indemnity and bailment. A surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor's unless the contract says otherwise. Pledge is a special bailment of goods as security.

points.heading: Companies, partnership and LLP
points.text: Bankers must verify borrowing powers of companies under the Companies Act and the articles, register charges with the Registrar of Companies within the time allowed, and know partners' implied authority under the Partnership Act. LLPs are separate legal entities with limited liability.

points.heading: Other laws
points.text: The Negotiable Instruments Act governs cheques and Section 138 dishonour; the Consumer Protection Act covers deficiency in service; the IT Act gives legal recognition to electronic records and signatures; the Right to Information Act applies to public sector banks; the DICGC Act insures deposits up to ₹5 lakh.

formulas: SARFAESI threshold: outstanding at least 20% of principal plus interest, and loan of ₹1 lakh or more.
IBC timeline: 180 days + one 90-day extension; outer limit 330 days including litigation.
traps: Section 22 of the BR Act is about licensing; Section 5(b) defines banking.
SARFAESI notice period is 60 days; the borrower's appeal to DRT is within 45 days.
IBC threshold for default is ₹1 crore, raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020.
STR is due within 7 days of concluding suspicion; CTR is monthly by the 15th.
A surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor's, not secondary by default.
items.recap: RBI Act: currency, monetary policy, NBFCs, CRR under Section 42. BR Act: 5(b) definition, 6 businesses, 22 licence, 24 SLR, 35A directions, 45 moratorium, 17 reserve fund 20%. PMLA: CTR monthly, STR within 7 days, five-year records. SARFAESI: 60-day notice, possession, DRT appeal in 45 days. DRT for ₹20 lakh+. IBC: ₹1 crore default, 180+90 days, 330 days outer, 66% CoC.
